title: Expected threat (xT)
text:
Expected Threat (xT) assigns a value to a pitch location according to the probability of eventually scoring from a possession that starts in that location, under the actions and transitions represented in the model (Singh 2018). Unlike expected goals (xG), which evaluates a shot, xT values positions before a shot occurs. A location far from goal can therefore have positive value if possession can progress towards more promising locations.
The xT surface is a location-based estimate that summarizes typical outcomes in the event data, independently of the particular players, defensive pressure or available passing options of an individual tracking frame. PRESS uses the fitted xT grid as a spatial input to its state-dependent action models.

title: Expected threat (xT)
text:
1. Mathematical formulation
Divide the pitch into cells. For each origin cell \(i\), the model needs two distinct quantities: how often each event occurs, and where the ball goes when that event occurs. The event frequencies are denoted by \(p\), the conditional destination distributions by \(T\), and the probability of scoring from a shot by \(p_{\mathrm{goal}}\).

Event frequencies: the \(p\) terms
For an origin cell \(i\), let \(n_{\mathrm{pass},i}\) count completed passes released from the cell, \(n_{\mathrm{carry},i}\) count within-possession displacements starting there, \(n_{\mathrm{shot},i}\) count shots, and \(n_{\mathrm{loss},i}\) count terminal losses, which include failed passes. A carry here is a within-possession displacement: it records the movement from the matched beginning to the matched end of individual control, irrespective of the terminal outcome. It covers all possessions and is distinct from the canonical one-second carry. A possession can contribute a displacement followed by a separate pass, shot or loss event.
The four counts share a common denominator,
\[
n_i=n_{\mathrm{pass},i}+n_{\mathrm{carry},i}+n_{\mathrm{shot},i}+n_{\mathrm{loss},i},
\qquad p_{a,i}=\frac{n_{a,i}}{n_i}.
\]
For an observed cell the four frequencies sum to one, and for a cell without events they are zero. They are frequencies in the xT event tables, computed independently of the PRESS action-selection and physical risk models.
Failed actions enter the denominator through the loss count. Hence \(p_{\mathrm{pass},i}\) is the probability that a possession in cell \(i\) continues with a completed pass, which already accounts for failed attempts, so the value equation below needs no additional pass-success factor. The same holds for \(p_{\mathrm{carry},i}\) and \(p_{\mathrm{shot},i}\).


Destinations: the \(T\) terms
For passes, let \(N^{\mathrm{pass}}_{ij}\) count completed passes from \(i\) to \(j\). Before the smoothing described below,
\[
T^{\mathrm{pass}}_{ij}
=\frac{N^{\mathrm{pass}}_{ij}}{\sum_kN^{\mathrm{pass}}_{ik}}
=P(\text{destination }j\mid\text{completed pass from }i).
\]
The carry matrix is constructed in the same way from the within-possession displacements. Passes and carries have separate destination counts, and terminal-loss events enter neither matrix. Each row sums to one.
Multiplying \(p_{\mathrm{pass},i}\) by \(T^{\mathrm{pass}}_{ij}\) combines the frequency of the completed-pass branch with the conditional destination distribution. Before smoothing, this product is simply
\[
p_{\mathrm{pass},i}T^{\mathrm{pass}}_{ij}
=\frac{N^{\mathrm{pass}}_{ij}}{n_i}.
\]


Value of a cell
Let \(p_{\mathrm{goal},i}=P(\mathrm{goal}\mid\mathrm{shot},i)\). The value satisfies
\[
\mathrm{xT}_i = p_{\mathrm{shot},i}p_{\mathrm{goal},i}
+ p_{\mathrm{pass},i}\sum_j T^{\mathrm{pass}}_{ij}\mathrm{xT}_j
+ p_{\mathrm{carry},i}\sum_j T^{\mathrm{carry}}_{ij}\mathrm{xT}_j.
\]
The first term is the immediate scoring contribution. The other terms propagate the value of destination cells through passes and displacements. Terminal loss contributes zero future value. Starting from zero values, this equation is iterated until the surface converges; the iteration converges because losses and shots remove probability mass from the continuing branches at every step.
The original xT formulation (Singh 2018) groups ball progression into a move branch. The separate pass, carry and zero-value loss branches are the project-specific construction used here.

title: Expected threat (xT)
text:
2. Estimation
The production surface is fitted on the event tables of the ten matches, on a 10 × 6 grid. The event frequencies \(p_{a,i}\) are computed directly from the counts, while the destination distributions \(T\) and the goal probability \(p_{\mathrm{goal}}\) are estimated from Gaussian-smoothed counts, with bandwidths of 8 m for passes, 5 m for carries and 5 m for goal given shot. The value equation is then iterated to convergence. The benchmark describes the event cohort, the smoothing, the iteration and the selection of the grid and the bandwidths.

title: Expected threat (xT)
text:
3. Fitted xT surface
The heatmap shows the exact production xT values fitted on all ten matches, with the same 10 × 6 cells and no visual interpolation. The saved array has shape (n_x, n_y); its first axis is longitudinal, and its second axis runs from the bottom to the top of the pitch. Both the display and get_xt_values use this convention, with attack from left to right.

from pathlib import Path
import sys
import json
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

root = next(p for p in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents] if (p / "_quarto.yml").is_file())
if str(root) not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(root))
from scripts.build_xt_vignette_figures import plot_xt_surface

# The actual surface distributed with the pretrained choice model.
artifact = json.loads((root / "PRESS/utils/data/pass_selection_model.json").read_text())
xt_grid = np.asarray(artifact["xt_grid"], dtype=float)
fig, ax = plot_xt_surface(xt_grid)
plt.show()

title: Expected threat (xT)
text:
4. Using xT in PRESS
PRESS expects an xT grid with shape (n_x, n_y) and uses centred pitch coordinates. The helper get_xt_values evaluates locations for both teams, accounting for attacking direction. The example below reads the locations of the passer and the matched receiver in the real Brisbane FC–Perth Glory pass used in the action-selection example, together with the fitted grid loaded above.

import os
from PRESS import PRESS
from PRESS.utils.state import get_xt_values

opendata = Path(os.environ.get("SKILLCORNER_OPENDATA", root.parent / "opendata"))
match_dir = opendata / "data/matches/1925299"
press = PRESS.from_skillcorner(match_dir)
release = press.get_frame(54295).iloc[0]
reception = press.get_frame(54309).iloc[0]
passer, receiver = release.player_possession, reception.player_possession
targets = np.asarray([
    [release[f"{passer}_x"], release[f"{passer}_y"]],
    [reception[f"{receiver}_x"], reception[f"{receiver}_y"]],
])
team_xt, opponent_xt = get_xt_values(targets, release.attacking_side, xt_grid)
for name, own, opposite in zip(["N. Acosta at release", "J. Hingert at reception"], team_xt, opponent_xt):
    print(f"{name}: team xT={own:.4f}, opponent xT={opposite:.4f}")

N. Acosta at release: team xT=0.0109, opponent xT=0.0083
J. Hingert at reception: team xT=0.0055, opponent xT=0.0140

title: Pressure case studies and player reports
text: This vignette uses the possession-loss hazard \(h\) and its difficulty bands, defined in the composed hazard vignette, to describe how pressure evolves during an individual possession and to summarize how players and teams perform under pressure. It first defines three pressure patterns, illustrates each with an observed possession and counts how often they occur. It then introduces the expected-minus-observed score, which compares the failures of a player or team in elevated-risk situations with those predicted by \(h\), and reports it for teams and players. The results use ten A-League 2024/25 matches.

title: Pressure case studies and player reports
text: This vignette uses the possession-loss hazard \(h\) and its difficulty bands, defined in the composed hazard vignette, to describe how pressure evolves during an individual possession and to summarize how players and teams perform under pressure. It first defines three pressure patterns, illustrates each with an observed possession and counts how often they occur. It then introduces the expected-minus-observed score, which compares the failures of a player or team in elevated-risk situations with those predicted by \(h\), and reports it for teams and players. The results use ten A-League 2024/25 matches.

title: Pressure case studies and player reports
text:
2. Pressure patterns
PRESS describes three patterns of how pressure evolves during an individual possession. The definitions are inspired by the pressure metrics of SkillCorner (SkillCorner 2026). PRESS defines them as retrospective indicators identified with the possession-loss hazard \(h\), as described next.

Pressure escape. A possession that begins under pressure, lasts at least 1 s and ends with the pressure relieved: the player leaves a pressured situation (Passarotti 2026b).
Drawing pressure. A possession that starts from a low-pressure reception, lasts at least 2 s and ends under high pressure: the player receives in space and draws opponents towards the ball (Passarotti 2026a).
Sustained successful carrying. The player completes at least two one-second carries, each starting in an elevated state: the player keeps the ball under sustained pressure (Passarotti 2026c).


Identification with h
The unit is the individual possession. All indicators use the 14,919-state band-analysis cohort, covering 7,265 verified outfield, non-shot possessions with a terminal canonical action, as described in the composed-risk benchmark. The overall predictive metrics of \(h\) use a 15,085-state population. Pattern frequencies are reported both over all 7,265 possessions and within the eligible subset for each pattern.
\(h\) is evaluated at the canonical checkpoints defined in Possession segmentation and context: one-second carry starts and pass releases. The initial state of a possession is its start, and the final state is the release of its terminal pass or the start of its final failed carry. A loss at 2.4 s has checkpoints at 0, 1 and 2 s, with the final state at 2 s, and a pass at 2.4 s has its final checkpoint at 2.4 s. The loss is the outcome of the final action and adds no decision state. A micropossession shorter than one second has a single checkpoint, which is both its initial and final state.
States are classified with the bands of the composed hazard vignette:

Below Medium: \(h<0.159104\).
Elevated (Medium or High): \(h\ge0.159104\).
High: \(h\ge0.292893\).

The implementation uses the exact half-life cutoffs; the rounded values above give the same memberships. A completed pass is terminal individual nonloss, and a failed pass or direct carry loss is terminal individual loss. Foul-suffered and clearance endings have no terminal canonical action and are outside this cohort, and shots are excluded. The patterns are defined as follows.







Pattern
Operational definition




Pressure escape
Elevated initial h, final h below Medium, completed terminal pass, and duration at least 1 s.


Drawing pressure
Reception with initial h below Medium, duration at least 2 s, and High at the final state. Any terminal outcome is allowed. Reception includes ordinary pass, free-kick, goal-kick, corner and throw-in reception start types.


Sustained successful carrying
At least two successful full one-second carries, each starting in an elevated state; the carries can be non-consecutive and a later action may fail.



A possession can match more than one pattern. Intervals on their shares are 95% Wilson intervals over distinct possessions (Wilson 1927). The intervals are descriptive and treat possessions of the same match as independent.


Examples
Case A illustrates a pressure escape, Case B drawing pressure and Case C sustained successful carrying. Every canonical evaluated checkpoint has a pitch panel: the attacking direction is stated and velocity arrows are scaled drawing aids. Panel titles show \(h\), its band, the distance of the nearest defender and the number of active annotated on-ball engagements (OBE, defined in the ball-drive benchmark). The values are held-out predictions of the matching outer-fold models at observed tracking states. Cases are selected for interpretation. Geometry, carrier movement, event origin, pass result, pass options and OBE timing were cross-checked against tracking and annotations.

Case A: receiving and advancing out of pressure
Ivan Vujica, Melbourne City–Macarthur FC, 2025-03-07, 66:34.4–66:37.3. Vujica receives in his own defensive third, closed by opponents and with few passing options. He carries the ball 5.35 m forward without losing it, and during the carry a simple passing line opens towards Luke Brattan, to whom he completes the pass. \(h\) follows 31.43% → 36.76% → 11.71%: the two carry checkpoints are High and the release is Low. The sequence illustrates a pressure escape (Passarotti 2026b). The last panel shows Brattan controlling the completed pass.

The figure summarizes the three cases through the weighted branch contributions to \(h\) along their checkpoints. The underlying values are available as case probabilities, event/outcome summaries, checkpoint geometry and engagement counts and context verification.



Patterns found
Each pattern has a starting situation without which it cannot occur: an escape needs initial pressure to escape from, drawing pressure needs a low-pressure reception, and sustained carrying needs carries made under pressure. The eligible possessions of a pattern are those that meet this starting situation. Among them, the pattern occurs when the remaining conditions of its definition also hold. Possessions outside the eligible set cannot show the pattern by construction.
Two shares describe each pattern, with the same count of possessions \(x\) in the numerator. The first divides by all 7,265 terminal-covered possessions, including single-checkpoint micropossessions, and gives the frequency of the pattern in the whole sample. The second divides by the eligible possessions and gives how often the starting situation develops into the pattern.

The eligible possessions of each pattern are:

Pressure escape: possessions with an elevated initial state (\(h\ge0.159104\)). Possessions starting below Medium have no pressure to escape from and fall outside the eligible set. Within it, a possession that ends in a loss, or lasts less than 1 s, does not count as an escape and remains in the denominator.
Drawing pressure: receptions with an initial state below Medium. Possessions that start with an elevated state, or with a start type other than a reception (ordinary pass, free-kick, goal-kick, corner or throw-in), fall outside the eligible set. Within it, receptions lasting less than 2 s, or not reaching High at the final state, do not count as occurrences and remain in the denominator.
Sustained successful carrying: possessions with at least one canonical carry attempted in an elevated state, including failed carries shorter than 1 s. Possessions without carries, or whose carries all start below Medium, fall outside the eligible set. Within it, possessions with fewer than two successful full one-second carries starting in an elevated state do not count as occurrences and remain in the denominator.

The sample covers ten matches, so some patterns have few occurrences and some eligible sets are small. The table therefore reports 95% Wilson intervals on each share, with \(n\) equal to 7,265 for the first and to the number of eligible possessions for the second. The Wilson interval remains inside \([0,1]\) and keeps a sensible width for small counts and for shares close to zero, which is the situation of the rarest patterns.



Pattern frequencies over all terminal-covered possessions (left) and the respective eligible subsets (right), with 95% Wilson intervals.


The patterns are also meant to profile a player by the types of possession to which they are exposed: how often they start under pressure and escape it, receive in space and draw opponents towards the ball, or keep the ball while carrying under sustained pressure. Such a profile needs enough possessions per player. The ten matches contain 239 pressure escapes, 56 drawing-pressure possessions and 257 sustained carrying possessions, spread over 192 players and 12 teams. This leaves on average about 1.2, 0.3 and 1.3 occurrences per player and about 20, 5 and 21 per team, too few for a breakdown by pattern. The typology is therefore reported at league level and describes the sample as a whole.

title: Pressure case studies and player reports
text:
3. Player and team report
The report describes how teams and players fare in the situations where \(h\) signals a high risk of losing the ball. It uses held-out \(h\) from the matching fold for 14,919 canonical states from 7,265 individual possessions, 192 players and 12 teams in the ten matches. Teams appear in one to four matches, and the results describe this sample.

Attribution
\(h\) measures the fragility of the team possession at a checkpoint. For player attribution, each canonical action is assigned to its current carrier, and a completed pass ends that individual’s involvement without ending the team sequence. The team report aggregates the actions of all the players of the team.


Elevated-risk actions
The report focuses on the canonical actions with \(h_i\ge0.159104\), those in Medium or High. They are the situations in which a loss is a real possibility. At lower \(h\) failures are rare, and differences between teams or players would rest on a handful of events. For an entity \(j\), a player or a team, \(A_j\) is the set of its elevated-risk actions, and \(y_i=1\) if the current action \(i\) fails (a failed pass or a lost carry) and \(y_i=0\) otherwise.


Expected minus observed: E−O per 100 actions
The prediction \(h_i\) is the probability that action \(i\) fails. Its mean over \(A_j\), \(\bar h_j\), is the failure frequency expected for the entity in its elevated-risk actions, and \(\bar y_j\) is the frequency observed. The score is
\[\mathrm{E{-}O}_j=100\,\frac{\sum_{i\in A_j}(h_i-y_i)}{|A_j|}=100\,(\bar h_j-\bar y_j).\]
A positive value means fewer failures than predicted and a negative value more failures. Over all 3,324 elevated-risk actions of the sample the mean \(h\) is about 25.2% and the observed failure frequency about 24.4%, so the score of the whole league is close to zero (about +0.8). Zero is therefore the natural reference for reading the scores of teams and players. The score summarizes resistance to pressure through the risk of losing the ball. The value of the actions can be assessed by combining \(h\) with a measure of expected possession value, such as the expected threat model of the expected threat vignette.


Quantities in the tables

Matches: the matches in which the entity appears.
Elevated actions: \(|A_j|\), the denominator of the score.
Exposed possessions: the distinct possessions containing at least one elevated-risk action of the entity. Summed over the twelve teams they give the 2,505 possessions reaching Medium or High.
Mean \(h\): \(\bar h_j\), the expected failure frequency.
Observed failures: \(\bar y_j\), the observed failure frequency.
High share: the share of elevated-risk actions with \(h\ge0.292893\) (High band), which shows how much of the exposure sits in the highest band.
E−O per 100: the score, equal to 100 times Mean \(h\) minus Observed failures, with its interval.

If \(A_j\) is empty, the score and these rates are undefined, and the complete table retains those players with their counts.


Uncertainty of the score
E−O is computed on a limited number of elevated-risk actions, so each score comes with a 95% interval from a bootstrap that resamples possessions (Efron and Tibshirani 1993). The bootstrap draws units that are assumed independent and keeps each drawn unit intact.

Resampling unit
Actions of the same possession share the carrier, the context and the pressure state, so they depend strongly on each other and are resampled together. The match would be a larger unit, but a team is represented in one to four matches, and a team observed in a single match offers one unit: resampling it returns the observed score at every replicate and the interval reduces to a point. The individual possession is the largest unit for which every team and every player with elevated-risk actions has several units. It is therefore the primary procedure. The match-bootstrap sensitivity is kept separately.


Quantities
For an entity \(j\), a player or a team, the blocks \(b=1,\dots,K\) are the distinct possessions that contain at least one action of \(A_j\). Each block carries three numbers computed once over its actions in \(A_j\):

\(n_b\), the number of actions;
\(H_b=\sum h_i\), the sum of the predicted failure probabilities;
\(Y_b=\sum y_i\), the number of observed failures.

Summing over blocks, the score is \[\mathrm{E{-}O}_j=100\,\frac{\sum_{b}(H_b-Y_b)}{\sum_b n_b}.\]


Procedure

Draw \(K\) blocks with replacement from the \(K\) blocks of \(j\). Some blocks are drawn several times and others not at all.
Add up \(n_b\), \(H_b\) and \(Y_b\) over the drawn blocks, counting a repeated block each time it is drawn, and compute the score \(\mathrm{E{-}O}^*\) with the number of actions of the drawn sample as denominator.
Repeat 2,000 times with seed 20261030, obtaining 2,000 values of \(\mathrm{E{-}O}^*\).
The interval is formed by the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of these values.

The predictions \(h_i\) and the membership in \(A_j\) stay fixed: the replicates change which possessions enter the sample and how many times. Each entity has its own deterministic random stream derived from the seed, so the result is independent of the order of the table.


Reporting
Players with at least 20 distinct exposed possessions show the interval. Below that count the table shows the score and its support.
The intervals describe the sampling variability of the possessions of these ten matches. They treat possessions of the same match or team as independent and are conditional on the fitted models.

The sample comes from the 2024/25 A-League Men season, in which Auckland FC, a new club, won the Premiers Plate and Melbourne City won the championship, with Western United third in the regular season (Wikipedia). The scores below describe how each team handled elevated-risk situations in its sampled matches. With one or two matches for most teams, the score of each team reflects the sampled matches and depends on the opponent and on how those games developed.
Three of the twelve intervals exclude zero: Melbourne City (+6.04) and Sydney FC (+4.93) above it, and Western United (−9.60) below it. Melbourne City and Sydney FC fail less often than predicted, with observed failure frequencies of 18.32% and 20.18% against mean \(h\) of 24.36% and 25.11%. Western United combines the highest High share of the league (31.49%) with an observed failure frequency (35.99%) well above its mean \(h\) (26.39%), so its elevated-risk actions concentrate in the highest band and fail more often than predicted. The other nine intervals include zero.
Teams with a high High share have scores of both signs: Wellington P FC and Newcastle have High shares close to that of Western United (30.81% and 30.59%) and scores near or above zero (+3.27 and +0.06).
The width of the intervals follows the support. A team observed in one match, such as CC Mariners with 100 elevated-risk actions, has a wide interval (−15.17 to +2.12), while Auckland FC, observed in four matches with 608 actions, has a narrow one (−4.98 to +1.70). With one to four matches per team, the intervals that exclude zero are descriptions of the sampled matches, and the nine that include zero show differences too small to separate from possession-to-possession variation.


Complement: possessions by maximum band
A complementary descriptive statistic classifies each possession by the maximum band reached across its checkpoints. Possessions with more checkpoints have more chances to reach Medium or High, so the statistic also reflects their duration. The exposure of a team is the share of its possessions reaching Medium or High, and its retention is the share of those that end with a completed pass. Across the sample, 2,505 of 7,265 possessions (34.48%) reach Medium or High, and 1,599 of those (63.83%) end with a completed pass. Both proportions have 95% Wilson intervals over possessions.



Maximum band per possession, elevated-risk exposure and terminal retention by team.


At league level, about one possession in three reaches Medium or High, and about two thirds of those end with a completed pass. Among the possessions that start in an elevated state, 13.07% end as a pressure escape, and among those with a carry attempted in an elevated state, 23.88% contain sustained successful carrying. Drawing pressure is the rarest pattern, at 1.23% of the receptions that start below Medium. These frequencies describe the ten sampled matches. A reference from other leagues would be needed to call them high or low, so they remain a description of these matches.


Player scores
The plot includes the 40 players with at least 20 distinct exposed possessions, the minimum for which the bootstrap interval is shown. Each player has a point with its interval. Marker shape distinguishes one represented match from several, and the counts beside the points show elevated-risk actions and exposed possessions. Players are grouped by team and name for display. The tables report the same quantities as for the teams.



Player E−O per 100 elevated-risk actions with 95% possession-bootstrap intervals; counts show actions and distinct possessions.


Of the 192 players, 189 have at least one elevated-risk action and 40 have an interval. Nine of these 40 have an interval that excludes zero, with between 29 and 72 elevated-risk actions each: seven above zero (Leonardo de Souza Sena +18.51, Alex Rufer +14.92, Nathaniel Atkinson +13.53, Sam Sutton +13.29, Callan Elliot +11.96, Anas Ouahim +11.79 and Anthony Cáceres +10.28) and two below (Nishan Velupillay −12.16 and Riku Danzaki −21.35). title: Composed-risk benchmark
text:
Model and example · All benchmarks
This benchmark evaluates the composed hazard \(h\) and the individual xLoss, which have distinct targets: failure of the current canonical action, and loss by the end of the carrier’s individual possession. An individual possession is the control of the ball by a single player, as segmented in Possessions and checkpoints, and it ends with a terminal action: a pass, a possession loss, a clearance, a shot or a foul suffered. A completed pass ends the individual possession without a loss, while a failed pass or a direct possession loss ends it with a loss. The model vignette introduces the composition, the difficulty bands and an executable example, and this benchmark documents the cohort, the evaluation procedure, the predictive performance and the band validation.
Let \(q(s)\) be the probability of selecting a pass, \(\pi_j\) the probability of the destination \(j\) and \(p_j\) the probability that a pass to \(j\) is completed, so that \(f(s)=\sum_j \pi_j(1-p_j)\) is the pass-failure probability averaged over the destination distribution. Let \(d(s)=1-D(s)\) be the loss probability of the canonical one-second carry, the complement of the carry-success probability \(D(s)\), and \(r(s)\) the probability of terminal individual loss conditional on a successful carry, evaluated from the current state. The composed predictions are
\[
h(s)=q(s)f(s)+\big(1-q(s)\big)d(s),
\]
\[
\operatorname{xLoss}(s)=h(s)+\big(1-q(s)\big)\big(1-d(s)\big)r(s).
\]
Each prediction is evaluated against its own observed target: \(h\) against the failure of the current action (a failed pass, or a loss during the one-second carry), and xLoss against the terminal individual loss.

title: Composed-risk benchmark
text:
1. Evaluation cohort

Effective task-specific exclusions
The cohort starts from the canonical action-selection checkpoints. A checkpoint is kept when the terminal outcome of its parent possession is verified: a loss-ending parent needs a valid associated OBE, defined in the ball-drive benchmark, and a terminal pass must belong to the verified continuous direct-receipt cohort. Verification concerns the parent’s terminal outcome, so earlier checkpoints of an affected possession are removed as well. Terminal passes are retained irrespective of observed flight duration. These criteria leave 15,085 verified-outcome checkpoints. Effective exclusion counts.
The overall predictive metrics of \(h\) and xLoss use all 15,085 checkpoints, including the earlier valid carry checkpoints of possessions ending in a foul suffered or a clearance. Every checkpoint has an observed current-action outcome for \(h\) and a verified terminal individual outcome for xLoss. The pooled metrics and calibration curves retain all checkpoints, irrespective of terminal coverage or possession duration.


Cohort for difficulty bands and possession profiles
The \(h\)-band validation and the subsequent possession-profile analysis additionally require coverage of the terminal canonical action. A pass supplies its release checkpoint, and a failed carry supplies the start of the final failed action, at most one second before loss. Micropossessions remain eligible with their single pass or failed-carry checkpoint. Possessions ending in a foul suffered or a clearance have no terminal canonical action, so their earlier successful-carry states are excluded from this cohort, which has 14,919 states from 7,265 possessions. The rule applies to the band analysis only, with predictions and component models unchanged.

title: Composed-risk benchmark
text:
2. Evaluation procedure
Both predictions are obtained by composing the component outputs directly. At each eligible outer-test checkpoint, their terms are composed from the matching six-fitting/two-validation model stack, using native action-selection and residual-risk outputs, calibrated pass-completion probabilities, and the temperature-calibrated flat pass-selection distribution. The same fold-specific upstream quantities enter every term, and the full-ten-match deployment fits are left out of the evaluation. Metrics are then recomputed on the pooled composed predictions against each target.

text:
3. Predictive performance
Both targets are evaluated on 15,085 held-out canonical checkpoints: 1,465 current-action failures for \(h\) and 2,888 terminal individual losses for xLoss. This verified-outcome set is smaller than the action-selection training set, which requires an identifiable choice. The one-second segmentation is described in Possessions and checkpoints. Scores are pooled across the five outer test folds for each target.

title: Composed-risk benchmark
text:
4. Band validation intervals
The \(h\) bands of the model vignette are validated on the 14,919 held-out states of the band cohort. Predictions and band thresholds are fixed, and the intervals quantify between-match variability in this sample.
Intervals are 95% percentile intervals from 2,000 whole-match bootstrap replicates, with seed 20261030 (Efron and Tibshirani 1993). Each replicate draws ten matches with replacement and includes all their eligible actions, preserving multiplicity. For every band, mean predicted \(h\) and the observed frequency of current-action failure are recomputed, and the bounds are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. The paired gap is the difference between the two means within each replicate, and its interval is taken from the same replicates. Action selection remains native, and pass completion retains its fold-specific isotonic calibration.
Whole matches are resampled because actions within a match are dependent. Band counts are unequal, so the denominators vary across draws: High contains 665–1,053 actions across replicates (median 841), and no band is empty in any replicate. With ten matches the 95% level is indicative, and the intervals quantify the sampling variability of the evaluation, conditional on the fitted models.

title: Residual risk
text:
Residual risk estimates the probability of a terminal individual-possession loss given that the player successfully completes the current one-second carry (see Possession segmentation and context). The model evaluates the state at the beginning of that carry, using only the information available at that frame. The outcome of the individual possession remains open after a successful carry, so the prediction concerns the remaining sequence of individual control.
An individual possession unfolds as an alternation of choice and execution: in each state the player chooses to pass or to carry, the chosen action is executed with some probability of success, and the possession continues from a new state. A successful carry leads to such a new state, and the probability that the possession eventually ends in a loss depends on all later choices and executions. Residual risk approximates this remaining iteration with a single classifier, which maps the state at the start of the carry directly to the probability of eventual terminal loss.
Let \(Y=1\) denote a terminal individual-possession loss, that is, a possession that ends in a failed pass, a direct possession loss or a clearance, and \(Y=0\) a possession that ends in a completed pass or a foul suffered, according to the conventions specified in the residual-risk benchmark. Using the same state notation as action selection, let \(s\) denote the current game state and \(A\) the selected action. For this state, the conditional target is
\[
r(s)=P(Y=1\mid s,\,A=\mathrm{carry},\,\text{successful one-second carry}).
\]
Consequently, the probability of a terminal outcome without loss, under the same condition, is \(1-r(s)\).
Related work addresses pressure-based possession outcomes, action-rate prediction and temporal possession modelling (Gu et al. 2024; Dick and Brefeld 2023; Le Coz, Boustila, and Imbach 2026). The benchmark discusses their relationship to this conditional terminal-loss task.
We estimate \(r(s)\) with a regularized XGBoost classifier (Chen and Guestrin 2016), which takes a vector of features summarizing the game state and returns the probability of terminal loss. The features are described first, followed by the likelihood used to train the model.

title: Residual risk
text:
2. Model inputs
Residual risk uses the same state-based features and construction procedures as the action-selection vignette, with two changes.

Carry probability \(P(\mathrm{carry})=1-q(s)\). The chance that the player chooses to carry in state \(s\), where \(q(s)=P(A=\mathrm{pass}\mid s)\) is the pass-choice probability defined in action selection. It is computed by the action-selection model from its own inputs, including the number of completed one-second carries, and is taken from that model without refitting. In training, it is cross-fitted so that every state is scored by an action-selection model that did not see its match, as described in the benchmark. Together with the carry-execution success probability \(1-d(s)\) (already among the shared features, the chance that the carry succeeds), it describes both the choice and the execution of carrying.
Elapsed time. The time elapsed since the beginning of the individual possession, measured at the prediction frame, that is, how long the player has already been on the ball. It replaces the count of completed one-second carries, enters residual risk only, and uses no information after the prediction frame.

These changes yield 31 conceptual inputs, including the two categorical context variables. The classifier returns its native logistic probabilities.
Context-label meanings and the previous_action convention are defined in the User guide.

title: Residual risk
text:
3. Likelihood and learning
For feature vector \(z_i\) and binary terminal label \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), the tree ensemble produces a score \(f_\psi(z_i)\) and the logistic residual-loss probability
\[
\widehat r_i=\frac{1}{1+\exp[-f_\psi(z_i)]}.
\]
The parameters are fitted by minimizing the Bernoulli negative log-likelihood with the usual tree-complexity penalty,
\[
\mathcal L(\psi)=-\sum_i\left[y_i\log\widehat r_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-\widehat r_i)\right]+\Omega(\psi).
\]
Training observations are states preceding completed, successful one-second carries, with the label taken from the eventual terminal outcome of the same individual possession. Cohort verification, outcome conventions, model selection and held-out evaluation are documented in the benchmark.

title: Residual risk
text:
4. Feature importance and interpretation
The figure reports XGBoost total split gain, normalized within each fitted ensemble. One-hot encoded levels are aggregated into their original conceptual features. Bars represent the installed full-data model, while the five outer-fold estimates indicate variability across fitted models; their ranges are descriptive.



Feature importance of the residual-risk model.


Accessible space and the configuration of subsequent passing options are prominent predictors. BCOS accounts for 14.21% of production split gain and ranks between first and fourth across the five outer folds. This suggests that the carrier’s available space provides information about terminal individual-possession loss even after conditioning on a successful one-second carry.
The number of opponents ahead of likely completed-pass destinations contributes 10.30% and ranks first or second across folds. The model therefore relies on immediate conditions around the carrier and on the spatial configuration of plausible subsequent passes. The estimated probability of successful one-second carrying (8.83%) and expected pass success (8.01%) are also prominent, linking the forecast to immediate execution conditions and available alternatives. The rank of expected pass success varies substantially across folds, so its production importance is less stable.
Team-line position under failed-pass outcomes (5.60%) and own-team xT under successful-pass outcomes (5.24%) further indicate that the model uses the tactical structure of potential continuations. Overall, these rankings are consistent with residual risk depending on both the carrier’s freedom of movement and the quality of available options.
Split gain describes how the fitted ensemble uses its inputs. Correlated inputs can substitute for one another, and features with more potential split points may receive higher gain. Further diagnostics are available in the feature-importance analysis.

title: Residual risk
text:
5. Application to a game state
Auckland FC–Newcastle: L. Gillion completes the one-second carry starting at checkpoint 32927, then loses possession; K. Grozos takes control for Newcastle. The second frame is the beginning of the next individual possession. Set SKILLCORNER_OPENDATA to your local open-data repository (Data setup).

from pathlib import Path
import os
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import jax

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
from PRESS import PRESS

opendata = Path(os.environ.get("SKILLCORNER_OPENDATA", Path.cwd().parent / "opendata"))
match_dir = opendata / "data/matches/1886347"
press = PRESS.from_skillcorner(match_dir)
frame_id = 32927

# Observed context: getters resolve the frame and possession annotations.
frame = press.get_frame(frame_id).iloc[0]
context = press.get_frame_context(frame_id)
match_clock_min = pd.to_timedelta(frame.timestamp).total_seconds() / 60

# Score is absent from these tracking rows: read the current possession's
# dynamical event rather than inserting a constant in the model call.
possessions = press.get_player_possessions()
current_possession = possessions.loc[
    possessions.frame_start.le(frame_id) & possessions.frame_end.ge(frame_id)
].iloc[0]
events = pd.read_csv(
    opendata / "data/matches" / match_dir.name / f"{match_dir.name}_dynamic_events.csv",
    low_memory=False,
)
origin = events.loc[
    events.event_type.eq("player_possession")
    & events.event_id.eq(current_possession.possession_id)
].iloc[0]
score_difference = float(origin.team_score - origin.opponent_team_score)

from PRESS.model import PassSelectionModel

xT_grid = PassSelectionModel.pretrained().xt_grid
result = press.compute_risk_frame(
    frame_id, xT_grid, keep_details=True,
    start_type=context["start_type"], previous_action=context["previous_action"],
    completed_canonical_drives=context["completed_canonical_drives"],
    match_clock_min=match_clock_min, score_difference_prefix=score_difference,
)

# Reuse the preliminary BCOS feature evaluated by the production workflow.
area = press.get_bcos_result(frame_id)["BCOS area"]

from PRESS.model import ActionSelectionModel, ResidualRiskModel

state = press.get_state(frame_id)
context = press.get_frame_context(frame_id)
field = result["PPCF"]
action_model = ActionSelectionModel.pretrained()
residual_model = ResidualRiskModel.pretrained()
features = residual_model.build_features(
    action_model=action_model, time_since_start=press.get_elapsed_time(frame_id),
    x_bc=state["x_bc"], v_bc=state["v_bc"],
    r_atts=state["r_atts"], r_defs=state["r_defs"],
    attacking_side=state["attacking_side"], targets=field["grid"],
    pass_selection_probabilities=field["Pass selection probabilities"],
    pass_success_probability=field["Pass probability"],
    bcos=area, ball_drive_loss=result["BALL_DRIVE_RISK"]["Ball drive risk"],
    start_type_raw=context["start_type"], previous_action_raw=context["previous_action"],
    match_clock_min=match_clock_min, score_difference_prefix=score_difference,
    completed_canonical_drives=context["completed_canonical_drives"],
    pitch_length=state["pitch_length"], pitch_width=state["pitch_width"],
)
c = float(residual_model.predict_features(features)[0])

from PRESS.visualization import plot_frame

fig, ax = plot_frame(press, frame_id, title=f"Residual risk · frame {frame_id} · P(loss | successful 1 s carry)={c:.1%}", show=False)
fig.savefig("figures/vignette_12_residual_real_pitch.png", dpi=170)
fig.savefig("figures/vignette_12_residual_real_pitch.svg")
plt.close(fig)

title: Pass selection
text:
A player in possession decides whether to pass and where to direct the ball. Pass selection models this decision as a probability distribution over potential destinations, conditional on attempting a pass. Pass probability estimates whether a pass to a specified destination will be completed. A destination can be attractive and risky, and a safe destination can be rarely chosen. These components describe different aspects of the same decision.
The distinction is central to spatial models of football. Spearman’s Beyond Expected Goals (Spearman 2018) places a pass selection model alongside control and scoring opportunity in a framework for evaluating off-ball attacking opportunities. Fernández, Bornn and Cervone (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021) explicitly model pass selection as a normalized spatial probability surface within an expected-possession-value framework. PRESS follows this probabilistic interpretation of destination choice, while learning the utility of each destination using gradient-boosted trees instead of a convolutional network.
At each observed passing decision, the pitch is discretized into candidate destinations on a one-metre grid. The observed endpoint is mapped to its nearest cell centre. The resulting probabilities sum to one across the complete candidate set; they are conditional on a pass being attempted, irrespective of whether the observed pass was successful.
Context-label meanings and the previous action convention are defined in Possessions and checkpoints.

Fernández, Bornn and Cervone (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021) explicitly model pass selection as a normalized spatial probability surface within an expected-possession-value framework. PRESS follows this probabilistic interpretation of destination choice, while learning the utility of each destination using gradient-boosted trees instead of a convolutional network.
At each observed passing decision, the pitch is discretized into candidate destinations on a one-metre grid. The observed endpoint is mapped to its nearest cell centre. The resulting probabilities sum to one across the complete candidate set; they are conditional on a pass being attempted, irrespective of whether the observed pass was successful.
Context-label meanings and the previous action convention are defined in Possessions and checkpoints.

title: Pass selection
text:
2. Probabilistic destination-choice model
Let \(s_i\) denote the tracked game state at passing decision \(i\), and let \(\mathcal G_i\) be its set of candidate destination cells. Each cell \(j\) is represented by features \(z_{ij}\) describing the pass and the current spatial configuration. A single shared function assigns a utility to each destination:
\[
u_{ij}=f_\psi(z_{ij}).\]
PRESS represents \(f_\psi\) as an additive ensemble of XGBoost regression trees. Utilities express relative preference among destinations. The multinomial-logit model converts them into a categorical distribution:
\[
\boxed{\pi_{ij}=P(Y_i=j\mid s_i,\text{pass})=
\frac{\exp(u_{ij})}{\sum_{k\in\mathcal G_i}\exp(u_{ik})}.}
\]
The normalization couples every candidate in the same decision: changing the utility of one destination changes the probabilities of the others.
The ensemble is estimated from observed destinations by minimizing the categorical negative log-likelihood,
\[\mathcal L(\psi)=-\sum_i\log \pi_{i,y_i}(\psi),\]
where \(y_i\) is the observed destination cell. The benchmark describes the boosting procedure, regularization, model selection and validation.
After fitting, a scalar temperature \(T\) calibrates the predicted distribution,
\[\pi_{ij}^{(T)}=\frac{\pi_{ij}^{1/T}}{\sum_k \pi_{ik}^{1/T}},\]
while preserving the ordering of destinations. The installed model uses the flat multinomial-logit specification; an exploratory cross-nested extension is evaluated separately in the benchmark.

title: Pass selection
text:
3. Model features
The model uses 21 conceptual features: 19 numerical and two categorical, in four groups. Each group answers one question about the decision. Each feature is described first in plain terms and then by how it is computed, and uses only information available at the passing decision; the realized receiver, pass outcome and subsequent events are excluded. Categorical variables are one-hot encoded using a vocabulary learned during fitting.








Group
Question
Count




Carrier state and ball retention
How fast is the carrier moving, and how risky is continuing the carry?
2


Spatial and tactical configuration
What is the current location’s value and team structure?
6


Passing opportunities
What are the geometry, accessibility and tactical properties of each candidate destination?
9


Possession and match context
How did control start, and what is the match situation?
4




Carrier state and ball retention (2 features)
These features describe how the carrier is moving and how risky it would be to keep the ball. They are shared by all destinations in the same decision.

Carrier speed. How fast the carrier is moving: running with the ball, or almost standing. It is the magnitude of the carrier’s current velocity, \(\lVert v_{\mathrm{bc}}\rVert\), in m/s.
Carry-loss probability \(d(s)\). The chance that the carrier loses the ball within one second if the carry continues. A high value means that keeping the ball is risky in the current situation. It is the probability of loss during a canonical one-second carry, from the ball-drive risk model.



Spatial and tactical configuration (6 features)
These features describe the value of the carrier’s location and how the teams are arranged around it. They are evaluated at the carrier’s current position and shared by all candidate destinations.

Own-team xT and opponent xT (2 features). How valuable it is to hold the ball at the carrier’s location: the first value is for the carrier’s team and the second for the opponent, each in its own attacking orientation. The construction follows Singh (Singh 2018) and is described in the xT vignette.
Nearest own-team line index and nearest opposition line index (2 features). Where the carrier is located relative to the pressure structure of each team. The current outfield longitudinal positions are clustered into three lines with complete linkage, following the spatial line representation of Fernández, Bornn and Cervone (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021). The lines use current player positions, with the carrier excluded from their own team’s construction and the extreme-x goalkeeper proxy removed from each roster. For each team, the three lines are numbered from the most advanced (1) to the deepest, closest to its own goal (3), and the index is that of the line closest to the point considered.
Teammates ahead and opponents ahead (2 features). How many players of each team are further toward the goal the carrier team attacks. They are counts strictly beyond the transverse line through the carrier, along the carrier team’s attacking direction, and both rosters use the same direction. The carrier is excluded, tracked goalkeepers are retained, and players exactly on the line are excluded.

For a player group \(G\), query point \(r\) and carrier-team attacking direction \(\delta\in\{-1,+1\}\), the shared count convention is
\[
N_G(r)=\sum_{k\in G}\mathbf 1\{\delta\,x_k>\delta\,r_x\}.
\]


Passing opportunities (9 features)
These features describe each candidate destination \(j\), evaluated from the current frame, with its own geometry and tactical descriptors.

Pass distance. How long the pass would be. It is the Euclidean distance from the carrier to the candidate destination, in m.
Pass angle. Whether the pass follows or departs from the direction in which the carrier is already moving. It is the signed angle from the carrier’s velocity to the carrier-to-destination vector, and is undefined for a stationary carrier.
Raw target pitch control \(C_{\mathrm{att}}\). How likely the attacking team is to control that point. It is the attacking team’s control probability at the destination, excluding the carrier. It uses raw pitch control; the calibrated completion probability comes from pass probability.
Own-team xT and opponent xT at the destination (2 features). How valuable it would be to hold the ball at the destination for each team, in its own attacking orientation.
Nearest own-team line index and nearest opposition line index at the destination (2 features). Where the destination is located relative to the pressure structure of each team. They use the same line definitions and ordering as at the carrier, evaluated at the candidate point.
Teammates ahead and opponents ahead of the destination (2 features). How many players of each team are further toward the attacked goal than the destination. They use the same strict longitudinal counts as at the carrier, with current player positions. A backward candidate may have more players ahead, since these are counts beyond each line.



Possession and match context (4 features)
These features describe how the possession began and the state of the match.

Start type (categorical). How the player got the ball: the event through which the current individual possession began.
Previous action (categorical). What the player did before: the previous canonical action. The start context is retained until a full one-second carry has been completed, after which it is ball_drive.
Match minute. How far the match has advanced: the time elapsed in the match at the passing decision.
Score difference. Whether the carrier’s team is ahead or behind: carrier-team goals minus opponent goals known at that frame.

These definitions use the general event meanings and segmentation conventions documented in Possessions and checkpoints.

title: Pass selection
text:
5. Application to a game state
Brisbane Roar FC–Perth Glory: N. Acosta chooses and completes a pass to J. Hingert (checkpoint 54295). Set SKILLCORNER_OPENDATA to your local open-data repository (Data setup). The dashed line shows the matched destination. Colors display relative preference: 100% is the most probable destination cell. The stored cell probabilities remain a distribution summing to one.
The action labels are retrieved with get_frame_context; the match minute is calculated from the timestamp returned by get_frame. The carrier-team score difference is read from the current possession’s dynamical event. It is supplied explicitly because these processed tracking rows do not contain score information.

from pathlib import Path
import os
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import jax

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
from PRESS import PRESS

opendata = Path(os.environ.get("SKILLCORNER_OPENDATA", Path.cwd().parent / "opendata"))
match_dir = opendata / "data/matches/1925299"
press = PRESS.from_skillcorner(match_dir)
frame_id = 54295

from PRESS.model import PassSelectionModel
from PRESS.visualization import plot_pass_map

choice = PassSelectionModel.pretrained()
context = press.get_frame_context(frame_id)
frame = press.get_frame(frame_id).iloc[0]

# Match minute comes from the observed tracking timestamp.
match_clock_min = pd.to_timedelta(frame.timestamp).total_seconds() / 60

# The context getter supplies action labels, not the score. Read the known
# score from the dynamical event of the current individual possession.
possessions = press.get_player_possessions()
current_possession = possessions.loc[
    possessions.frame_start.le(frame_id) & possessions.frame_end.ge(frame_id)
].iloc[0]
events = pd.read_csv(
    opendata / "data/matches/1925299/1925299_dynamic_events.csv", low_memory=False,
)
origin = events.loc[
    events.event_type.eq("player_possession")
    & events.event_id.eq(current_possession.possession_id)
].iloc[0]
score_difference = float(origin.team_score - origin.opponent_team_score)

press.compute_ppcf(frame_id)
press.compute_ball_drive_risk(frame_id)
press.compute_pass_selection(
    frame_id, choice.xt_grid,
    start_type_raw=context["start_type"], previous_action_raw=context["previous_action"],
    match_clock_min=match_clock_min, score_difference_prefix=score_difference,
)
plot_pass_map(press, frame_id, field="pass_selection", pass_target=(-12.15, -28.05))
plt.savefig("figures/vignette_03_pass_selection_pitch.png", dpi=170)
plt.savefig("figures/vignette_03_pass_selection_pitch.svg")
plt.close()




Pass selection on the real checkpoint; color intensity is relative to the most probable cell.

title: Pass selection
text:
6. Using the fitted model
The model can also be loaded directly, with its saved feature vocabulary and fitted physical-model dependencies:
from PRESS.model import PassSelectionModel
choice = PassSelectionModel.pretrained()
press = PRESS(tracking, pass_selection_model=choice)
press.compute_ppcf(frame_id)
press.compute_ball_drive_risk(frame_id, t_press=1.0)
probability = press.compute_pass_selection(
    frame_id, xT_grid,
    start_type_raw=context["start_type"], previous_action_raw=context["previous_action"],
    match_clock_min=match_clock_min, score_difference_prefix=score_difference,
)
Here context, match_clock_min and score_difference are the observed values recovered in the preceding example; retrieve them again when selecting another frame. The positional xT_grid argument remains for API compatibility; the installed choice model retains its fitted xT representation. The benchmark reports the evaluation protocol, training details, exploratory nested alternative and comparison with Fernández et al. (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021).

title: Ball-drive risk
text:
The ball-drive risk component estimates the probability that the current ball carrier loses possession during a canonical one-second ball drive, as segmented in Possessions and checkpoints. It is the action-specific risk \(d_t\) used by PRESS to construct the possession-loss hazard. The event is the loss of possession by the current player during the drive.
The model combines two ideas from the literature. Bekkers’ arrival formulation provides the idea of intercepting a moving ball carrier: the time a defender needs to reach the carrier’s projected position determines whether an intervention is possible (Bekkers 2025). Spearman’s pitch-control framework provides the uncertainty on arrival times and the idea of control: a player arriving at a location establishes control at a certain rate (Spearman et al. 2017; Spearman 2018). PRESS adapts these ideas to a player already in possession: a defender must reach the carrier and, once there, can generate a successful defensive intervention at a certain tackle rate. This rate plays a role analogous to the control rate in pitch control, but measures the intensity of possession loss, and the uncertainty on arrival turns each defender’s arrival time into a probability of reaching the carrier. PRESS does not reproduce Bekkers’ aggregate pressing score.
Each defender contributes a time-varying cause-specific hazard. A shared survival process combines these contributions into the probability of retaining the ball over one second. The one-second action convention follows the modular EPV perspective of Fernández, Bornn and Cervone (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2019; Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021).
The approach is physics-informed: motion and reachability follow an explicit physical approximation, whereas tackle intensity is estimated from observed outcomes. The tackle rate is represented by a penalized additive spline model fitted to observed outcomes.

title: Ball-drive risk
text:
2. Motion and defender interception time

Projected ball-carrier trajectory
Let \(x_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)\) and \(v_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)\) denote the carrier’s observed position and velocity at the evaluation frame. During the hypothetical drive, the carrier follows a constant-velocity projection:
\[
x_{\mathrm{bc}}(t)=x_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)+v_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)t,\qquad 0\le t\le 1.
\]
Let \(x_i(0)\) and \(v_i(0)\) denote the observed position and velocity of defender \(i\) at the evaluation frame. At each integration time, defender \(i\) targets the projected carrier position \(x_{\mathrm{bc}}(t)\). The carrier is represented as a 2D point. Let \(r_i(t)=\lVert x_{\mathrm{bc}}(t)-x_i(0)\rVert\) denote the defender’s distance to that target, and let \(u_i=\lVert v_i(0)\rVert\) be the defender’s observed initial speed.


Travel and turning time
For initial speed \(u_i\le v_{\max}\), the motion approximation uses linear acceleration \(a=a_{\mathrm{linear}}\) up to an effective speed \(v_{\max}\). Define
\[
t_a=\max\left\{\frac{v_{\max}-u_i}{a},0\right\},
\qquad
d_a=u_it_a+\frac12 at_a^2.
\]
The estimated travel time to the projected target is
\[
t_{\mathrm{move},i}(t)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\sqrt{u_i^2+2ar_i(t)}-u_i}{a}, & r_i(t)\le d_a,\\[6pt]
t_a+\dfrac{r_i(t)-d_a}{v_{\max}}, & r_i(t)>d_a.
\end{cases}
\]
If the observed initial speed exceeds \(v_{\max}\), the model retains that initial speed without additional acceleration and uses \(t_{\mathrm{move},i}(t)=r_i(t)/u_i\). Thus \(v_{\max}\) is not a hard cap on observed initial speeds.
Following Pleuler’s use of a heading-dependent turning penalty (Pleuler 2020), PRESS parameterizes the defender’s reorientation with a simplified turning delay. With turning angle \(\theta_i(t)\) in radians and turning-acceleration parameter \(a_{\mathrm{turn}}\),
\[
t_{\mathrm{turn},i}(t)=\frac{u_i\theta_i(t)}{a_{\mathrm{turn}}}.
\]
This expression follows from a turning radius \(R=u_i^2/a_{\mathrm{turn}}\) and arc time \(R\theta_i/u_i\). The implementation adds a delay but does not propagate the defender along a turning arc. The arrival-time estimate is
\[
\tau_i(t)=t_{\mathrm{move},i}(t)+t_{\mathrm{turn},i}(t).
\]
For the existing near-target convention, \(\tau_i(t)=0\) whenever \(r_i(t)\le0.1\) m. This does not imply certain reachability.

title: Ball-drive risk
text:
3. Probabilistic defender reachability
As in the pitch-control approach, deterministic arrival times are converted into a smooth reachability gate. With logistic arrival-time dispersion \(s\) (in seconds), defender \(i\) has reachability
\[
F_i(t)=\left[1+\exp\left\{-\frac{\pi\,[t-\tau_i(t)]}{\sqrt{3}\,s}\right\}\right]^{-1}.
\]
The parameter \(s\) is the standard deviation of the corresponding logistic arrival-time uncertainty. The gate increases when the defender can reach the projected carrier position sooner relative to elapsed time.

title: Ball-drive risk
text:
4. Tackle intensity

Additive spline tackle rate
The second ingredient is the instantaneous rate at which a defender who has reached the carrier can cause loss of control. Inspired by the control-rate mechanism of pitch control, PRESS assigns defender \(i\) a nonnegative tackle rate \(\lambda_i(t)\), with units s\(^{-1}\):
\[
\boxed{\log\lambda_i(t)=\alpha+g_v(\lVert v_{\mathrm{bc}}\rVert)+g_B(B(t))+g_\phi(\phi_i(t)),\qquad \alpha=\log\lambda_0.}
\]
Here \(\lambda_0\) is the baseline tackle rate, and \(g_v\), \(g_B\), \(g_\phi\) are smooth functions that scale it multiplicatively according to the carrier’s speed, the distance to the pitch boundary and the approach angle of the defender, so that \(\lambda_i(t)=\lambda_0\exp\{g_v+g_B+g_\phi\}\). As the control rate in pitch control sets how quickly a player establishes control, \(\lambda_i(t)\) sets how quickly a defender at the carrier can dispossess him. The difference is that it depends on the state of the carrier and the defender. Whether the defender can reach the carrier in time is described separately by the reachability gate \(F_i(t)\) of Section 3. The functions are additive, without interactions, and the angle contribution is masked when its direction is unavailable, as defined below. The cause-specific hazards vary with time through defender reachability and the evaluated covariates. The form of the functions, their regularization and the estimation of their parameters are described in Section 7.


Why these covariates?
Carrier speed. Schepers et al. identify movement speed as an important predictor of dribbling outcomes (Schepers et al. 2025). Greater speed can make fine ball control more difficult, increasing vulnerability to intervention. The function \(g_v\) allows the magnitude and shape of that effect to be estimated without imposing a strictly log-linear response.
Boundary proximity. Available space is a central aspect of defensive pressure, including SkillCorner’s emphasis on spatial constraints (SkillCorner 2026). Near a boundary, the carrier has fewer possible directions in which to evade an intervention. PRESS uses the signed minimum distance to all four pitch boundaries, recomputed along the projected path:
\[
B(t)=\min\!\left\{\frac L2-x_{\mathrm{bc}}(t),\frac L2+x_{\mathrm{bc}}(t),\frac W2-y_{\mathrm{bc}}(t),\frac W2+y_{\mathrm{bc}}(t)\right\}.
\]
Here \(L\) and \(W\) denote the pitch length and width. This differs from a sideline-only distance and can become negative beyond the pitch boundary.
Defender approach angle. Spatial constraints also depend on whether a defender approaches from ahead, behind, or the side. Motivated by the role of the carrier’s available field of view and escape directions in pressure interpretation, PRESS measures \(\phi_i(t)\) between carrier velocity and the defender’s predicted final approach direction. For \(r_i(t)>0.1\) m, define
\[q_i(t)=x_{\mathrm{bc}}(t)-x_i(0),\qquad
\phi_i(t)=\arccos\!\left[\frac{v_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)\cdot q_i(t)}{\lVert v_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)\rVert\,\lVert q_i(t)\rVert}\right].\]
Thus \(0\) means an approach from behind in the carrier’s direction of motion, \(\pi/2\) a lateral approach, and \(\pi\) a frontal approach. This is distinct from the defender’s turning angle \(\theta_i(t)\) in the arrival-time calculation. At distance \(r_i(t)\leq0.1\) m, the implementation substitutes the defender’s initial velocity \(v_i(0)\) for \(q_i(t)\) to define its approach direction. The angle is recomputed along the projected carrier path using only the initial observed state. It is a geometric proxy, not observed body orientation or gaze. Its contribution is masked when carrier speed is below 1 m/s or the direction is undefined.
These three covariates describe complementary mechanisms: control difficulty at speed, geometric restrictions near the pitch boundary, and the direction of defensive engagement.

title: Ball-drive risk
section: 5. From defender hazards to possession-loss probability
text:
5. From defender hazards to possession-loss probability
For each defender \(i\in\mathcal D\), where \(\mathcal D\) is the set of defenders, let \(P_i(t)\) be the probability that defender \(i\) has caused the first possession loss by time \(t\). Define \(S(t)\) as the probability that the carrier has retained possession up to time \(t\). Since the possible first-loss causes compete for the same possession,
\[
S(t)=1-\sum_{j\in\mathcal D}P_j(t).
\]
The model assigns defender \(i\) the following differential equation:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{dP_i(t)}{dt}
=\underbrace{\left[1-\sum_{j\in\mathcal D}P_j(t)\right]}_{S(t)}
\underbrace{\lambda_{\mathrm{tackle}}\!\left(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{bc}}(t),\mathbf v_{\mathrm{bc}}(t),\mathbf x_i(0),\mathbf v_i(0)\right)}_{\lambda_i(t)}
\underbrace{F_i\!\left(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{bc}}(t),t\right)}_{F_i(t)}.
}
\]
The initial conditions are \(P_i(0)=0\) for every defender and \(S(0)=1\). The reachability term \(F_i(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{bc}}(t),t)\) is the logistic gate defined above, evaluated for the moving projected carrier position. The tackle intensity is the fitted nonnegative rate described in Sections 4 and 7; its compact state-dependent notation here is shorthand for the specified speed, boundary-distance and approach-angle covariates, not an additional fitted dependence on the full position or velocity vectors. The defender state \(\mathbf x_i(0),\mathbf v_i(0)\) is observed at the evaluation frame and is not propagated as a simulated defensive trajectory.
The factor \(S(t)\) makes the causes mutually exclusive: once possession has been lost, no other defender can produce its first loss. Thus a high tackle intensity contributes little when the defender is unlikely to reach the carrier, and even a defender who can reach the carrier contributes only while possession survives.
Equivalently, defining the cause-specific hazard \(h_i(t)=\lambda_i(t)F_i(t)\) gives
\[
\frac{dS(t)}{dt}=-S(t)\sum_{i\in\mathcal D}h_i(t),
\qquad
S(t)=\exp\!\left[-\int_0^t\sum_{i\in\mathcal D}h_i(u)\,du\right].
\]
The corresponding integral form is
\[
P_i(t)=\int_0^t S(u)h_i(u)\,du,
\qquad
\boxed{P(\mathrm{loss\ by}\ t\mid\mathrm{drive})=\sum_{i\in\mathcal D}P_i(t)=1-S(t).}
\]
The one-second ball-drive risk passed to the wider PRESS framework is \(d_t=1-S(1)\), where the evaluation state is understood to be fixed at the start of the hypothetical action. Multiple defenders affect risk through their individual reachability and rates; coordinated defensive behaviour is not explicitly modelled.

title: Ball-drive risk
text:
6. Motion parameters
The model uses \(v_{\max}=7\) m/s and \(a_{\mathrm{linear}}=a_{\mathrm{turn}}=7\) m/s\(^2\). These are effective common movement capabilities, motivated by published models and checked against the tracking distribution.








Parameter
Literature rationale
Tracking consistency check




Defender speed \(v_{\max}=7\) m/s
Approximately the 25.1 km/h sprint threshold in Bradley et al. (Bradley et al. 2009).
Defensive-engagement event frames with speed \(>2\) m/s: Q95 = 7.050 m/s.


Linear acceleration \(a_{\mathrm{linear}}=7\) m/s\(^2\)
The acceleration used by Spearman’s movement model (Spearman 2018).
Engagement acceleration peaks above 3 m/s\(^2\): Q99 = 6.966 m/s\(^2\).


Turning acceleration \(a_{\mathrm{turn}}=7\) m/s\(^2\)
A heading-dependent delay follows the idea in Pleuler (Pleuler 2020); PRESS sets its scale equal to the linear-acceleration parameter.
Equality with linear acceleration is a modelling convention; it is not separately identified by these quantiles.



The speed filter removes stationary/walking observations for this descriptive check. These conditional quantiles are consistency checks for rounded model scales, not physiological ceilings or independently estimated caps. Event-frame observations and event peaks use different sampling units. The speed audit, engagement quantiles and kinematic conventions provide the definitions and sources.
Positions and velocities enter the model directly; observed acceleration is not an input. The current velocities use the offline centred seven-frame tracking estimate.

title: Ball-drive risk
section: 7. Specification, likelihood, priors and parameter estimation
text:
7. Specification, likelihood, priors and parameter estimation

Form of the tackle-rate functions
Each effect in Section 4 is the sum of a linear term and a nonlinear component built on restricted cubic splines. With \(b_{jk}\) the nonlinear basis functions of covariate \(j\),
\[g_v(v)=\beta_v v+\sum_{k=1}^{3}\gamma_{vk}b_{vk}(v),\qquad
g_B(B)=\beta_B B+\sum_{k=1}^{3}\gamma_{Bk}b_{Bk}(B),\]
\[g_\phi(\phi)=\beta_\phi z_\phi(\phi)+\sum_{k=1}^{2}\gamma_{\phi k}b_{\phi k}(\phi),\qquad z_\phi(\phi)=\frac{\phi-\mu_\phi}{\sigma_\phi},\]
where \(\mu_\phi\) and \(\sigma_\phi\) are the mean and standard deviation of the angle over valid directions in the fitting data. Knots are placed at equally spaced empirical quantiles of the fitting data. The bases have linear tails beyond the boundary knots and do not impose monotonicity, and further mathematical details on their construction and on the curvature penalty are in the appendix on the spline basis.
The covariates are split into two blocks with a different complexity budget. The carrier block, speed and boundary distance, is the main description of carrier vulnerability, in line with Schepers et al. (Schepers et al. 2025), and receives a moderately flexible basis, with five knots and three nonlinear components per covariate, and one shared smoothing multiplier \(\rho_{\mathrm{bc}}\) (bc for ball carrier). The engagement block, the approach angle, is a geometric complement and receives a slightly smaller basis, with four knots and two nonlinear components, and its own multiplier \(\rho_\phi\). Sharing the multiplier within the carrier block contains the search over smoothing strengths, and the separate multiplier controls the new component. The basis functions, penalty matrices and coefficients of speed and boundary remain distinct, so the shared multiplier does not force the two effects to have the same shape. The additive structure, without interactions between covariates, serves the same purpose of moderating the complexity of the specification.
These are constraints of an exploratory specification. They are not presented as the only correct choices, and four knots for the angle are not claimed to be necessary. The performance of the specification is evaluated with the protocol documented in the benchmark.


Likelihood: the outcome of a one-second carry
For carry \(j\), let \(Y_j=1\) denote a loss and \(Y_j=0\) successful retention over the canonical horizon. Given the observed initial state and parameters \(\theta\), the competing-risk model supplies
\[d_j(\theta)=1-S_j(1;\theta).\]
The probability \(d_j(\theta)\) depends on the spline coefficients through the defender-specific tackle rates. For defender \(i\) in carry \(j\),
\[
\lambda_{ij}(t;\theta)=\exp\!\left\{\alpha+g_v(\lVert v_{\mathrm{bc},j}\rVert)+g_B(B_j(t))+g_\phi(\phi_{ij}(t))\right\},
\]
where the angle contribution is masked when unavailable. Combined with the reachability gate, these rates determine the survival probability:
\[
S_j(1;\theta)=\exp\!\left[-\int_0^1\sum_{i\in\mathcal D_j}\lambda_{ij}(t;\theta)F_{ij}(t;s)\,dt\right].
\]
The outcome likelihood is Bernoulli:
\[\boxed{\mathcal L(\theta;D)=\prod_j
d_j(\theta)^{Y_j}\,[1-d_j(\theta)]^{1-Y_j}.}\]
Equivalently,
\[\log\mathcal L=\sum_j\left\{Y_j\log[1-S_j(1)]+(1-Y_j)\log S_j(1)\right\}.\]
A loss before one second contributes \(1-S_j(1)\): its observed failure time does not shorten the forecast horizon. A successful full second contributes \(S_j(1)\). The fit learns which initial configurations make the one-second outcome more or less likely; it does not fit the exact tackle time or the observed tackler’s identity.


Priors
The linear parameters have independent standard normal priors,
\[\alpha\sim\mathcal N(0,1),\qquad
\beta_v,\ \beta_B\sim\mathcal N(0,1),\qquad
\beta_\phi\sim\mathcal N(0,1).\]
The scale of the linear terms defines the meaning of these priors. The priors on \(\beta_v\) and \(\beta_B\), which refer to speed in m/s and boundary distance in m, are motivated by preliminary tests with a log-linear model in the original units, which gave values compatible with a standard Gaussian. For the angle, which was added later, the prior is placed on the effect of one standard deviation, which normalizes its scale. This is statistically legitimate, since the covariates do not need a common standardization. Thus \(\lambda_0=e^{\alpha}\) has a lognormal prior with log-location 0 and log-SD 1.
The arrival dispersion has a Gamma prior,
\[\boxed{s\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\text{shape}=2.5,\ \text{rate}=5).}\]
It keeps \(s\) positive, has mean 0.5 s and SD 0.316 s, and places it on the same broad time scale as the arrival dispersion in Spearman’s models (Spearman et al. 2017; Spearman 2018). These exact prior choices belong to PRESS. The priors on the nonlinear spline coefficients follow from the curvature penalty described next.


Smoothing penalty
The nonlinear coefficients \(\boldsymbol\gamma_j\) are regularized by a curvature penalty, \(\frac{\rho_j}{2}\boldsymbol\gamma_j^\top\Omega_j\boldsymbol\gamma_j\), where \(\Omega_j\) is the normalized curvature penalty matrix of the basis and \(\rho_j\) controls the regularization. It discourages unnecessary curvature without constraining the direction of the fitted effect, and it applies only to the nonlinear coefficients, while the linear coefficients have the priors above. With \(\rho_v=\rho_B=\rho_{\mathrm{bc}}\) and \(\rho_\phi\) separate, the complete nonlinear penalty is
\[\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{bc}}}{2}\left(
\boldsymbol\gamma_v^\top\Omega_v\boldsymbol\gamma_v+
\boldsymbol\gamma_B^\top\Omega_B\boldsymbol\gamma_B\right)
+\frac{\rho_\phi}{2}\boldsymbol\gamma_\phi^\top\Omega_\phi\boldsymbol\gamma_\phi.\]
The penalty corresponds to a zero-centred Gaussian prior on each coefficient vector with precision \(\rho_j\Omega_j\),
\[p(\boldsymbol\gamma_j\mid\rho_j)\propto\exp\!\left(-\frac{\rho_j}{2}\boldsymbol\gamma_j^\top\Omega_j\boldsymbol\gamma_j\right).\]
The multipliers are selected by cross-validation and then held fixed, and no hyperprior is placed on them. The deployed model uses \(\rho_{\mathrm{bc}}=1\) and \(\rho_\phi=100\). The grid explored and the selection procedure are described in the benchmark.


MAP estimation
The posterior combines the one-second likelihood with these priors,
\[p(\theta\mid D)\propto\mathcal L(\theta;D)\,p(\theta).\]
Optimization uses \(\ell=\log s\), so the prior density of \(\ell\) includes the transformation Jacobian, \(p_\ell(\ell)=p_s(e^\ell)e^\ell\propto\exp\{2.5\ell-5e^\ell\}\). With the smoothing multipliers held fixed, the negative log posterior is, up to constants,
\[
\mathcal J(\theta)=-\log\mathcal L(\theta;D)+\tfrac12\left(\alpha^2+\beta_v^2+\beta_B^2+\beta_\phi^2\right)+5e^\ell-2.5\ell+\tfrac12\sum_{j\in\{v,B,\phi\}}\rho_j\boldsymbol\gamma_j^\top\Omega_j\boldsymbol\gamma_j.
\]
The full parameter vector, including the baseline tackle rate, arrival dispersion and spline coefficients, is estimated jointly by maximum a posteriori (MAP) optimization. The objective is minimized with L-BFGS-B, with gradients obtained by automatic differentiation, and the optimization procedure is described in the benchmark. The resulting point estimates parameterize the model distributed with PRESS, and predictions are not averaged over posterior draws.
The joint MAP fit on the complete development cohort gives an arrival-time dispersion of \(s=0.299632\) s and a baseline tackle rate of \(\lambda_0=0.344563\) s\(^{-1}\). These are fitted parameters of the deployed model.
The dispersion parameter is model-specific. Spearman’s pass model reports 0.45 s, while a later OBSO formulation reports a MAP estimate of 0.54 s under a different estimation setup (Spearman et al. 2017; Spearman 2018). These values give context for the magnitude of \(s\) and are not a like-for-like comparison. The pass-probability vignette discusses its independently fitted arrival parameter.
Posterior covariance is estimated with a local Laplace approximation: the joint posterior in the fitted log-scale/coefficient coordinates is approximated by a Gaussian at the MAP, with covariance
\[\widehat\Sigma=\left[\nabla^2_{\theta}\{-\log p(\theta\mid D)\}\big|_{\hat\theta}\right]^{-1}.\]
This uses the full joint Hessian, including the priors and spline penalties. Approximate marginal variances and intervals are conditional on the selected smoothing strengths and model specification, and they differ from fold-to-fold variability. Numerical summaries are reported in the benchmark.


Fitted spline curves
The conditional spline curves illustrate how the fitted tackle rate varies with the three covariates before multiplication by defender reachability.



Conditional tackle-rate curves from the bundled MAP fit. Each panel varies one covariate, holding the others at the values shown above it. Rates are shown before multiplication by defender reachability. The speed panel starts at 1 m/s, where the angle term is active.


In the fitted curves, tackle intensity increases with carrier speed, in line with the dribbling literature (Schepers et al. 2025), decreases with distance from the boundary, and increases as the approach angle grows. A plausible reading is that higher speed leaves the carrier with less control over the ball and less time to react to a challenge, while proximity to the boundary reduces the space available to evade a defender and leaves less margin for error. The angle effect is consistent with the geometry of the encounter: a defender arriving from behind must first close the gap and then reach the ball, whereas one engaging frontally meets the carrier along the direction of travel. All three effects agree with the physical arrival model, in which speed, space and relative geometry shape the interception opportunities of defenders.
The ball-drive benchmark documents regularization selection, posterior uncertainty, cross-validation results, comparisons of predictive performance and the evaluation limits.

title: Ball-drive risk
text:
8. Real-match examples
The examples apply the pretrained model to two frames of SkillCorner open data. Set SKILLCORNER_OPENDATA to your local open-data repository (Data setup). For each case, compute_ball_drive_risk evaluates the one-second drive risk \(d_t\) at the starting frame, plot_ball_drive_risk draws the pitch at that frame and plot_frame shows a later frame after the observed loss.
In the first figure of each case, the colours show each defender’s share of the total loss risk, and the title reports the absolute probability \(d_t\).

Melbourne Victory–Auckland
D. Arzani loses possession, followed by an Auckland recovery by F. Gallegos.

from pathlib import Path
import os
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PRESS import PRESS
