title: Pass selection benchmark
text:
7. Discussion and limitations
The flat multinomial logit lowers the cross-entropy by 34.3% relative to the uniform-choice reference (5.827787 against 8.873286), using information available at the decision: pass geometry, pitch control, expected threat, pressure lines, ball-drive risk and match context. The temperature fitted in each fold is close to one, which suggests that the raw choice probabilities are already close to calibrated on the validation pair, and temperature scaling changes cross-entropy only marginally. The nested specification gave only a small gain over the flat model, so the flat model is deployed for its simplicity and the CNL is kept as an exploratory alternative. A plausible explanation is that the predictors (pass geometry, raw pitch control and the other contextual features) are already informative and that XGBoost uses them flexibly, which leaves little for the nest structure to add. The CNL evaluated here has one dissimilarity parameter shared by all nests and memberships fixed by individual pitch control, so the comparison covers this specific nesting structure.
Hyperparameter screening compares five configurations per model family on a single development partition. The computational cost of boosting over the full candidate grid limits the search to this size and to a single partition. Early stopping and temperature scaling share the same two validation matches within each fold. The evaluation covers ten matches from a single competition and season, and the comparison with Fernández et al. is reported as context because dataset, split and candidate grid differ. Generalization to other competitions, tracking providers and annotation conventions remains to be assessed.
Unsuccessful passes enter the training data with their recovery location as the observed destination. This location is a proxy for the intended destination and may be an interception point away from the intended destination. If so, the model assigns probability to regions that are contested more often than the intended destinations are, and the resulting distribution leans towards riskier destinations. This explanation remains to be tested; a direct check would refit the choice model on completed passes only and compare the downstream results.

title: Pass selection benchmark
text:
8. Supplementary resources
For reproducibility, the screening table, pooled metrics, fold summaries, per-match results , feature-importance summaries and installed artifact provenance are provided as supplementary resources.

title: Expected threat benchmark
text:
Model and example · All benchmarks
The xT benchmark documents the training of the expected-threat surface and the selection of its grid resolution and smoothing bandwidths. The model vignette introduces the value equation, the fitted surface and its use in PRESS. This benchmark describes the event cohort, the training procedure and the selection, which relies on leave-one-match-out validation of the destination and goal-given-shot components.

title: Expected threat benchmark
text:
1. Evaluation cohort
The production surface uses the archived event tables from all ten matches: 9,071 within-possession displacements, 6,355 completed passes, 212 shots (23 goals) and 2,214 terminal losses. A displacement records movement from the matched start to the matched end of individual control, and is distinct from the canonical one-second carries of the ball-drive classifier. Passes connect release to matched reception. Shot and loss locations use the end of individual control. Coordinates are oriented so the team in possession attacks from left to right.
These counts come from the archived event cohort, which is more permissive than the verified pass-probability cohort: it includes goalkeeper passers and passes later excluded there by the association and flight-duration checks, and it covers the completions whose origin and destination fall inside the fixed 105 × 68 m grid.
The components scored in the selection are the pass-destination, carry-destination and goal-given-shot estimates. The goal-given-shot component is the sparsest and rarest of them and is the one used to compare grid resolutions.

title: Expected threat benchmark
text:
2. Training procedure
The fit proceeds in four steps. The event frequencies \(p_{a,i}\) are computed from the counts without smoothing. The destination distributions \(T\) and the goal probability \(p_{\mathrm{goal}}\) are estimated from smoothed counts. The smoothing bandwidths are selected by leave-one-match-out validation, as described in Smoothing bandwidth selection. Finally, the value equation is iterated to convergence.

What is smoothed
Gaussian smoothing is applied to the destination distributions and to the goal probability given a shot. In the formulas below, \(\varepsilon=10^{-8}\) is a small numerical constant.

Destination distributions. For each fixed origin \(i\), the destination-count field \(N^a_{ij}\) is smoothed over neighbouring destination cells \(j\), separately for passes and carries. The smoothed counts are then normalized:
\[
T^a_{ij}=\frac{\widetilde N^a_{ij}+\varepsilon}
{\sum_k(\widetilde N^a_{ik}+\varepsilon)},
\qquad \widetilde N^a_{i\cdot}=K_{h_a}*N^a_{i\cdot}.
\]
Smoothing acts over destination cells, for each fixed origin. An origin with no observed transitions has a uniform destination row.
Goal probability given a shot. The spatial goal counts \(G_i\) and shot counts \(S_i\) are smoothed separately, then divided:
\[
p_{\mathrm{goal},i}=\frac{(K_{h_g}*G)_i}{(K_{h_g}*S)_i+\varepsilon}.
\]

The four event frequencies \(p_{a,i}=n_{a,i}/n_i\) are computed directly from the counts. Bandwidths \(h\) are expressed in metres; the Gaussian standard deviations in grid units are \(h/\Delta x\) and \(h/\Delta y\).


Value iteration
The iteration of the value equation starts at zero and stops when the maximum change is below \(10^{-12}\).

title: Expected threat benchmark
text:
3. Smoothing bandwidth selection
The smoothing bandwidth of each component (pass destinations, carry destinations and goal given shot) is selected by leave-one-match-out validation on the matches available for fitting. Whole matches are held out, so that each held-out set plays the role of a new match. The candidates are 0, 3, 5, 8, 12 and 18 m, where zero means no Gaussian smoothing. For a set of \(M\) matches the procedure is:

Rotation. Each match is held out in turn. The component is estimated on the other \(M-1\) matches and scored on the held-out match. The score is the negative log-density of the observed destination for passes and carries, and the Bernoulli cross-entropy of the outcome for shots.
Pooling. The \(M\) rotation scores of each candidate are combined with weights proportional to the number of events in the held-out match.
Uncertainty. A delete-one-match jackknife of the paired score differences between each candidate and the best one gives the standard error of each difference.
Choice. The largest bandwidth whose score lies within one standard error of the best is retained, so that the rule favours the stronger smoothing.

The same procedure is applied at three levels, which differ in the number \(M\) of matches that supply the fit.

Held-out matches therefore never enter the selection, and each fold map uses the bandwidths selected in its own fold.

title: Expected threat benchmark
text:
4. Grid resolution
Binning determines the spatial resolution of the fitted value function. Smaller bins preserve more local variation but provide fewer events per cell and sparser transition estimates; larger bins stabilize estimates but can obscure meaningful spatial structure. Smoothing can reduce sampling noise, at the cost of spatial detail.
The grid is chosen among four resolutions (8 × 5, 10 × 6, 12 × 8 and 16 × 12) on the event cohort of the ten matches. This is a second validation layer, built around the bandwidth selection above. The matches are divided into five outer folds, each with eight development and two test matches, and the test matches are disjoint across folds. For each resolution, every fold proceeds as follows:

The bandwidths are selected on the eight development matches with the rule above (7 + 1 rotations).
xT is refitted on the development matches with these bandwidths fixed.
The goal-given-shot component, the sparsest and rarest one, is scored on the two test matches.

The out-of-fold scores are pooled with shot-weighted averages. A delete-one-match jackknife of the shot-weighted paired differences, with the out-of-fold predictions held fixed, gives the standard error of each resolution against 10 × 6. Among the resolutions within one standard error of the best, the coarsest is retained, which favours lower complexity. Positive ΔCE indicates worse performance than 10 × 6.

The production surface is fitted on all ten matches with a 10 × 6 grid and the bandwidths selected at the production level (8 m passes, 5 m carries, 5 m goal given shot). title: Appendix: construction of the restricted cubic spline bases
text: This appendix describes the change of basis used for the nonlinear effects in the ball-drive risk model. The construction separates the constant and linear components, improves the empirical scaling and conditioning of each nonlinear block, and diagonalizes its curvature penalty. The resulting penalty can be expressed through independent Gaussian priors on the transformed coefficients. The benchmark describes the selection of the smoothing strengths.

title: Appendix: construction of the restricted cubic spline bases
text:
1. Normalization and knots
For one covariate \(x\), let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) be the fitting values. Normalize them using their fitting-set range,
\[
z_i=\frac{x_i-x_{\min}}{x_{\max}-x_{\min}}.
\]
The \(K\) knots \(\kappa_1<\cdots<\kappa_K\) are empirical quantiles of \(z\). PRESS uses \(K=5\) for carrier speed and boundary distance, and \(K=4\) for the approach angle. The quantile levels are \(0,1/4,1/2,3/4,1\) and \(0,1/3,2/3,1\), respectively, so \(\kappa_1=0\) and \(\kappa_K=1\). There are \(q=K-2\) nonlinear basis functions: three for speed and boundary distance, and two for angle.
All knots, normalizations and transformations below are determined from the fitting data and reused for new observations. Angle values are restricted to observations with a valid direction.

title: Appendix: construction of the restricted cubic spline bases
text:
2. Restricted cubic basis
Define \(t_j(z)=(z-\kappa_j)_+^3\), where \((u)_+=\max(u,0)\). For \(j=1,\ldots,K-2\), let
\[
c_j(z)=t_j(z)
-\frac{\kappa_K-\kappa_j}{\kappa_K-\kappa_{K-1}}\,t_{K-1}(z)
+\frac{\kappa_{K-1}-\kappa_j}{\kappa_K-\kappa_{K-1}}\,t_K(z).
\]
These combinations are piecewise cubic between knots and linear beyond the boundary knots. A general function in the spline space can be written as
\[
f(z)=a_0+a_1z+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\delta_jc_j(z).
\]
Here \(\boldsymbol\delta\) denotes coefficients in the raw basis; \(\boldsymbol\gamma\) below denotes coefficients in the final transformed basis. The change of basis preserves the represented spline space when the constant and linear components are retained separately.
This is a generic representation in the normalized coordinate \(z\); the fitted linear speed and boundary terms retain the original covariate units, as detailed below.

title: Appendix: construction of the restricted cubic spline bases
section: 3. Orthogonalization against the constant and linear terms
text:
3. Orthogonalization against the constant and linear terms
Let \(C_{ij}=c_j(z_i)\) and \(L=[\mathbf 1,z]\). Remove the least-squares projection onto the constant and linear design,
\[
A=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_A\|C-LA\|_F^2,
\qquad E=C-LA,
\qquad L^\top E=0.
\]
For full-column-rank \(L\),
\[
A=(L^\top L)^{-1}L^\top C.
\]
Thus, \(E\) represents nonlinear deviations that are empirically orthogonal to the separate constant and linear terms. Separating linear and nonlinear components is a standard motivation for reparameterizing penalized spline effects; see Scheipl, Fahrmeir, and Kneib (2012, sec. 2.1). The matrix \(A\) is retained for evaluating the same transformation on new observations.
Since \(x=x_{\min}+(x_{\max}-x_{\min})z\), the designs \([\mathbf 1,x]\) and \([\mathbf 1,z]\) span the same space. Residualization against \([\mathbf 1,z]\) therefore also removes the projection onto a linear effect expressed in the original units of \(x\).

title: Appendix: construction of the restricted cubic spline bases
text:
4. Empirical whitening
The Gram matrix of the residualized basis is
\[
G=\frac{E^\top E}{n}.
\]
Assuming \(G\) is positive definite, write \(G=U\Lambda U^\top\) and define
\[
W=U\Lambda^{-1/2},
\qquad E_w=EW.
\]
Then
\[
\frac1n E_w^\top E_w
=W^\top GW
=I_q.
\]
The columns are orthonormal under the empirical inner product on the fitting set. Because they are already centered by the projection onto \(L\), they also have unit empirical variance. This removes scale differences and empirical correlations within the nonlinear block, improving its numerical conditioning. It is the PCA-whitening transformation written for observations arranged in rows (Kessy, Lewin, and Strimmer 2018).

title: Appendix: construction of the restricted cubic spline bases
text:
5. Curvature penalty and rotation
Define the curvature matrix with derivatives taken with respect to the normalized coordinate \(z\),
\[
R_{jk}=\int_0^1 c_j''(z)c_k''(z)\,dz.
\]
Subtracting a constant and a linear function leaves second derivatives unchanged, so residualization does not change this curvature matrix. The second derivatives \(c_j''\) vanish outside \([\kappa_1,\kappa_K]=[0,1]\), so the integral over \([0,1]\) covers the whole line. The integral is evaluated over consecutive knot intervals. Within each interval the second derivatives are linear and their products are quadratic; two-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature therefore evaluates these integrals exactly, apart from floating-point rounding.
Diagonalize the penalty in the whitened coordinates,
\[
W^\top RW
=V\operatorname{diag}(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_q)V^\top,
\qquad V^\top V=I_q.
\]
Set \(T=WV\). The final basis is \(\widetilde E=ET\) and satisfies
\[
\frac1n\widetilde E^\top\widetilde E=I_q,
\qquad
T^\top RT=\operatorname{diag}(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_q).
\]
With the row vector \(\boldsymbol c(z)=[c_1(z),\ldots,c_q(z)]\), the final basis functions evaluated at \(z\) are
\[
\widetilde{\boldsymbol c}(z)=\bigl[\boldsymbol c(z)-[1,z]A\bigr]T,
\]
and the nonlinear component of the covariate effect is \(f_{\mathrm{nonlinear}}(z)=\widetilde{\boldsymbol c}(z)\boldsymbol\gamma\), where \(\boldsymbol\gamma\) are the coefficients in the final basis. The components of \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol c}(z)\) are the nonlinear basis functions \(b_{jk}\) of the model vignette, for covariate \(j\). The rotation preserves empirical orthonormality while making the curvature penalty diagonal. This is a Demmler–Reinsch-type change of basis (Demmler and Reinsch 1975); an explicit matrix derivation of simultaneous design and penalty diagonalization is also given by Lang et al. (2012, sec. 4).

title: Appendix: construction of the restricted cubic spline bases
section: 6. Independent Gaussian priors in the transformed basis
text:
6. Independent Gaussian priors in the transformed basis
For nonlinear coefficients \(\boldsymbol\gamma\) in the final basis, the integrated squared curvature is
\[
\int_0^1\left[f_{\mathrm{nonlinear}}''(z)\right]^2\,dz
=\boldsymbol\gamma^\top T^\top RT\boldsymbol\gamma
=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\eta_j\gamma_j^2.
\]
PRESS normalizes the eigenvalues by their minimum,
\[
\omega_j=\frac{\eta_j}{\min_k\eta_k},
\qquad \Omega=\operatorname{diag}(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_q).
\]
For a fixed smoothing strength \(\rho>0\), this gives the independent Gaussian priors
\[
\gamma_j\sim\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac1{\rho\omega_j}\right),
\]
with negative log density
\[
-\log p(\boldsymbol\gamma\mid\rho)
=\frac{\rho}{2}\boldsymbol\gamma^\top\Omega\boldsymbol\gamma
+\text{constant}
=\frac{\rho}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{q}\omega_j\gamma_j^2
+\text{constant}.
\]
The constant is independent of \(\boldsymbol\gamma\) for fixed \(\rho\) and basis. Directions with greater curvature receive stronger shrinkage. Dividing by the smallest eigenvalue is a normalization convention: it rescales the overall curvature penalty while preserving its relative weights. The diagonal representation simplifies the prior specification, and the coefficients remain dependent in the posterior.

title: Appendix: construction of the restricted cubic spline bases
section: 7. Linear terms in the original units
text:
7. Linear terms in the original units
In the fitted PRESS model, the carrier effects are parameterized as
\[
g_v(v_{\mathrm{bc}})=\beta_v v_{\mathrm{bc}}
+\widetilde{\boldsymbol c}_v(z_v)\boldsymbol\gamma_v,
\qquad
g_B(B)=\beta_B B
+\widetilde{\boldsymbol c}_B(z_B)\boldsymbol\gamma_B.
\]
Thus, \(\beta_v\) multiplies speed in m/s and \(\beta_B\) multiplies boundary distance in m; min–max normalization is used internally for the nonlinear bases. The intercept \(\alpha=\log\lambda_0\) remains a separate model parameter. The priors and preset initial values motivated by the preliminary log-linear model refer to these original-unit linear coefficients.
For comparison, after the nonlinear change of basis, the same one-covariate function could be written in either coordinate as
\[
\alpha_x+\beta_x x+\widetilde{\boldsymbol c}(z)\boldsymbol\gamma
=a_0^*+a_1^*z+\widetilde{\boldsymbol c}(z)\boldsymbol\gamma,
\]
where \(a_0^*=\alpha_x+\beta_x x_{\min}\) and \(a_1^*=\beta_x(x_{\max}-x_{\min})\). These are equivalent functions with different linear coefficients. Preserving the prior under this reparameterization would require transforming its joint distribution as well; independent standard normal priors on \(a_0^*\) and \(a_1^*\) would define a different prior. PRESS retains the original-unit parameterization for speed and boundary distance. The linear approach-angle term is treated separately: it multiplies the angle standardized by its fitting-set mean and standard deviation, as specified in the model vignette.

title: Appendix: construction of the restricted cubic spline bases
text:
8. Evaluation on new observations
For a new value \(x\), use the fitting-set normalization \(z=(x-x_{\min})/(x_{\max}-x_{\min})\) and evaluate \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol c}(z)\) as defined in Section 5. The fitting-set matrices \(A\) and \(T\) are unchanged. Orthogonality and unit empirical variance hold on the fitting set and can differ on a different sample. Values outside the fitting range are evaluated using the spline’s linear tails.

title: Appendix: construction of the restricted cubic spline bases
text:
References


Demmler, A., and C. Reinsch. 1975. “Oscillation Matrices with Spline Smoothing.” Numerische Mathematik 24 (5): 375–82. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01437406.


Kessy, Agnan, Alex Lewin, and Korbinian Strimmer. 2018. “Optimal Whitening and Decorrelation.” The American Statistician 72 (4): 309–14. https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2016.1277159.


Lang, Stefan, Nikolaus Umlauf, Peter Wechselberger, Kenneth Harttgen, and Thomas Kneib. 2012. “Multilevel Structured Additive Regression.” Working Papers in Economics and Statistics 2012-07. University of Innsbruck. https://www2.uibk.ac.at/downloads/c4041030/wpaper/2012-07.pdf.


Scheipl, Fabian, Ludwig Fahrmeir, and Thomas Kneib. 2012. “Spike-and-Slab Priors for Function Selection in Structured Additive Regression Models.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 107 (500): 1518–32. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2012.737742.

title: Benchmarks
text:
The PRESS benchmarks evaluate five modeling tasks, and the predictions composed from them, under a common match-level cross-validation protocol. This page describes the dataset, the two model families, the shared evaluation design and the performance metrics. Each task-specific benchmark reports its cohort, its model-specific training and calibration choices and its predictive results.
Research pipeline and source download · Project roadmap

title: Benchmarks
text:
1. Dataset overview
The benchmarks use ten A-League 2024/25 matches from SkillCorner Open Data (SkillCorner, n.d.). All component benchmarks concern outfield ball carriers. Reliability is checked at the temporal boundaries needed for the target. Two data-preparation branches share these principles: possession-based tasks use matched individual-control intervals, whereas pass tasks use matched release and the immediate next reception/recovery start. The matching with tracking data relies on the SkillCorner event labels, as described in Dataset and preprocessing.
For the possession branch used by ball-drive, action-selection and residual-risk training, the frozen preparation audit starts from 9,566 raw individual possessions. A possession is kept when its individual-control interval is matched with tracking data at both boundaries, its terminal event and outcome supply a supported component label, its carrier is an outfield player and it does not end in a shot. These criteria leave 8,451 possessions.
These are parent-possession counts before task segmentation (see Possessions and checkpoints). Individual tasks then select the actions and verified outcomes required by their target, and their benchmark pages give the task-specific criteria and the resulting cohort sizes. Features and predictions can still be computed for states outside these training populations. Effective exclusion counts and source-audit provenance.

Verified pass links
Pass-outcome verification links the matched release to the matched start of the immediate next individual possession, in the same match and period. The next control must follow release, with no intervening annotated interruption and complete observed ball XY over the interval. A completion requires the identified recipient to be the next carrier of the same team, with a matched reception; a failure requires an accepted opponent interception or recovery. The recovery location supplies the destination proxy for a failed pass. Only the matched release and the matched start of the next possession are required.
These checks establish the outcome and endpoint needed by the pass models. Flight-duration limits and the observations needed for trajectory fitting are task-specific and are stated in the corresponding benchmarks. Possession-based tasks additionally specify whether a failed verification excludes an entire parent possession or only an observation. Definitions of actions, checkpoints and contextual labels are centralized in Possession segmentation and context.

title: Benchmarks
text:
2. Model families
The tasks use two model architectures, which are developed and evaluated differently.
Physical models with estimated parameters. Ball-drive risk and pass probability have an explicit physical structure, and only a small number of parameters is learned from data by maximizing a likelihood. Model-selection choices, such as the strength of spline regularization, are few and are made on inner validation splits. The model produces probabilities directly, and any post-hoc calibration step is described in the task benchmark.
Gradient-boosted tree models. Pass selection, action selection and residual risk are XGBoost models trained on feature sets that include the outputs of upstream models. Their hyperparameters and number of trees are selected on a validation pair of matches by early stopping, and a probability calibration can be fitted afterwards.
The composed risk (h and xLoss) combines the predictions of the components.

Component notation
The model pages use the same component symbols when passing predictions between tasks. All quantities below are conditioned on the current state \(s\).







Symbol
Meaning




\(q(s)\)
Probability of choosing a pass; \(1-q(s)\) is the carry-choice probability


\(\pi_j(s)\)
Probability of destination \(j\), given a pass attempt


\(C_{\mathrm{att}}\)
Raw attacking-team pitch control, before pass-probability calibration


\(p_j(s)\)
Probability of completing a pass to destination \(j\)


\(d(s)\)
Loss probability during a canonical one-second carry


\(r(s)\)
Terminal individual-possession loss probability conditional on a successful current carry


\(h(s)\)
Current canonical-action loss probability, marginalized over choice and pass destination


\(\mathrm{xLoss}(s)\)
Terminal individual-possession loss probability, including the residual continuation

title: Benchmarks
text:
3. Common evaluation protocol

Shared outer match folds
All five tasks use the same partition of the ten matches into five outer folds. Each fold holds out two complete matches and uses the remaining eight for development. The five test pairs are disjoint: every match, and every eligible observation for a task, contributes to the pooled test evaluation once. Task cohorts differ according to the target and the reliability checks required to observe it.
6 + 2 + 2 describes match roles. The two model families follow different development procedures within each outer fold:








Model family
Development procedure within each outer fold
Model evaluated on the two test matches




Physical models
Four disjoint 6-fitting + 2-validation rotations within the eight development matches, used to select regularization or to produce cross-fitted scores for calibration
Parameters refitted on all eight development matches


Tree models
One fixed 6-fitting + 2-validation split, used for hyperparameter selection, early stopping and any calibration
The six-match tree fit at the selected checkpoint



For the tree models, the two validation matches remain fixed throughout that fold’s search, early stopping and any calibration. The pair can change between outer folds because test matches must be excluded. The task benchmarks give the exact procedure of each task.


Hyperparameters, early stopping and probability calibration
For XGBoost, a hyperparameter configuration is trained on the six fitting matches, and its uncalibrated validation cross-entropy selects the tree prefix by early stopping. Where a grid is used, the best configuration is selected by this same native validation criterion. Numerical XGBoost predictors are used without standardization, and the categorical vocabulary and encoding are learned from fitting matches only.
Any temperature scaling is fitted after configuration/checkpoint selection. It minimizes validation choice or binary negative log-likelihood, with trees, selected hyperparameters and stopping point held fixed. The same two validation matches are reused for this calibration, so selection and calibration share the validation pair. Only after these choices are frozen is the corresponding outer-test score computed.


Features and dependent models
Some tasks use the outputs of upstream models as features. For a given outer fold, the upstream models are fitted on that fold’s fitting matches only, and the full-ten-match versions are used only for deployment. Snapshot quantities that require no learned parameters can be shared across folds, while model-dependent features have a separate version for each fold. Verified caches are reused with their fold-specific predictions, and full-data deployment weights enter only the deployment.
The validation pair supports both upstream calibration and downstream selection where those components are required. Fitting-row features can therefore be in-sample with respect to upstream models, so cross-fitting and independent validation apply layer by layer. Each task benchmark states which layers are refitted and which remain frozen.


Aggregation and performance metrics
Cross-validated performance is computed on the concatenation of the five outer-fold held-out prediction sets. Each observation contributes once to the pooled evaluation. Fold-level results serve to inspect stability, and the pooled estimates are the reported ones.
For the binary-outcome tasks, with observed labels \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) and predicted probabilities \(p_i\), the primary probabilistic metric is binary cross-entropy (CE), also called log loss:
\[
\mathrm{CE}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right].
\]
A task-specific null model supplies a reference cross-entropy \(\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{null}}\), estimated without the outer test labels and defined in each benchmark where needed. The relative improvement over the reference is
\[
\mathrm{Gain}=1-\frac{\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{model}}}{\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{null}}},
\]
and a positive gain indicates lower cross-entropy than the null model.
The Brier score is the mean squared probabilistic error:
\[
\mathrm{Brier}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(p_i-y_i)^2.
\]
Calibration is summarized with the expected calibration error (ECE). Held-out predictions are divided into ten approximately equal-count quantile bins. For bin \(b\), let \(n_b\) be its number of observations, \(\bar p_b\) its mean prediction and \(\bar y_b\) its observed event frequency. Then
\[
\mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^{10}\frac{n_b}{N}\left|\bar p_b-\bar y_b\right|.
\]
Calibration plots compare observed event frequencies with mean predicted probabilities in these bins, and ECE and the bins are recomputed on the pooled outer-test predictions. Where relevant, ROC AUC assesses ranking across classes, and precision–recall AUC (PR AUC) summarizes discrimination for the positive class, particularly when outcomes are uncommon. Not every metric applies to or is reported for every task. Task-specific numerical conventions, including any probability clipping used for log loss, are recorded alongside the corresponding results.
Multiple-choice tasks are evaluated with the likelihood assigned to the observed choice among the available alternatives, and the improvement over a task-specific null choice model is summarized by McFadden’s pseudo-\(R^2\):
\[
R^2_{\mathrm{McFadden}}=1-\frac{\log L_{\mathrm{model}}}{\log L_{\mathrm{null}}},
\]
where \(L_{\mathrm{model}}\) and \(L_{\mathrm{null}}\) are the likelihoods of the observed choices under the fitted and null models, evaluated on the held-out observations. The task benchmark specifies its choice set and null model, and the nested cross-validation and the pooling of held-out predictions are unchanged.


Model stability and final refitting
The cross-validation results evaluate predictive performance and stability across the outer folds before a specification is accepted. The accepted specification is then refitted on all ten matches to obtain the parameters distributed with the PRESS package. The reported held-out estimates come exclusively from the cross-validation.
Deployment calibration may use labels paired with frozen cross-fitted predictions from all ten matches, after evaluation is complete. The saved benchmark predictions remain the reported held-out results. Final tree counts and configurations are chosen from validation records; the exact aggregation rule is task-specific.


Scope of the development benchmark
Outer-test labels are excluded from that fold’s model fitting, stopping rule and calibrator estimation. The ten matches were repeatedly examined during model development, so the complete development process serves as a development benchmark, and generalization to other competitions and annotation conventions remains open. The task benchmarks describe any development choice shared across folds and distinguish this scope from the match-disjoint fitting of the reported fold models.
The benchmark uses ten matches, with two held out in each outer fold. Observations within a match are dependent, so the number of independent units is the number of matches. Differences between models and between folds should be read with that uncertainty in mind. The same sample size motivates the choice of simple models with few parameters, as described in Modelling choices.

title: PRESS
text: PRESS is an independent, work-in-progress research and software framework for estimating possession-loss risk in football from tracking data. It combines physics-informed models of passing and ball carrying with learned decision-making policies to quantify possession vulnerability at complementary horizons: the risk of losing team possession during the next action and the probability that the current ball carrier’s individual possession eventually ends in a loss. A primary application is the evaluation of player performance under defensive pressure, with broader uses in possession and tactical analysis.

title: PRESS
text:
Motivation
PRESS investigates how the current game state shapes the risk of losing possession in football, with particular interest in the difficulty players face under defensive pressure. Player performance is evaluated in relation to that difficulty by comparing observed possession outcomes with model-based expectations.
As an exploratory research and software development project, PRESS draws on pitch control and possession valuation (Spearman et al. 2017; Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021). Following the modular philosophy of Expected Possession Value (EPV), it separates action selection, pass destination choice, and the success or loss probability of each action. PRESS examines this decomposition from a possession-retention perspective and translates its components into reusable software, transparent implementations, and reproducible analyses of real tracking and event data.
The project also explores alternative formulations for individual EPV components. One example is a physics-based model of ball-drive success. Building on the arrival formulation of Bekkers (Bekkers 2025) and the pitch-control framework of Spearman (Spearman et al. 2017), PRESS investigates whether the relative movement and interception capabilities of defenders and the ball carrier can support a probabilistic model of retaining control during a ball drive. This offers a physically motivated alternative to black-box models of ball-drive success based on spatial and contextual features.
For action and pass destination selection, PRESS experiments with tree-based discrete-choice models suited to decision tasks. In particular, we adopted a multinomial gradient-boosted tree model for pass destination. These choices are driven by player decisions, and the models can incorporate features derived from physical components. One example is the open space available to the carrier, measured by Ball Carrier Open Space (BCOS), a concept introduced in (Bandara et al. 2025) that PRESS formalizes within a competing-risks framework. BCOS describes the area of the pitch the carrier can reach before any opponent. It captures potentially controlled space over a horizon longer than the one-second ball-drive risk model, making it a candidate predictor of action choice and terminal possession loss alongside tactical and contextual features. This hybrid strategy combines physical models of action feasibility and risk with learned tree-based models of player decisions.
The components yield two complementary measures. Evaluated along observed possessions, the possession-loss hazard supports retrospective risk profiles, survival-based descriptions of possession difficulty, and player-performance reports. xLoss provides a prospective measure, with potential applications in tactical analysis, and PRESS computes it modularly as the hazard plus a residual-risk term. Both measures are defined from the current game state.
The framework is developed on a publicly available ten-match sample, which supports end-to-end modelling and reproducible evaluation on real game situations while limiting the generalizability of fitted models and empirical findings. The modelling choices favour parsimonious models, in line with this sample and the project’s exploratory scope; their assumptions and implications are discussed in Modelling choices.

title: PRESS
text:
Framework overview

Possession as a Markov decision process
PRESS adopts a Markov Decision Process (MDP) perspective on football possession, following the modular approach to Expected Possession Value (EPV) developed by Fernández, Bornn and Cervone (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021). In this formulation, possession is viewed as a sequence of decisions and actions undertaken by successive ball carriers, where each action has an uncertain outcome.
This perspective provides a convenient way to separate three fundamental aspects of possession: which actions are available, how likely they are to succeed, and how players choose among them. This decomposition is central to the EPV framework, where individual components can be estimated separately and subsequently combined to evaluate possession outcomes.
PRESS builds on this modular decomposition to estimate possession-loss risk. Let \(s_t\) denote the game state at time \(t\), represented by the positions and movements of players and the ball, together with relevant tactical and contextual information.
We consider two canonical on-ball actions: ball drive and pass. A ball drive corresponds to retaining control of the ball for a conventional interval of one second, whereas a pass represents an attempt to transfer the ball to a selected destination while maintaining team possession. Unlike a ball drive, a pass has a variable duration, determined by the execution and completion of the attempt.
The framework combines four probabilistic components:

Ball-drive risk: the probability of losing possession during the one-second ball drive,
\[
d_t=P(\mathrm{loss}\mid s_t,A_t=\mathrm{drive}).
\]
Pass probability: the probability of retaining team possession through a pass towards destination \(j\),
\[
p_{j,t}=P(\mathrm{success}\mid s_t,A_t=\mathrm{pass},J_t=j).
\]
Pass selection: the probability of choosing destination \(j\), conditional on attempting a pass,
\[
\pi_{j,t}=P(J_t=j\mid s_t,A_t=\mathrm{pass}),
\qquad \sum_j\pi_{j,t}=1.
\]
Action selection: the probability of choosing a pass over a ball drive,
\[
q_t=P(A_t=\mathrm{pass}\mid s_t).
\]

The pass-success and ball-drive components characterize the physical difficulty of executing potential actions, while action and destination selection describe how players are expected to choose among the available alternatives. The latter are learned from observed behaviour using tree-based models, incorporating features derived from the physics-based components alongside tactical and contextual information.



PRESS model flow


The diagram shows how the individual model components are combined to estimate possession-loss hazard and xLoss.


Possession-loss hazard
The canonical actions introduced above provide a conventional way to segment possession into a discrete sequence of on-ball action opportunities (see Possession segmentation and context). Each opportunity is associated with a predefined checkpoint at which the current game state is evaluated. A successful ball drive allows the same player to continue controlling the ball, whereas a successful pass transfers control to a teammate. Since the event of interest is the loss of team possession, a completed pass does not terminate the process: the sequence continues across successive ball carriers until possession is lost.
This conventional segmentation allows possession to be represented as a discrete survival process. Let \(T\) denote the number of canonical on-ball actions until team possession is lost, and let \(s_n\) represent the game state at the \(n\)-th checkpoint. The probability of losing possession during the next action, conditional on having retained it up to the current opportunity, defines the discrete hazard:
\[
\boxed{
h_n=P(T=n+1\mid T>n,s_n).
}
\] PRESS estimates this probability by marginalizing action-specific risks over the decision-making policy learned from observed play, including the choice between carrying and passing and the distribution of pass destinations. The estimate depends on the current state only, whatever action the player actually chose:
\[
\boxed{
h(s_t)=(1-q_t)d_t+
q_t\sum_j\pi_{j,t}(1-p_{j,t}).
}
\] The first term represents the contribution of ball-drive risk, while the second averages pass-failure risk across potential destinations. Together, they quantify the vulnerability of team possession in the current state.
Importantly, the possession segmentation provides the discrete interpretation of the hazard, while \(h(s_t)\) can be computed at any reliable state \(s_t\), including frames between canonical checkpoints, to monitor possession difficulty throughout play. At every frame it remains a per-action quantity: the probability of losing possession during the next canonical action, equal to \(h_n\) when \(s_t\) is the state at checkpoint \(n\). Intermediate evaluations add observations of risk without adding canonical actions.


Pressure intensity and possession difficulty
Defensive pressure is a collective phenomenon. Defenders can restrict the space available to the ball carrier, close passing lanes, reduce the accessibility of teammates, and force the attacking team towards less favourable decisions. Its impact therefore depends not only on the proximity of individual defenders but also on the opportunities available to the player in possession. Related work studies pressure through pressure maps (Gu et al. 2024), minimum arrival time (Narizuka et al. 2026), ball retention under high pressure (Poli, Ravenel, and Besson 2024) and turnover models (Peters et al. 2024), and models the actions of the ball carrier through action rates (Dick and Brefeld 2023) and EPV components (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021).
The possession-loss hazard captures these interacting effects and provides an operational measure of possession difficulty under defensive pressure.
The segmentation into canonical actions also supports a survival analysis interpretation. Under a hypothetical constant hazard, possession half-life is the number of actions required for the probability of retaining possession to fall to \(50\%\). Higher hazard therefore corresponds to shorter reference half-life. This measures current difficulty; risk evolves throughout play.
Evaluating the hazard at successive canonical checkpoints along an observed possession defines a retrospective survival curve, \(S_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-h(s_k))\), with \(S_0=1\). This summarizes the cumulative possession-loss risk encountered along the observed sequence of game states.
Following SkillCorner’s approach of classifying defensive pressure into bands (SkillCorner 2026), PRESS defines possession-difficulty bands from the possession-loss hazard, using this survival-based interpretation; their construction and thresholds are described in the hazard and risk bands vignette.
A primary application is the retrospective evaluation of how individual players retain possession under pressure. Hazard trajectories reveal recurring patterns, such as escaping pressure (initially high risk followed by a decline) or drawing pressure (initially low risk followed by an increase). These patterns are inspired by the pressure metrics of SkillCorner (SkillCorner 2026) and are defined here from the hazard; they can help characterize individual playing styles. Comparing observed outcomes with model-based expectations across difficulty levels provides a complementary assessment of player performance. These applications are illustrated in the case studies vignette.


From possession-loss hazard to xLoss
The possession-loss hazard measures the probability of losing team possession during the next on-ball action. A complementary perspective concerns the eventual outcome of the current ball carrier’s individual possession, which may extend beyond the next action (SkillCorner 2025, 52). PRESS computes this object modularly, by composing the hazard with a residual-risk component.
The distinction arises primarily from ball carrying. A successful one-second drive preserves individual possession but does not determine its eventual outcome: the player may continue carrying the ball, attempt a pass, or lose control later. Conversely, a successful pass terminates the current player’s individual possession without causing a loss of team possession.
To account for this longer horizon, PRESS adds a residual-risk component. Conceptually, the eventual outcome of an individual possession is an absorption probability, which would follow from iterating the evaluation over successive states, each with its own action choice and loss risk, until the possession ends. Since the space of possible continuations is unbounded, the residual-risk component approximates this quantity directly from observed outcomes, as the probability that the current individual possession eventually terminates in a loss, conditional on successfully completing the initial ball drive:
\[
r_t=
P(\mathrm{eventual\ individual\ possession\ loss}
\mid s_t,\mathrm{successful\ drive}).
\]
The probability of eventual loss through the ball-drive branch therefore combines the risk of losing the ball during the initial drive with the residual risk following its successful completion:
\[
d_t+(1-d_t)r_t.
\]
Combining the two action branches gives the expected loss probability:
\[
\boxed{
\mathrm{xLoss}(s_t)=
(1-q_t)\left[d_t+(1-d_t)r_t\right]
+
q_t\sum_j\pi_{j,t}(1-p_{j,t}).
}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
\mathrm{xLoss}(s_t)=h(s_t)+(1-q_t)(1-d_t)r_t.
}
\]
The additional term represents the probability contribution from an initially successful drive followed by an eventual loss of individual possession. Unlike the hazard, which concerns the next action, xLoss incorporates this longer-horizon risk through the residual-risk component, without explicitly modelling the subsequent sequence of decisions.
Together, \(h(s_t)\) and \(\mathrm{xLoss}(s_t)\) provide complementary state-conditioned measures: hazard supports retrospective analysis of possession difficulty, while xLoss supports prospective assessment of individual possession outcomes.

title: PRESS
text:
Vignettes and benchmarks
Each component is described in a dedicated vignette, covering its mathematical formulation, input variables, implementation, and application to real match situations using tracking and event data.
Each modelling task is also accompanied by a dedicated benchmark page, where its predictive performance is evaluated and compared, whenever possible, with results reported in the academic literature for similar tasks. The main references for these comparisons are Fernández, Bornn and Cervone (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2019) and Stalpaert et al. (Stalpaert 2022). These benchmarks provide a basis for assessing the performance of individual components in relation to existing approaches, while accounting for differences in datasets, modelling assumptions, and evaluation protocols.
The case studies and player-level reports illustrate these applications in real match situations.

title: PRESS
text:
Data and reproducibility
PRESS uses ten matches from the publicly available SkillCorner A-League sample as its primary source of tracking and event data. The analyses and examples are based on real match situations, allowing the framework to evaluate possession vulnerability in the context of observed player movements, defensive configurations, and on-ball decisions.
Raw tracking files are not redistributed with the package. Analyses and notebooks can be reproduced using the pinned Python environment and the corresponding match data. Instructions for obtaining and preparing the dataset are provided in the dataset and preprocessing guide, alongside installation and reproducibility information in the repository README.

title: PRESS
text:
Start using the package
To get started with PRESS, follow the user guide or explore the match-use example, which illustrates the analysis of real match situations using tracking and event data.
The workflow begins by loading and validating a match, then selecting team possessions, individual frames, and canonical action checkpoints. The relevant model components can subsequently be evaluated to estimate possession vulnerability and generate risk profiles.
For implementation details, consult the Python API reference and scientific solver reference. The project roadmap outlines ongoing development and planned extensions.

title: Ball-drive risk benchmark
text:
Model and example · All benchmarks
This benchmark documents the selection, estimation, and predictive evaluation of the PRESS ball-drive risk model. The target is the loss of individual possession within a canonical one-second carry, conditional on carrying. The model vignette defines the player-motion approximation, probabilistic defender reachability, tackle intensity, and competing-risk equations. Here we focus on the evidence supporting the fitted specification.

title: Ball-drive risk benchmark
text:
1. Evaluation cohort
The final cohort comprises 9,114 carry attempts, including 456 losses (5.003%), from ten SkillCorner matches. The one-second segmentation of individual possessions is described in Possession segmentation and context. For this specific task, loss-ending possessions without an associated on-ball engagement (OBE) are excluded, since such losses are not guaranteed to result from defensive pressure. The OBE is used only to verify outcomes, and successful-ending possessions do not require one.
Only the final failed section of a possession is labelled as a loss. A loss observed before one second still contributes the one-second failure probability, \(1-S(1)\); a successful canonical second contributes \(S(1)\). The fit uses only the binary outcome of the canonical second. Individual possession loss can include out-of-play events without a team turnover; failed passes are excluded from this task.
The shared evaluation procedure described in Benchmarks defines the five outer match folds, the nested 6+2 validation rotations, pooled held-out evaluation, and performance metrics. For Ball-drive risk, the four inner rotations select the spline smoothing specification using the six fitting and two validation matches. The task-specific null model predicts the loss prevalence estimated from the eight development matches of each outer fold. The final physical model is fitted without resampling or post-hoc calibration.

title: Ball-drive risk benchmark
text:
2. Model specification and features
The evaluated model is the reachability-gated competing-risk specification with an additive spline tackle intensity,
\[
\log\lambda_i(t)=\alpha+g_v(\lVert v_{\mathrm{bc}}\rVert)+g_B(B(t))+g_\phi(\phi_i(t)),\qquad \alpha=\log\lambda_0.
\]
The terms describe carrier speed, signed distance to the pitch boundary, and defender approach angle, respectively. Restricted cubic spline bases allow nonlinear effects while retaining the common possession-survival process. The model vignette documents the kinematic conventions, the form of the spline functions, reachability functions, complexity allocation, priors, and competing-risk equations. The construction of the bases is in the appendix on the spline basis.
Every fit is a maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate under the priors defined in the model vignette: standard normal priors on the linear parameters \(\alpha\), \(\beta_v\), \(\beta_B\) and \(\beta_\phi\), and a Gamma prior on the arrival dispersion \(s\) with shape 2.5 and rate 5 (mean 0.5 s). The nonlinear spline coefficients are regularized by a curvature penalty, equivalent to a zero-centred Gaussian prior, whose multipliers are selected as described below.

title: Ball-drive risk benchmark
text:
3. Model selection and validation

Optimization
Every MAP fit in this study follows the same procedure: the fits of the nested validation, the refits on the eight development matches, and the final fit on all ten matches. The negative log-posterior is minimized with L-BFGS-B, using gradients from automatic differentiation. Before optimizing, the objective is evaluated, without moving them, at 33 initial points: one preset point and 32 random points drawn from the prior. The optimization starts from the point with the lowest objective, and if that point differs from the preset one, the optimization is also run from the preset point. Among the converged solutions, the one with the lowest final objective is retained. The preset point has \(\lambda_0=0.4\) s\(^{-1}\), \(s=0.4\) s, \(\beta_v=0.1\) and \(\beta_B=-0.02\), with all nonlinear coefficients and the linear coefficient of the angle set to zero. This set of values is a practical starting point, consistent with preliminary explorations using a log-linear model that includes only the ball-carrier block. Initialization uses only the fitting data of each fit.


Regularization grid and selection
Write \(\rho_{\mathrm{bc}}\) for the shared nonlinear smoothing multiplier of the ball-carrier block (speed and boundary), and \(\rho_\phi\) for the multiplier of the engagement block (approach angle). The smoothing strengths were explored in an exploratory run over three values of different scale for each block, designed to contain the computational cost of nested cross-validation. Tuning speed and boundary separately would require nine combinations instead of three for each angle specification, so the carrier block shares one multiplier. The knot counts, the additive structure and the linear-coefficient priors are fixed, and validation selects the smoothing strengths and whether the angle is included.







Component
Candidate specifications




Speed and boundary together
Linear terms only; or splines with \(\rho_{\mathrm{bc}}\in\{0.01,1,100\}\)


Approach angle
Absent; or linear-plus-spline effect with \(\rho_\phi\in\{0.01,1,100\}\)



The three smoothing strengths, 0.01, 1 and 100, span four orders of magnitude and cover weak, intermediate and strong curvature regularization. The Cartesian product contains 16 configurations (four choices for speed and boundary times four for the angle). When angle is present, its linear coefficient keeps its prior, and \(\rho_\phi\) penalizes only its two nonlinear coefficients. Exact candidate grid and priority order.
The selection is carried out separately in each of the five outer folds, using only the eight development matches of that fold.

Inner splits. The eight development matches are divided into four rotating 6 + 2 splits: in each split, six matches fit the model and two matches validate it, and every development match is a validation match exactly once.
Fitting. Each of the 16 configurations is fitted on the six fitting matches of each split. Knot locations and basis transformations are estimated on those matches and reused unchanged on the validation matches, and each MAP fit follows the optimization procedure above and runs to numerical optimizer convergence.
Scoring. Each configuration is scored by cross-entropy on the two validation matches of its split, which gives a cross-entropy for every development match.
Reference candidate. The candidate with the lowest observation-weighted cross-entropy across the eight validation matches is the reference.
Paired comparison. For each candidate \(c\) and validation match \(m\), let \(\Delta_m=\mathrm{CE}_{c,m}-\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{best},m}\), and let \(\bar\Delta_c\) be the observation-weighted mean difference. Its standard error is estimated by deleting one validation match at a time (match jackknife). A candidate is eligible when \(\bar\Delta_c\leq\mathrm{SE}_{\mathrm{jackknife}}(\bar\Delta_c)\).
Choice by priority. Among the eligible candidates, the first in a prespecified priority order is selected: angle-absent configurations first, followed by angle multipliers 100, 1 and 0.01; within each group, linear main effects precede spline multipliers 100, 1 and 0.01. The order favours simpler and smoother configurations when their validation disadvantage is small relative to the uncertainty between matches. A more flexible configuration is therefore selected only when its reduction in cross-entropy exceeds the uncertainty between matches.
Refit and test. The selected configuration is refitted on all eight development matches and evaluated on the two held-out test matches.

The choice was identical across all five outer folds, and the selected configuration includes the approach angle: multipliers 1 for speed and boundary and 100 for approach angle. Fold selection details.

CatBoost with training-set resampling
In (Stalpaert 2022) a CatBoost architecture is adopted to model ball-drive risk, providing a substantial improvement when the training set is resampled (table above). We tested the same approach on our data by training CatBoost on the same 9,114 sections and 456 losses used to evaluate the final physical model. Its 50 snapshot-derived features cover carrier speed, boundary geometry, defender times to interception, encounter probabilities, and local spatial relationships, broadly overlapping the information used in (Stalpaert 2022), although not reproducing every feature transformation or convention. Observed future positions, outcomes, engagement annotations, durations, receiver identities and player/team identities are excluded from the features.

The encounter curve is \(E(t)=1-\prod_i[1-F_i(t)]\), where \(F_i(t)\) is the logistic defender-reachability probability (Bekkers 2025). The dispersion \(s\) is taken from the corresponding physical training fit for each inner or outer fold. Thus the same fold separation is respected in both sampling arms.
Resampling was applied only within training subsets, retaining all losses and sampling nine successful sections per loss; validation and test data preserved their natural prevalence. The resampled model’s probabilities were adjusted for the known change in class prevalence.
The CatBoost comparison follows the rotating design of the physical model tasks. In each outer fold, four 6+2 rotations evaluate 36 configurations (depth 4/6/8, learning rate 0.02/0.05/0.10 and L2 1/3/10/30) and tree prefixes every 25 trees up to 3,000. Selection minimizes pooled inner-validation CE, applying the analytical prevalence correction in the resampling arm. Models are trained to the fixed search ceiling and scored at saved prefixes.

6. Production model and parameter uncertainty
The selected specification was fitted to all ten matches and all 9,114 verified sections. Following the shared deployment protocol, this fit supplies the package parameters.
The likelihood is Bernoulli on the one-second loss outcome, and the coefficients, baseline tackle rate, and logistic arrival-time dispersion are estimated jointly by maximum a posteriori (MAP) under the priors defined in the model vignette. A local Laplace approximation to the joint posterior supplies approximate marginal uncertainty. In the final fit, the preset initial point had the lowest initial objective, so a single optimization was run. In log coordinates, the reported approximations are

title: Ball-drive risk benchmark
text:
7. Discussion and limitations
The spline model achieves strong held-out discrimination and good pooled calibration while retaining an explicit interpretation in terms of defender reachability and tackle intensity. On the same observations, CatBoost trained at natural prevalence reaches a slightly lower cross-entropy (0.139855 against 0.143483). The physical model remains close to it while providing defender-level rates and reachability, which the composed hazard uses.
The scope of the model is described in the model vignette, which also includes executable real-match examples.

title: Ball-drive risk benchmark
text:
8. Supplementary resources
The final physical metrics, fold parameter estimates, regularization selection, CatBoost comparison, posterior summaries and production provenance support the reported results. The research pipeline provides the procedural source and input/output layout.

title: BCOS: transport with killing and competing risks
text: This appendix develops a model of deterministic transport with interior killing and boundary absorption, and describes its application to BCOS in PRESS. The forward equation for diffusion with killing and absorption studied by Holcman, Marchewka and Schuss (Holcman, Marchewka, and Schuss 2005) motivates the mathematical structure. Here, deterministic transport is combined with a probabilistic reference law and competing terminal events.

title: BCOS: transport with killing and competing risks
text:
1. Reference transport model
Consider a particle on \((-\infty,L)\), with absorption at \(L>0\). Conditional on its initial position, its motion is deterministic until killing or absorption. Let \(\tau:(-\infty,L]\to\mathbb R\) be continuous, strictly increasing, locally absolutely continuous, with \(\tau'>0\) almost everywhere and \(\tau(\ell)\to-\infty\) as \(\ell\to-\infty\). Define the transport velocity almost everywhere by
\[
\nu(\ell)=1/\tau'(\ell).
\]
For \(\kappa>0\), introduce the logistic reference function
\[
F(\ell,t)=[1+\exp\{-\kappa[t-\tau(\ell)]\}]^{-1}.
\]
It is the probability that the particle has reached \(\ell\) by time \(t\) in the absence of killing; the particle reaches \(\ell\) at time \(\tau(\ell)+T\), with \(T\) a logistic delay common to all positions. The corresponding density of the particle’s position, \(p_0\), and its current are
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_0(\ell,t)&=-\partial_\ell F(\ell,t)=\kappa\tau'(\ell)F(\ell,t)[1-F(\ell,t)],\\
\nu(\ell)p_0(\ell,t)&=\partial_tF(\ell,t)=\kappa F(\ell,t)[1-F(\ell,t)].
\end{aligned}
\]
Equality of the mixed derivatives, in the distributional sense, gives
\[
\partial_tp_0+\partial_\ell(\nu p_0)=0.
\]

title: BCOS: transport with killing and competing risks
text:
2. Initial conditioning
The initial condition is the reference density at time zero, conditioned on non-absorption. At \(t=0\), the reference law assigns mass \(F(L,0)\) to the destination or beyond; removing it and retaining all mass on \((-\infty,L)\) gives
\[
Z=1-F(L,0),\qquad p_k(\ell,0)=p_0(\ell,0)/Z,\quad -\infty<\ell<L.
\]
Since \(F(-\infty,0)=1\), the initial density integrates to one. The reference law has median at the point where \(\tau(\ell)=0\), when that point exists. In particular, if \(\tau(0)=0\), its unconditioned median is zero; truncation at \(L\) shifts the conditioned median. The negative half-line can represent a latent waiting state, as in the BCOS application below.

title: BCOS: transport with killing and competing risks
text:
3. Transport with killing
Let \(k(\ell,t)\ge0\) be measurable and bounded on the domain over each finite time interval. The surviving density satisfies
\[
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
\partial_tp_k+\partial_\ell(\nu p_k)&=-kp_k, &&\ell<L,\\
p_k(\ell,0)&=p_0(\ell,0)/Z.
\end{aligned}}
\]
The absorbing outflow boundary \(L\) is the only finite boundary of the domain, and the density there is determined by the transport. The current vanishes at \(-\infty\), as follows from the characteristic solution below.

title: BCOS: transport with killing and competing risks
text:
4. Solution by characteristics
Use the transport-time coordinate \(\zeta=\tau(\ell)-\tau(0)\). The density in this coordinate is the current \(J_k=\nu p_k\), since \(\mathrm d\ell=\nu\,\mathrm d\zeta\) almost everywhere. The conservative equation becomes
\[
\partial_tJ_k+\partial_\zeta J_k=-kJ_k,
\]
where \(k\) is evaluated at \(\ell=\tau^{-1}(\zeta+\tau(0))\). The characteristic ending at \((\ell,t)\) is
\[
X_\xi=\tau^{-1}(\tau(\ell)-t+\xi),\qquad 0\le\xi\le t.
\]
Every backward characteristic reaches the initial line because \(\tau\) tends to \(-\infty\) at the left end. This construction also specifies the passage through points where the spatial velocity vanishes: transport proceeds at unit speed in \(\zeta\) through such points.
Along a characteristic,
\[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\xi}J_k(X_\xi,\xi)=-k(X_\xi,\xi)J_k(X_\xi,\xi).
\]
The reference function and current are constant along characteristics because \(\xi-\tau(X_\xi)=t-\tau(\ell)\). The initial current is therefore \(\partial_tF(\ell,t)/Z\). Integration yields
\[
\boxed{p_k(\ell,t)=\frac{p_0(\ell,t)}{Z}w(\ell,t),\qquad w(\ell,t)=\exp\!\left[-\int_0^t k(X_\xi,\xi)\,\mathrm d\xi\right].}
\]
The weight \(w\) is the probability of surviving killing along the entire characteristic since time zero. Since \(0\le w\le1\), the current \(J_k=\partial_tF\,w/Z\) vanishes as \(\ell\to-\infty\). Without killing, \(p_k=p_0/Z\).

title: BCOS: transport with killing and competing risks
text:
5. Competing risks
The terminal fluxes are
\[
\boxed{j_L(t)=\nu(L)p_k(L^-,t),\qquad j_k(t)=\int_{-\infty}^L k(\ell,t)p_k(\ell,t)\,\mathrm{d} \ell.}
\]
Integration of the transport equation over \((-\infty,L)\) gives
\[
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\int_{-\infty}^L p_k(\ell,t)\,\mathrm d\ell= -j_L(t)-j_k(t).
\]
The total at-risk probability is the surviving mass:
\[
\boxed{S(t)=\int_{-\infty}^L p_k(\ell,t)\,\mathrm d\ell.}
\]
With \(C_L\) and \(C_k\) denoting cumulative incidences of absorption and of killing, respectively,
\[
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
S'&=-j_L-j_k, & S(0)&=1,\\
C_L'&=j_L, & C_L(0)&=0,\\
C_k'&=j_k, & C_k(0)&=0.
\end{aligned}}
\]
Adding the equations yields \(S(t)+C_L(t)+C_k(t)=1\). These balances hold almost everywhere in time under the stated assumptions.
For \(S(t)>0\), the cause-specific hazards are
\[
\boxed{h_L(t)=\frac{j_L(t)}{S(t)},\qquad h_k(t)=\frac{j_k(t)}{S(t)}.}
\]
The total hazard is \(h_L+h_k=-S'/S\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(t)&=\exp\!\left[-\int_0^t [h_L(\xi)+h_k(\xi)]\,\mathrm{d}\xi\right],\\
C_L(t)&=\int_0^t h_L(\xi)S(\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi,\qquad C_k(t)=\int_0^t h_k(\xi)S(\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi.
\end{aligned}
\]
Bounded killing on finite time intervals implies \(S(t)>0\) at every finite time.

Multiple killing causes
Suppose killing can occur through several competing causes indexed by \(i\), with local intensities \(k_i(\ell,t)\). Conditional on the particle’s trajectory, assume independent killing processes, so that
\[
k(\ell,t)=\sum_i k_i(\ell,t).
\]
Along a characteristic, the survival weight factorizes as
\[
w(\ell,t)=\prod_{i}\exp\!\left[-\int_{0}^t k_i(X_\xi,\xi)\,\mathrm d\xi\right].
\]
The additive sink partitions the killing flux into mutually exclusive terminal causes:
\[
j_i(t)=\int_{-\infty}^L k_i(\ell,t)p_k(\ell,t)\,\mathrm{d}\ell,\qquad
j_k(t)=\sum_i j_i(t).
\]
The cause-specific hazards and cumulative incidences are
\[
h_i(t)=\frac{j_i(t)}{S(t)},\qquad C_i(t)=\int_0^t S(\xi)h_i(\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi.
\]
Consequently \(S(t)+C_L(t)+\sum_i C_i(t)=1\). The individual fluxes depend on all killing intensities through the surviving density \(p_k\).

title: BCOS: transport with killing and competing risks
text:
6. Terminal probabilities
Since \(0\le w\le1\), we have \(0\le S(t)\le [1-F(L,t)]/Z\to0\). Consequently, the terminal probabilities satisfy
\[
C_L(\infty)=\int_0^\infty j_L(t)\,\mathrm{d} t,\qquad C_k(\infty)=\int_0^\infty j_k(t)\,\mathrm{d} t,\qquad C_L(\infty)+C_k(\infty)=1.
\]
Substituting the characteristic solution into the boundary current gives
\[
C_L(\infty)=\frac1Z\int_0^\infty \partial_tF(L,t)w(L,t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
\]
If \(k(\ell,t)=k(\ell)\), changing variables along each characteristic gives \(\mathrm d\xi=\mathrm d\eta/\nu(\eta)\) almost everywhere. The terminal probability is
\[
C_L(\infty)=\int_{-\infty}^L \frac{p_0(y,0)}{Z}\exp\!\left[-\int_y^L\frac{k(\eta)}{\nu(\eta)}\,\mathrm d\eta\right]\,\mathrm dy.
\]
Without killing, \(w=1\) and \(j_L(t)=\partial_tF(L,t)/Z\), so \(C_L(\infty)=[1-F(L,0)]/Z=1\).
For multiple killing causes, \(C_L(\infty)+\sum_i C_i(\infty)=1\).

title: BCOS: transport with killing and competing risks
text:
7. Application to BCOS in PRESS

Time to intercept and reference law
The function \(\tau(\ell)\) of the transport model is the time to intercept (TTI) of the carrier along the candidate route, and the killing is the interception of the carrier by the defenders. For a player \(j\) and a target location \(x\) on the pitch, the nominal TTI is
\[
\tau_j(x)=t_{\mathrm{turn},j}(x)+t_{\mathrm{move},j}(x),
\]
the sum of the turning delay and the acceleration-limited travel time, both computed from the observed position and velocity of the player. The maximal speed and acceleration of the movement model are set separately for the carrier, who moves with the ball, and for the defenders. For a defender, \(\tau_j(x)\) is the nominal time to reach a potential interception location; for the carrier, it is the nominal time to reach \(x\). Following Spearman (Spearman et al. 2017; Spearman 2018), the uncertainty around the TTI is logistic, with arrival-time distribution and arrival hazard
\[
F_j(x,t)=\left[1+\exp\{-\kappa\,[t-\tau_j(x)]\}\right]^{-1},\qquad
\lambda_j^{\mathrm{arr}}(t\mid x)=\frac{\partial_tF_j(x,t)}{1-F_j(x,t)}=\kappa F_j(x,t).
\]
Here \(\kappa=\pi/(\sqrt{3}\,s)\), where \(s\) is the standard deviation of arrival-time uncertainty.
For a carrier initially at \(x_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)\), the route is \(x(\ell;z)=x_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)+\ell(z-x_{\mathrm{bc}}(0))/L\) for \(0\le\ell\le L\), with \(L=\|z-x_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)\|\). Along this route, \(\tau(\ell)\) is the nominal TTI of the carrier at \(x(\ell;z)\), and \(F(\ell,t)\) is its logistic arrival-time distribution. Time is measured from the observed instant: the carrier first turns and then moves along the route. The extension to negative transport coordinates represents waiting at the observed origin, as specified below.


Transport velocity
The TTI of the carrier along a straight ray follows from the acceleration-limited movement model of PRESS. Let \(\ell\) denote distance along a straight ray from the carrier’s initial position. The observed speed is \(u\ge0\), and \(a>0\) and \(v_{\max}>0\) are the carrier’s acceleration and maximal speed. The angle \(\theta\) is fixed along the ray. The turning contribution is the constant
\[
t_{\mathrm{turn}}=\frac{u\theta}{a_{\mathrm{turn}}},\qquad a_{\mathrm{turn}}>0.
\]
For \(u<v_{\max}\), set
\[
t_a=\frac{v_{\max}-u}{a},\qquad d_a=ut_a+\tfrac12at_a^2.
\]
The function defining the transport is
\[
\tau(\ell)=t_{\mathrm{turn}}+\begin{cases}
(\sqrt{u^2+2a\ell}-u)/a,&0\le \ell\le d_a,\\[3pt]
t_a+(\ell-d_a)/v_{\max},&\ell>d_a.
\end{cases}
\]
For \(u\ge v_{\max}\), use \(\tau(\ell)=t_{\mathrm{turn}}+\ell/u\): the observed speed is maintained, including when it exceeds \(v_{\max}\). For the accelerating case,
\[
\tau'(\ell)=\begin{cases}
1/\sqrt{u^2+2a\ell},&0<\ell\le d_a,\\
1/v_{\max},&\ell>d_a,
\end{cases}
\qquad
\nu(\ell)=\begin{cases}
\sqrt{u^2+2a\ell},&0<\ell\le d_a,\\
v_{\max},&\ell>d_a.
\end{cases}
\]
At \(d_a\), \(u^2+2ad_a=v_{\max}^2\), so \(\tau\) is \(C^1\).
Write \(t_{\mathrm{move}}(\ell)=\tau(\ell)-t_{\mathrm{turn}}\) for \(\ell\ge0\). Extend the movement time antisymmetrically:
\[
\boxed{\tau(\ell)=t_{\mathrm{turn}}+\begin{cases}
-t_{\mathrm{move}}(-\ell),&\ell<0,\\
t_{\mathrm{move}}(\ell),&\ell\ge0.
\end{cases}}
\]
This extension is strictly increasing and tends to \(-\infty\) at the left end. For \(u>0\), it is \(C^1\) at zero, with \(\tau'(0)=1/u\). For \(u=0\), the derivative has an integrable singularity at zero; the velocity tends to zero from both sides. The transport-time coordinate specifies passage through zero, as in the characteristic construction above. The extension uses only the movement parameters already defined.
The inverse of the positive movement time is, for \(r\ge0\) and \(u<v_{\max}\),
\[
t_{\mathrm{move}}^{-1}(r)=\begin{cases}
ur+\tfrac12ar^2,&0\le r\le t_a,\\
d_a+v_{\max}(r-t_a),&r>t_a.
\end{cases}
\]
For \(u\ge v_{\max}\), \(t_{\mathrm{move}}^{-1}(r)=ur\). Thus the extended inverse is
\[
\tau^{-1}(t)=\operatorname{sgn}(t-t_{\mathrm{turn}})\,t_{\mathrm{move}}^{-1}(|t-t_{\mathrm{turn}}|).
\]
The constant turning delay cancels from the characteristic trajectories but affects the reference weights and initial conditioning. Negative coordinates are latent waiting states, whose physical location is the observed origin:
\[
x(\ell;z)=x_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)+\frac{\max(\ell,0)}{L}(z-x_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)),\qquad \ell\le L.
\]
Since all negative coordinates share this location, the form of the extension is a convention.
For \(\tau(0)=t_{\mathrm{turn}}\ge0\), the initial physical position concentrates at the observed origin as \(\kappa\to\infty\): for \(0<\epsilon<L\), the conditioned probability of being beyond \(\epsilon\) is \([F(\epsilon,0)-F(L,0)]/Z\to0\). When the turning delay is positive, the latent reference median lies on the negative half-line, which maps to the origin.


Interception intensities
Interception occurs when a defender reaches the location occupied by the carrier while the carrier is still in possession. In pitch control, the arrival of each player is evaluated at every point of the ball trajectory, and each point represents an opportunity for interception. Here the arrival of each defender is evaluated in the same way at every point of the carrier’s route, and we model the local interception intensity by the defender’s arrival hazard at that location. Conditional on the carrier’s characteristic and the observed tracking state, the defenders’ interception processes are assumed independent; their intensities therefore add. For the route \(x(\ell;z)\), PRESS specifies the local killing intensity as
\[
k(\ell,t)=\sum_{i\in\mathrm{opp}} k_i(\ell,t),\qquad
k_i(\ell,t)=\lambda_i^{\mathrm{arr}}\big(t\mid x(\ell;z)\big)=\kappa F_i(x(\ell;z),t).
\]
On the negative half-line, the same intensity is evaluated at \(x_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)\), so interception can occur during waiting and turning. For a finite number of defenders, \(0\le k\le n_{\mathrm{opp}}\kappa\), satisfying the boundedness assumption above.


Accessibility and defender-specific risks
The accessibility probability is \(p_{\mathrm{bc}}(z)=C_L(\infty)\). The terminal incidence \(C_i(\infty)\) is the probability that defender \(i\) causes the first interception. Hence
\[
p_{\mathrm{bc}}(z)+\sum_{i\in\mathrm{opp}} C_i(\infty)=1.
\]
These incidences quantify the contributions of individual defenders under the joint model. Evaluating \(p_{\mathrm{bc}}(z)\) across candidate destinations produces the BCOS accessibility surface.

title: Pass probability benchmark
text:
Model and example · All benchmarks
This benchmark documents the cohort, estimation and predictive evaluation of the PRESS pass-probability model. The target is the completion of a pass by the attacking team, given the release state and a candidate destination. The pass vignette defines the model: the control rate and the arrival-time dispersion are estimated by maximum likelihood on the reconstructed physical trajectories of observed passes, and the fitted mechanism is then used to compute a potential pitch control field (PPCF) for hypothetical destinations, whose raw scores are calibrated with an isotonic map. Here we report the evidence supporting this specification.

title: Pass probability benchmark
text:
1. Evaluation cohort
The benchmark contains 6,706 passes: 5,742 completions and 964 failures (14.38%), across ten SkillCorner matches, selected from 7,078 outfield pass candidates by the matching criteria and the duration interval described below (effective exclusion counts). Passers are outfield players; goalkeepers remain in the state and can receive or intercept passes.
Pass endpoints satisfy the shared verified-pass-link criteria. Native-coordinate conversion, the release tracking state and the first five ball observations are also checked for the physical trajectory fit.
Passes are retained when the duration from release to matched reception or recovery lies within the inclusive interval [0.5, 10] s. The lower bound ensures sufficient tracking observations to estimate the ball-flight initial conditions, whereas the upper bound limits the trajectory integration horizon. This interval is also consistent with the temporal selection adopted by Spearman (Spearman et al. 2017). Passes with curvature above 5%, excluded in the original paper, are retained.

title: Pass probability benchmark
text:
2. Model specification and features

Ball-flight initial conditions
The physical flight and player-reachability models, including their kinetic parameters and the selected player-speed setting \(v_{\max}=5.5\) m/s, are described in the model vignette. Here we assess the reconstruction of the ball’s initial conditions, which determines the trajectories used to fit the control parameters.
For each pass, the release position is observed and the first five ball positions, at 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 s, are used to estimate the launch state. We compared two approaches: an initial velocity derived from the mean observed ball velocity and a position-based fit of the physical flight trajectory. The latter estimates launch speed and direction while keeping the observed release position fixed.
The two estimators were compared by their free-flight position-prediction error after 0.6 s and before the next ball control. Errors were averaged equally across matches. The choice was repeated separately for each physical fit, using only its training matches: six matches in each inner rotation, eight in each outer refit, and ten in the final production fit. One estimator was selected for the whole training partition.
Position-based fitting was selected in every outer fold and in the final fit, and in 19 of the 20 inner fits; the remaining inner fit selected the mean-velocity estimator. This reconstruction uses observations after release and is therefore an offline estimation procedure.

title: Pass probability benchmark
text:
3. Model selection and validation
The control rate \(\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}\) and arrival-time dispersion \(s\) are estimated by maximum likelihood, maximizing the Bernoulli log-likelihood defined in the pass vignette.
The resulting parameters are then applied to hypothetical passes towards candidate destinations. Because these predictions use a destination-based control calculation, which differs from the observed-flight calculation used for fitting, the raw potential pitch control field (PPCF) scores are calibrated against pass outcomes.

Optimization
The negative Bernoulli log-likelihood of the passes on the reconstructed trajectories is minimized over \(\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}\) and \(s\). The optimization is carried out in the coordinates \((\eta_\lambda,\eta_s)=(\log\lambda_{\mathrm{control}},\log s)\), so that both parameters remain positive.
Three complete and independent optimizations are run, starting from the following points:
