Each optimization uses BFGS, with gradients obtained by automatic differentiation. BFGS determines the step by line search, with a maximum of 500 iterations and a gradient tolerance of \(10^{-4}\). A solution is admissible when its parameters and objective are finite and the maximum absolute gradient is below 0.01, and among the admissible solutions the one with the lowest final negative log-likelihood is retained. The procedure uses only the fitting data and is the same for the fits on six, eight and ten matches.
In the fit on the ten matches, the three starts converge to practically the same solution (\(\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}=5.437830\) s\(^{-1}\), \(s=0.294560\) s) in 6, 6 and 11 iterations. The third start is retained, with an objective difference of the order of numerical precision.


Evaluation and calibration
Evaluation is match-wise, with five outer folds of two held-out matches each. Within each fold the procedure is the following.

Inner rotations. Within the eight outer-training matches, four rotations train the physical model on six matches and generate predictions for the remaining two. The four held-out pairs are disjoint within the development set, so each development pass supplies one raw PPCF calibration score from a physical fit that omitted its match.
Calibration map. These out-of-fold predictions are used to fit an isotonic calibration map. A Platt calibrator is evaluated using the same calibration examples.
Refit. The physical parameters are re-estimated on all eight outer-training matches.
Test. The fitted calibration map is applied to the predictions for the two outer-test matches.

The initial-condition estimator is selected using training data only. The physical trajectory MLE, the initial-condition estimator choice and the isotonic/Platt fitting are separate operations, and the calibration step leaves \(\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}\) and \(s\) unchanged. The retained calibration method is a development decision based on the reported comparison.

Curvature is measured as maximum perpendicular deviation from the release-to-endpoint line, relative to endpoint distance. Performance is substantially weaker for more curved passes. The absence of spin and Magnus effects is one plausible explanation; the subsets also differ in difficulty, geometry and failure prevalence.
Further limitations include the use of the observed recovery location as a proxy for the intended destination of failed passes, uncertainty in endpoint annotations, and simplified player motion. The initial-condition reconstruction requires at least 0.5 s of observed flight; shorter passes are outside the evaluated population.

title: Action selection benchmark
text:
Model and example · All benchmarks
The action-selection model estimates the probability that the ball carrier passes, \(q(s)=P(\mathrm{pass}\mid s)\), at a given game state \(s\); the probability of carrying is \(1-q(s)\). The target is the observed choice of action. The classifier is a native XGBoost model with a binary logistic objective (Chen and Guestrin 2016), with native probabilities retained for deployment; temperature scaling is evaluated as a diagnostic. The model vignette introduces the 30 input features, the probabilistic summaries of hypothetical passing options and an executable example.

title: Action selection benchmark
text:
1. Evaluation cohort
The final cohort comprises 16,918 decisions across ten SkillCorner matches, of which 7,770 are passes and 9,148 are carries. Carriers are outfield players, and individual possessions that end in a shot are excluded. Pass labels occur at the actual release. Carry labels are complete one-second successful carries and failed carries, including failures before one second. The segmentation of individual possessions into decision checkpoints is discussed in Possessions and checkpoints.

Effective task-specific selection
After the shared possession-level preparation, a decision is canonical when it is a pass at its release or a one-second carry attempt. Short-control tails, terminal-clearance snapshots and terminal-foul snapshots are noncanonical: they remain available for state evaluation and are excluded from the choice-training examples. The target is the observed pass or carry decision, so the terminal execution outcome is exempt from the OBE and pass-flight verification filters, and all failed canonical carries are retained. Unknown start and previous-action contexts are kept as predictor categories. These criteria leave the 16,918 decisions. Effective exclusion counts and snapshot counts.

title: Action selection benchmark
text:
2. Model specification and features
The model uses 30 features, 28 numerical and two categorical, in four groups. Their definitions are given in the vignette. The original start and previous-action categories, including unknown, are kept, and missing or unseen levels receive an explicit encoding. All features are built from information available at the decision frame, so future execution outcomes, receivers, remaining possession duration, player identity and role are excluded.
The upstream components are refitted for each evaluation split. Pass-completion physics, physical carry risk and arrival dispersion, and destination-choice utilities are fitted on the same six training matches as the action classifier, and the smoothed xT surface is estimated from those same six matches. BCOS uses the fold-specific carry-arrival dispersion (see the kinematic conventions). Benchmark inputs are created only with components fitted on the training matches.

Likelihood and calibration diagnostic
For score \(f_\psi(z_i)\) and \(q_i=\operatorname{sigmoid}(f_\psi(z_i))\), the regularized Bernoulli loss is
\[
\mathcal L(\psi)=-\sum_i\big[y_i\log q_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-q_i)\big]+\Omega(\psi),
\qquad y_i=\mathbf1\{\mathrm{pass}\}.
\]
The native gradient and curvature with respect to the score are \(q_i-y_i\) and \(q_i(1-q_i)\), so training uses the standard XGBoost logistic objective.
A separate diagnostic fits a single temperature parameter \(T>0\) on the existing validation matches with the selected trees held fixed (Guo et al. 2017):
\[q_T=\operatorname{sigmoid}\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{logit}(q)}{T}\right).\]
The diagnostic temperature minimizes validation negative log likelihood after the native grid and tree prefix have been selected. The selected configuration, trees and stopping rule remain unchanged. The same validation pair is reused for this diagnostic. The installed classifier returns native probabilities.

title: Action selection benchmark
text:
3. Model selection and validation

Hyperparameter search
In each of five match-disjoint 6 + 2 + 2 partitions, all 144 configurations of a grid were fitted, giving 720 fits. The grid varied maximum depth (3, 4, 6, 8), minimum child weight (1, 5, 20), L2 leaf regularization (0.1, 1, 3, 10) and learning rate (0.03, 0.05, 0.10). Row and column sampling were fixed at 0.8, and training allowed at most 2,000 trees with early-stopping patience 100. Match-wise held-out evaluation
In each partition, six matches fit the XGBoost classifier and the upstream feature components. Two fixed validation matches select the configuration and, by early stopping, the number of trees. This pair remains fixed for every grid candidate in that outer fold. A later temperature diagnostic reuses it with the selected ensemble held fixed, and the six-match fit is evaluated directly on the test matches. The remaining two test matches were reserved exclusively for performance evaluation. One-hot vocabularies and encoded columns were fitted on training matches only. Each of the 16,918 decisions appears exactly once among the pooled test predictions.


Context extensions
Two context extensions were also assessed without changing the feature set: the verified origin of the team-possession chain and the previous completed-pass count. With fixed hyperparameters, paired fits and three seeds, the origin feature changed null gain by an average of +0.105 percentage points, the count by +0.039 and both together by +0.053, with the joint change ranging from −0.056 to +0.148 points. These small, variable changes did not motivate adding the features.

The fold temperatures were 1.0875, 1.0256, 1.0279, 1.0153 and 1.0537. Relative to the raw output, temperature scaling reduces pooled ECE from 1.026% to 0.817%, with a CE change of −0.000180 and a null-gain change of +0.026 percentage points. The gain is small. These are diagnostic scores. Because the improvement from temperature scaling is marginal, the installed model keeps the native probabilities (calibration.method = "none"), consistent with the main calibration plot.

Stalpaert et al. (Stalpaert 2022) study the same binary pass–carry choice. PRESS has a lower CE and a higher gain than Stalpaert’s model with major action categories, and the model that includes specific action types reaches a higher gain; with our labels we could not obtain a comparable benefit.
Fernández et al. (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021) motivate the decomposition of action choice and execution. Their shoot/pass/carry classifier has a different label space and serves as context for this binary task.

title: Action selection benchmark
text:
6. Production model
The production model is a native XGBoost refit on all ten matches and 16,918 decisions, with 277 trees and native probabilities. Its configuration (depth 6, minimum child weight 1, L2 10, learning rate 0.03) has the lowest mean validation CE across the five fold-specific search grids. For this configuration, the best tree prefixes in the five folds are 242, 329, 369, 253 and 277, and their median, 277, fixes the tree count. These deployment values are selected from validation records.
Production features use the full-data pass-risk, carry-risk, destination-choice and xT models, and BCOS uses the full-data carry dispersion. All held-out scores above refer to the five outer-fold models.

title: Action selection benchmark
text:
7. Discussion and limitations
The studies differ in dataset, class balance (null CE 0.6602 versus 0.690053), available features and validation protocol, and the values are reported as context.

title: Action selection benchmark
text:
8. Supplementary resources
For reproducibility, the selected configurations, encoded feature schemas, pooled metrics, fold scores, per-match scores, temperature values, literature values and locators, importance tables, context-extension results with seed-level comparisons, refit provenance and benchmark provenance are provided as supplementary resources.

title: 1 · Datasets, installation and preprocessing
text: This is the first part of the User guide. Continue with possession segmentation and context and use on a match.

title: 1 · Datasets, installation and preprocessing
text:
The source data
PRESS was developed on the ten Australian A-League matches from the 2024/25 season released by SkillCorner and PySport. The broadcast tracking is sampled at 10 Hz. Players have two-dimensional positions in metres; the ball also has an estimated height. The origin is the pitch centre, x follows its length and y its width. Native pitch dimensions are retained. Detection flags distinguish observed and extrapolated objects (SkillCorner, n.d.).
Download the files from the SkillCorner open-data repository. Each match has its own directory:
opendata/data/matches/2006229/
  2006229_match.json
  2006229_tracking_extrapolated.jsonl
  2006229_dynamic_events.csv
  2006229_phases_of_play.csv







File
What PRESS uses




*_match.json
Pitch dimensions, team identities, player identities and shirt numbers.


*_tracking_extrapolated.jsonl
Frame, match clock, period, player and ball positions, provider possession and detection flags.


*_dynamic_events.csv
Individual-possession boundaries, boundary-matching flags, reception/recovery context, pass links and outcomes.


*_phases_of_play.csv
Available in the source release; unused by this preprocessing command and the fitted PRESS predictors.



Event IDs and possession IDs are local to a match. Identify an individual possession by (match_id, possession_id). The original provider files remain separate from derived tables.

title: 1 · Datasets, installation and preprocessing
text:
Install PRESS
From a local PRESS checkout, create a Python 3.11 environment and install the package with the data readers and notebook dependencies:
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e '.[io,vignettes]'
export SKILLCORNER_OPENDATA="/path/to/opendata"
The environment variable points to the downloaded SkillCorner open-data root containing data/matches/. The fitted models are included and can be used without training.

title: 1 · Datasets, installation and preprocessing
text:
Preprocess one observed match
The example uses Melbourne City FC–Macarthur FC, 7 March 2025, match 2006229. It is the match containing Ivan Vujica’s pressure-escape example in the case studies.

Load the original files
With the environment variable above set, load the original files directly:
import os
from pathlib import Path
from PRESS import PRESS

match_dir = Path(os.environ["SKILLCORNER_OPENDATA"]) / "data/matches/2006229"
press = PRESS.from_skillcorner(match_dir)
match_dir is the original match folder shown above. PRESS reads the metadata, tracking and dynamic events, calculates kinematics, prepares annotated possessions and builds canonical actions in memory. A single call replaces intermediate Parquet files and a separate preprocessing command. The following steps describe what this loader does.


What preprocessing does

Load observations and identities. Preserve frame IDs, period, timestamps, pitch dimensions and detection flags. Map provider player IDs to canonical labels such as away_13, retaining the original mapping.
Estimate kinematics. Apply a centred Savitzky–Golay derivative with polynomial order two: seven frames for players and five for the ball. Estimate acceleration by differentiating velocity again. Runs are split at missing frames, period changes and nonfinite coordinates; runs shorter than three observations have unavailable derivatives. This step keeps positions at their original scale and leaves gaps unfilled.

The centred velocity estimate uses observations after the selected frame: three future frames in an interior player window. These inputs reconstruct a recorded match; a causal live-data smoother would be a separate preprocessing choice. Detection flags are retained, and finite extrapolated players are allowed. Missing players remain distinguishable from observed players.
The loader also constructs the possession/action structure described in part 2:

Match individual control intervals. Retain recognized individual possessions with explicitly matched start and end. Preserve the full event audit separately, including excluded intervals and reasons.
Link passes and team possessions. Verify release and the immediate subsequent control. A completed pass can link two individual possessions into one team possession. A break in verified continuity starts a new reconstructed team interval.
Build actions. Export canonical carries and pass releases separately from additional snapshots. Part 2 defines their timing and context labels.

title: 1 · Datasets, installation and preprocessing
text:
The annotated input tables
The loader retains these tables in the PRESS object. They can also be supplied explicitly to PRESS(...) when prepared separately. They are in-memory DataFrames; saving them is optional.







Table
Structure and use




Tracking
One row per frame; timestamp, period, player_possession, attacking_side, pitch_length, pitch_width, ball fields and player fields. Player fields follow <player>_x, _y, _vx, _vy, with speed, acceleration and detection/provenance fields retained.


Individual possessions
possession_id, player_id, inclusive frame_start and frame_end, start_type, end_type, pass_outcome, target_pass, frame_receipt, boundary flags and team_possession_id.


Actions
possession_id, frame_start, frame_end, action, previous_action, start_type, is_canonical, snapshot_reason, duration and eligibility flags.


Team possessions
Linked team intervals with a team ID and the number of constituent individual possessions. PRESS can derive these from the individual table at initialization.


Player map / audit
Correspondence to provider identities and the complete audit of individual-boundary selection.



Positions use metres, velocity m/s and acceleration m/s². A frame ID is an observation index; the input frequency converts frame differences to elapsed time.
The match-use example loads the original files, initializes the object, evaluates a generic frame and all canonical checkpoints, and saves and reloads the calculated results. The five fitted models distributed with PRESS include their parameters, category vocabularies and fitted xT surfaces; the models can be used as distributed.

title: 1 · Datasets, installation and preprocessing
text:
Other tracking sources
The physical solvers consume canonical positions and velocities. Supply canonical tables to PRESS(...). The optional PRESS.io.convert_long_tracking(...) helper converts long tracking tables before initialization. If individual controls/actions are missing, call PRESS.io.segment_possessions(...) on the aligned canonical tracking and events. Convert coordinates and units, provide the actual frame frequency and map event labels to the concepts in part 2. The external-data guide explains the input contract and the Bundesliga example shows a complete workflow. The initialization reference specifies both input schemas. Calibration on another dataset remains to be assessed.
The pipeline page describes the research stages beyond this one-match example; task-specific outcome filters and validation protocols are documented in the benchmarks.

title: 4.2 · Use with other providers: Bundesliga example
text:
This is part 4.2 of the User guide, following the data requirements and preparation guide. It applies the installed PRESS models to match J03WMX (27 May 2023). Original event and tracking XML are from IDSSE, provided by the Deutsche Fußball Liga (DFL), under CC BY 4.0 (Bassek et al. 2025; German Sport University Cologne, n.d.). Download the original data through the official repository.
DataBallPy 0.7.3 is used as an optional external preprocessing tool for alignment and a tracking-based control estimate (Oonk, Grob, and Kempe 2026; Oonk and Grob, n.d.). PRESS performs the canonical segmentation and context reconstruction. All models are used as fitted. The example demonstrates software interoperability, and predictive generalization to Bundesliga data remains to be assessed. See input requirements and limitations.

title: 4.2 · Use with other providers: Bundesliga example
text:
Original files and synchronization
Install PRESS with its io extra. In a separate Python 3.10 environment install databallpy==0.7.3 and pyarrow. Set PRESS_IDSSE_DATA to the downloaded XML directory and PRESS_SYNC_PYTHON to that environment’s Python executable. PRESS_IDSSE_OUTPUT optionally selects a cache/output directory. The bridge reads the original XML, refines alignment and exports tables. The source files remain unchanged.
The adapter applies event revisions and deletions, preserves provider event IDs, and maps players and teams consistently between events and tracking. DataBallPy aligns the action/contact events and estimates the tracked controller. Synchronization categories and football labels are kept apart: a foul, recovery or clearance keeps its own PRESS label whatever generic contact category the synchronizer uses.
Passes, shots, tackles, control starts, fouls and clearances require direct synchronization links to be used by the segmenter. Other events may retain an explicitly labelled clock-interpolated link for audit; these links do not establish possession boundaries. Unlinked and excluded events remain in the event audit. Already aligned bridge outputs can be reused explicitly.

import json
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

title: 4.2 · Use with other providers: Bundesliga example
text:
Canonical input and custom segmentation
DataBallPy’s static home/away coordinates already orient the home side towards positive x in both periods. They keep that orientation. The adapter maps provider/player IDs to stable home/away aliases, keeps native pitch metres, differentiates finite contiguous position runs, and reconstructs past score and clock context.
Possession reconstruction and canonical action segmentation are separate steps. The first uses synchronized events and the estimated controller to identify individual control intervals. PRESS then applies its own one-second carry and pass-release convention to those intervals. The segmentation guide defines the common action, checkpoint and context conventions; the rules below describe how this example obtains their input intervals from IDSSE.
The procedure has four steps, described in the sections below. (1) Possession starts: a start is created by a successful pass reception or by an annotated acquisition of control. (2) Terminal events: from each start, the first eligible terminal event closes the interval. If none is available before a missing tracking range, a period boundary, an eligible stoppage or restart, or an intervening event of another player, the first change of estimated controller bounds the interval and the ending is unknown. (3) Pass-link verification: each pass ending is cross-checked against estimated control and flagged with outcome_verified. (4) Context labels and canonical checkpoints: PRESS labels each start, assigns the carrier to the interval and constructs the canonical actions and checkpoints.

Possession starts
This example sets include_unannotated_starts=False. The following rules determine starts:

Successful pass reception. After a synchronized successful release, take the identified receiver and the receiver’s next synchronized actor event in the same period. The start is the first frame after the release, up to and including the frame of that event, in which the estimated control belongs to the receiver. If the receiver is not in control within this window, the frame immediately before that event is used as the start when the observed ball–receiver distance there is at most 1.5 m (reception_fallback_max_distance); this candidate must exist in the same period and strictly follow the release. If the receiver is not identified, has no later synchronized event, or neither control nor the fallback candidate is found, no reception start is created.
Annotated acquisition of control. A synchronized BallClaiming establishes a start at the event’s synchronized frame for its identified player, subject to the overlap reconciliation below. Type="InterceptedBall" supplies pass_interception; a generic Type="BallClaimed" supplies recovery. The identified player starts the interval whichever player the control estimator identifies at the exact contact frame. A won TacklingGame is a terminal event and creates no start.

Receptions use observed control or the distance-checked fallback candidate; control acquisitions use the source annotation. No other source creates a start. The optional include_unannotated_starts=True also admits tracking-only starts and opponent controls after failed passes, and a reception search without a later receiver event then extends to the end of the period; it is not used here.
Intervals are constructed chronologically without overlap. When a recovery/interception start falls inside the preceding accepted interval, compare its source event with that interval’s terminal event. Reconcile the overlap only if the preceding interval ends in a tackle loss, the incoming player is that tackle’s winner on the opposing team, and the named loser, if available, is the outgoing carrier. The recovery/interception and tackle must be adjacent relevant events: no intervening pass, shot, tackle, acquisition of control, foul, clearance, stoppage or restart may separate them. Both controls must remain in the same period.
For a coherent pair, retain the outgoing end at the synchronized tackle frame and move the incoming start to the following observed frame. That frame must exist in the same period. This resolves the small timing disagreement without assigning one frame to two carriers. The report’s overlap_reconciliations records the original and aligned start frames and supporting event IDs; the interval retains original_frame_start and start_reconciled_with_event_id. An overlap without this support is recorded in overlapping_start_annotations and does not create another interval. No general time-tolerance rule shifts unrelated events.
The returned tracking retains the estimator’s original controller as estimated_player_possession. Within each reconstructed interval, player_possession names that interval’s carrier, so its checkpoints and frame-level state use the same player. Attacking direction and score difference remain relative to that carrier’s team. This assignment follows the event-supported interval and leaves player and ball positions unchanged.


Terminal events and outcomes
For each accepted start, search forward within the same period for the first eligible terminal event. An identified ending is assigned exactly to that event’s synchronized frame; the individual interval includes both its start and end frames. Passes, shots, fouls suffered and clearances must name the current carrier. A won tackle has a separate winner rule:



IDSSE annotation
PRESS ending and interpretation




Play by the carrier
pass, with the provider’s mapped success/failure annotation. The link is verified as described below.


TacklingGame with WinnerResult="ballClaimed" or "ballcontactSucceeded", and an identified winner different from the carrier
possession_loss. The annotated winner determines the loss, whether or not the tracked controller changes or an opponent possession follows. The explicitly named loser can be a player other than the carrier. PossessionChange is retained for audit only. A duel won by the carrier is not a loss.


TacklingGame with WinnerResult="fouled", or an eligible explicit Foul, naming the carrier as the fouled player
foul_suffered, a non-loss ending. A contact and the following decision for the same fouled player and fouler are linked and counted once. Handballs are excluded. A foul terminates the interval only with a direct synchronization link.


OtherBallAction by the carrier with DefensiveClearance="true"
clearance, a non-loss ending outside the terminal pass/carry actions. Only clearance-qualified OtherBallAction records terminate possession. The clearance must have a direct synchronization link.


ShotAtGoal by the carrier
shot, kept as an identified ending and excluded from the fitted pass–carry outcome cohort.



A synchronized terminal annotation can close an interval even when the control estimator changes player earlier. It stops at a missing tracking range, a period boundary, an eligible stoppage/restart, or an intervening pass, shot, foul or clearance attributed to another player. If no eligible terminal event is available before these limits, the first change to another estimated controller also bounds the interval. The ending is then unknown and remains distinct from a verified loss.
For a lost tackle, frame_end is the tackle frame. When no eligible terminal event identifies the end, the interval ends at the frame immediately before the limit that interrupts it, or at the last available frame when the period simply ends, and the ending remains unknown. The checkpoint of the final failed carry precedes frame_end: it is the start of the last canonical one-second attempt.


Pass-link verification
The pass annotation and its tracking cross-check are stored separately. pass_outcome retains the mapped provider result: successful, unsuccessful or unknown. Both IDSSE success annotations, Evaluation="successful" and Evaluation="successfullyCompleted", map to successful; missing or unrecognized success annotations remain unknown. A missing recipient leaves this known outcome unchanged and prevents receiver-link verification. For outcome_verified=True, the first different estimated controller after release, within the same period, must be the identified receiver for a successful pass, or an opponent for a failed pass. A known provider result is retained when this check fails, but the interval is marked outcome_verified=False. Thus an unverified link can reflect a disagreement with estimated control; the source outcome can still be known.
The reception search used to create the next possession and the first-different-controller check used to verify the outgoing pass are distinct operations. An intervening estimated touch can fail the latter even if the identified receiver is subsequently found. The example below selects an interval with a verified completed pass.


Context labels and canonical checkpoints
For a successful reception, the preceding pass’s restart qualifier gives pass_reception, throw_in_reception, corner_reception, free_kick_reception or goal_kick_reception. An unavailable or unsupported qualifier gives unknown. Direct BallClaiming starts use the interception/recovery labels above; the restart origin is read from annotations only. These labels use the existing fitted vocabularies. The general rule for previous_action is unchanged: the start type before one complete second, then ball_drive.
The code passes tracking, individual intervals and metadata to PRESS, without an externally supplied action table. PRESS constructs the canonical actions and checkpoints at initialization. Complete successful carries supply one-second blocks; a pass supplies a release checkpoint; a direct loss supplies the final failed carry even below one second. Fouls and clearances retain preceding complete carries but supply no terminal pass/carry checkpoint. The common segmentation guide covers micropossessions, partial tails and optional snapshots in detail.
These intervals are event-supported estimates, distinct from annotated SkillCorner possessions. The event audit, source event IDs, verification flags and segmentation report allow the reconstructed boundaries to be inspected separately from model predictions.

title: 4.2 · Use with other providers: Bundesliga example
text:
One observed possession
Select an outfield reception followed by a verified completed pass, with at least two whole seconds of carrying. Among eligible controls, use the first chronological case whose initial ball is within the 1.5 m control zone and an opponent is within eight metres. This is an illustrative selection.
The rule selects Leroy Sané (Bayern), followed by a completed pass to Benjamin Pavard. The start, whole-second carry checkpoints and release are different canonical decision states. The next control illustrates the annotated outcome; the state predictors use only information up to the checkpoint.

outfield = set(players.loc[players.is_goalkeeper.eq(False), "player_id"])
candidates = possessions.loc[
    possessions.outcome_verified & possessions.end_type.eq("pass")
    & possessions.start_type.eq("pass_reception") & possessions.frame_receipt.notna()
    & possessions.player_id.isin(outfield)
    & (possessions.frame_end-possessions.frame_start).between(2*press.fps, 5*press.fps)
].sort_values("frame_start")
selected = None
for row in candidates.itertuples():
    state = press.get_state(int(row.frame_start))
    ball = press.get_frame(int(row.frame_start))[["ball_x", "ball_y"]].to_numpy()[0]
    nearest = np.linalg.norm(state["r_defs"]-state["x_bc"], axis=1).min()
    if np.linalg.norm(ball-state["x_bc"]) < 1.5 and nearest < 8:
        selected = row
        break
if selected is None:
    raise ValueError("No case meets the documented selection rule; inspect the preparation report.")
selected_actions = press.get_actions(possession_id=selected.possession_id)
frames = selected_actions.frame_start.astype(int).tolist()
name = players.set_index("player_id").full_name
print(name[selected.player_id], "→", name[selected.target_pass])

text:
Complete PRESS inference
Each checkpoint uses the production pass-risk, ball-drive, pass-selection, action-selection and residual-risk models. The predictors receive only information available at the checkpoint. h describes current-action fragility; xLoss additionally includes predicted loss after that action succeeds. Each checkpoint computes only the preliminary effective-hazard BCOS required by the frozen classifiers, pending retraining. The final transport map is requested separately for the single descriptive example below.

predictions = []
for frame in frames:
    # Retain spatial fields only for the checkpoint plotted below.
    press.compute_risk_frame(frame, include_residual=True, keep_details=(frame == frames[0]))
    predictions.append(dict(
        frame=frame, elapsed_seconds=press.get_elapsed_time(frame),
        p_pass=press.get_action_selection_result(frame)["Pass probability"],
        drive_loss=press.get_ball_drive_risk_result(frame)["Ball drive risk"],
        h=press.get_hazard_result(frame)["Hazard"],
        residual_loss=press.get_residual_risk_result(frame)["Residual loss probability"],
        xloss=press.get_xloss_result(frame)["xLoss"],
        bcos_feature_m2=press.get_bcos_result(frame)["BCOS area"],
    ))
checkpoint_summary = pd.DataFrame(predictions)
display(checkpoint_summary.round(4))
checkpoint_summary.to_csv(output_dir / "checkpoint_predictions.csv", index=False)
print("Observed terminal action:", selected.end_type, selected.pass_outcome)
print("Mean h:", checkpoint_summary.h.mean(), "· maximum h:", checkpoint_summary.h.max())

Pitch control and BCOS at the same frame
Both panels use the same real tracking state and the package plotting functions. Pitch control describes competition for a destination; BCOS describes reaching a destination without interception along a hypothetical route. The surfaces answer different questions.

from PRESS.spatial_features import BCOS

frame = frames[0]
# Optional descriptor requested for this plot, independently of classifier inference.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 6))

          title=f"Same frame · final BCOS = {bcos_display.get_result(frame)['BCOS area']:.1f} m²")

title: User guide
text:
The guide follows the path from raw observations to a possession-level risk profile. All examples use observed match data and the models distributed with PRESS.

Datasets, installation and preprocessing. Obtain the SkillCorner files, install PRESS, load a match and inspect the prepared input tables.
Possession segmentation and context. Understand individual and team possessions, canonical actions, checkpoints and context labels.
Use on a match. Navigate a real match, calculate h and xLoss, plot frames and checkpoints, and save and reload results.
Use with other providers.

4.1 · Data requirements and preparation defines the input contract and synchronization/segmentation workflow.
4.2 · Bundesliga example applies it to Köln–Bayern.


The SkillCorner loader in part 1 prepares the original match files in memory. For another provider, follow part 4 to map and align the data before initializing PRESS. Individual possessions can be reconstructed through the segmentation interface; PRESS then constructs canonical actions and checkpoints.
The four-part reference documents individual classes and functions: initialization, solvers, getters and plots. The model pages explain the mathematical components; the benchmarks describe their training and held-out evaluation.
Models, calculation configurations and frame results explains where fitted coefficients, spline designs, physical settings and predictions are stored, with ball-drive, pitch-control and BCOS examples.

title: Reference: solvers
text:
1 · Initialization and classes · 2 · Solvers · 3 · Getters and saved results · 4 · Plot functions.
The match-level methods extract the current frame and store results; the numerical functions below operate directly on arrays. Positions are centred metres, velocities m/s and time seconds. Input frame frequency and numerical integration step are independent.

title: Reference: solvers
text:
Complete frame and possession calculations
outputs = press.compute_risk_frame(frame_id, include_residual=True)
h = outputs["HAZARD"]["Hazard"]
band = outputs["HAZARD"]["band"]
xloss = outputs["XLOSS"]["xLoss"]
compute_risk_frame(frame_id, xT_grid=None, *, start_type=None, previous_action=None, bcos_value=None, ppcf_kwargs=None, ball_drive_kwargs=None, bcos_kwargs=None, pass_selection_kwargs=None, match_clock_min=None, score_difference_prefix=None, completed_canonical_drives=None, include_residual=False, time_since_start=None, keep_details=False) computes prerequisites in order. It evaluates any usable frame, not only training checkpoints. Current context is read from annotations unless supplied explicitly. xT uses the frame argument when supplied, then the object map, then the fitted production surface. The resolved map is passed to both choice-model feature builders; residual risk reuses their feature record. Separately called action selection reuses the map stored by pass selection and rejects a conflicting map.
It always recomputes the requested frame and returns copied PPCF, BALL_DRIVE_RISK, ACTION_SELECTION and HAZARD results. With include_residual=True, it also returns RESIDUAL_RISK and XLOSS. Elapsed individual-possession time must be observed or explicitly supplied in seconds; a missing value raises an error and is never replaced by zero. A custom bcos_value reuses an already computed area in m²; otherwise only the preliminary effective-hazard BCOS required by the fitted trees is calculated. The standalone compute_bcos() default remains final transport. BCOS can be the expensive part of a full-frame calculation.
compute_possession(possession_id, xT_grid=None, *, frame_ids=None, include_snapshots=True, **frame_kwargs) evaluates a team interval. compute_risk_player_possession(player_possession_id, ...) evaluates an individual interval. Both return a chronological DataFrame with frame IDs, canonical/snapshot kind, P(pass), h and its automatically assigned band; xLoss is included when requested. Default frames come from the canonical actions constructed by PRESS from individual possessions, or from an explicitly supplied action table. Explicit frame_ids must be nonempty, unique integer usable frames within the chosen interval. No new segmentation or observed outcome is inferred.
The band field in each HAZARD result classifies h as None, Low, Medium or High, using the existing half-life cutoffs. It is assigned during risk calculation and returned by get_hazard_result; no additional band calculation is required. These are h bands, not classifications of xLoss.
Complete risk calculations use keep_details=False by default. Every dependency is evaluated before discarding spatial fields, integration curves and feature records. Scalar component probabilities, BCOS area, h, its band and optional xLoss remain in press.results. keep_details=True additionally retains the arrays needed for spatial plots and feature inspection. Both modes produce the same numerical predictions. The possession methods accept the same option through their frame keywords.
press.result_configurations stores physical/numerical settings and the xT input once per distinct configuration. Results refer to them through configuration_id. press.result_models holds fitted model instances once per distinct artifact, including custom per-call physical parameters. Inspect them with get_result_configuration(frame_id, component=None) and get_result_model(component, frame_id). The latter returns the shared model; use .to_dict() for an editable copy. Coefficients and spline transformations are not copied into each frame’s result.
Individual component calls retain their detailed outputs for step-by-step computation, but physical/numerical settings are still stored in shared configurations. No match-level component result repeats fitted coefficients, spline design, lambda_control, s or calibration; retrieve the fitted quantities from its model. BCOS dispersion is an explicit physical input in its configuration. Spatial plots never trigger model calculation: when a map was discarded, rerun the complete calculation with keep_details=True, or calculate the required component explicitly. plot_risk works with compact outputs.
Additional snapshot forecasts can overlap canonical actions. They are useful for plotting, but must not be multiplied blindly into a survival sequence. Frame sampling never changes the modeled one-second carry action.

title: Reference: solvers
text:
Individual component methods
Call these methods in dependency order when only some outputs are needed.







Method
Prerequisites and output




compute_ppcf(frame_id, r_max=150, step=1.0, physics_kwargs=None, model=None)
Current physical state → raw player/attacking control and isotonic pass completion on a candidate grid. Stores PPCF; returns None.


compute_ball_drive_risk(frame_id, t_press=1.0, physics_kwargs=None, model=None)
Current physical state → total and cause-specific drive loss over t_press seconds. Stores BALL_DRIVE_RISK; returns None.


compute_pass_selection(frame_id, xT_grid=None, *, start_type_raw=None, previous_action_raw=None, match_clock_min=None, score_difference_prefix=None)
Requires PPCF and one-second drive loss. Uses raw control for destination choice, stores Pass selection probabilities inside PPCF, and returns that normalized vector.


compute_bcos(frame_id, r_max=40.0, step=1.0, physics_args=None, *, formulation="transport")
Current state and physical drive dispersion → spatial field and area. Stores BCOS and returns its copied mapping.


compute_action_selection_probability(frame_id, xT_grid=None, start_type=None, previous_action=None, bcos_value=None, *, match_clock_min=None, score_difference_prefix=None, completed_canonical_drives=None)
Requires PPCF, destination choice, one-second drive loss and a BCOS area. The builder converts the stored loss d to drive_success_1s = 1 - d and uses calibrated pass completion. Stores ACTION_SELECTION; returns native P(pass).


compute_hazard(frame_id)
Requires the preceding pass/drive/choice/policy results. Returns and stores raw marginal next-action loss; no post-hoc h calibrator.


compute_residual_risk(frame_id, *, time_since_start=None, model=None)
Requires the current action feature record and its matching action model. Reuses the record plus native P(carry) and the observed elapsed time. Returns/stores terminal individual loss conditional on a successful carry.


compute_xloss(frame_id, *, time_since_start=None, model=None)
Requires pass/drive/choice/policy results. Computes residual risk if needed and composes the terminal individual loss. Returns/stores xLoss.




Reusing calculations within inference
A complete frame call extracts the physical state and context once and shares the pressure-line centres. The pass solver reuses player TTI for receiver-based flight selection and control, without changing the nearest-receiver convention. Candidate ball trajectories are reused across frames only when their launch and ball-physics settings match; this numerical cache is bounded to eight configurations. Frame-dependent flight times, control fields and predictions are recalculated.
Residual risk reuses the native P(carry) already returned by the matching production action model, retaining its model-dependency check. xLoss reuses the current h; changing an upstream component invalidates its dependent results. Frame-state reuse ends when the call returns or raises, so later calls see tracking/annotation edits. These are computational reuse rules; training and cross-fitting procedures are unchanged.
The autonomous final BCOS solver reuses defender TTI at the physical origin during waiting and omits zero-duration integration segments. Quadrature nodes, weights, precision, spatial grid and model equations are unchanged. Complete risk calls compute only the preliminary BCOS needed by the fitted tree models.


Frame inspection and many-possession analysis








Purpose
Call/storage setting
Available afterwards




Inspect one component at one frame
Call its compute_* method directly.
Detailed component outputs; model and physical/numerical configuration are referenced separately.


Inspect a complete frame
compute_risk_frame(..., keep_details=True, include_residual=True)
Scalar predictions, spatial maps, defender contributions, survival curve and action-selection feature record.


Process many possessions
compute_risk_player_possession(..., include_snapshots=False, keep_details=False, include_residual=True)
Scalar predictions and h bands for canonical checkpoints, shared models/settings; maps and feature records are discarded after calculation.



Both retention levels use the same model inputs and produce identical predictions. plot_risk and plot_action_selection work with compact predictions. Spatial maps and defender-risk coloring require details; plotting never starts a new model calculation.
The tree feature schema (names, order, categories and encoding) belongs to the fitted model. The feature values at a frame are calculation inputs: pass-selection’s destination-wise matrix and the encoded residual matrix are temporary; action selection retains its named Features record for residual risk and detailed inspection. Compact complete calls discard that record only after all requested predictions finish. These frame values are neither fitted model parameters nor predicted outcomes.


Example: change the model or the configuration
# Configuration change: same fitted coefficients/bases, different defender motion.
press.compute_ball_drive_risk(frame_id, physics_kwargs={"v_max": 6.5})

# Model change: custom coefficients/dispersion, with omitted bases inherited.
press.compute_ball_drive_risk(frame_id, model={"s": 0.35, "gamma_v": [0, 0, 0]})
fitted_model_used = press.get_result_model("BALL_DRIVE_RISK", frame_id)
parameters_used = fitted_model_used.parameters
physical_settings_used = press.get_result_configuration(frame_id, "BALL_DRIVE_RISK")["BALL_DRIVE_RISK"]

# Complete calculation: scalar results, shared configuration and automatic h band.
outputs = press.compute_risk_frame(frame_id, include_residual=True)
settings_used = press.get_result_configuration(frame_id)
h = outputs["HAZARD"]["Hazard"]
band = outputs["HAZARD"]["band"]
The first two calls replace the stored ball-drive result and invalidate its dependants; they do not change the default model. The final call omits overrides and recomputes the complete analysis with the object’s default models/settings. Model parameters and spline bases remain in the shared model, physical/numerical inputs in the shared configuration, and frame predictions in the results. The three levels, with movement-setting examples.


Fitted-model settings
The default pass-risk artifact uses v_max=5.5, a_max=a_turn=7, overspeed-preserving TTI, dt_ball=0.04, t_max_flight=10, dt_pc=0.01, t_max_pc=15, exact target distances and exponential integration. Launch candidates span 5–25 m/s and 0–45 degrees, 30 values on each axis; drag settings are rho=1.22, Cd=0.25, A=0.038, m=0.42, g=9.81, controllable height z_max=2. The full-data parameters are lambda_control=5.437830, s=0.294560; isotonic knots are separate from those physical estimates. Export provenance.
The default drive artifact uses the verified additive splines and angle term, v_max=7, independent linear/turning acceleration settings, preserved initial overspeed, signed boundary distance, constant carrier velocity and exponential integration with partial final steps. The wrapper supplies native pitch dimensions. Physical overrides and named fitted-parameter dictionaries are supported; omitted settings retain their model defaults. Model and spline definitions.
The operational pass-selection model is the verified flat refit, with its saved vocabulary, xT surface and temperature. Candidate cells use the native one-metre grid at the default settings. Coarse/restricted grids are supported as explicit sensitivities and recorded as differing from the benchmark. Action selection and residual risk retain their native probabilities without scaling. No training occurs in these methods.


Composition
For stored native P(pass) = p, drive loss d, destination-weighted pass failure f and conditional residual loss r:
\[h=(1-p)d+pf,\]
\[xLoss=pf+(1-p)\{d+(1-d)r\}.\]
A completed pass terminates the individual possession without loss; h describes the current action, not the outcome of the whole individual possession. PRESS.model.compose_individual_xloss(*, p_pass, drive_loss, pass_failure, residual_loss) exposes the same probability-only composition for scalar/broadcastable array inputs. It loads no model. Residual risk and xLoss.

title: Reference: solvers
text:
Numerical functions
Low-level defaults can differ from fitted model settings. Use explicit parameters when reproducing an integration and prefer the match/model wrappers for pretrained inference. These functions expect valid, compatible arrays and physical parameters; they do not validate canonical match tables or manage dependency caches.

Pitch control
Import integrate_pitch_control from PRESS.model.
integrate_pitch_control(r_grid, p_pos, p_vel, ball_carrier_idx, T_ball,
    lambda_control=4.3, s=0.45, v_max=5.0, a_max=5.0,
    t_max_pc=8.0, dt_pc=0.01, tol=1e-6,
    integration_method="exponential")
r_grid is (N,2) candidate positions; p_pos and p_vel are (M,2) players; ball_carrier_idx identifies the excluded carrier; T_ball is (N,) ball-arrival time. lambda_control is a rate in inverse seconds, s arrival dispersion in seconds, and v_max/a_max the motion settings. Returns player-by-target control (M,N). Control begins when the ball arrives (Spearman et al. 2017; Spearman 2018). Exponential Euler allocates the available uncontrolled mass exactly for rates frozen over each step, preserving total control at most one; it is first order for time-varying rates. The full configured horizon is used, including partial final steps. tol is a compatibility argument and no longer changes the integration schedule. Sum attacking rows, then use the saved isotonic map through PassRiskModel. integration_method="euler" is an explicit numerical sensitivity; archived sources preserve the original clipped solver. Mathematics and frame example.


Pass probability along a trajectory
Import from PRESS.model.solver_pitch_control.
integrate_pass_prob(p_pos, p_vel, attacker_idx, ball_carrier_idx,
    ball_trajectory, lambda_control=4.3, s=0.45, v_max=5.0,
    a_max=5.0, dt=0.04, z_max=2.0, tol=1e-6,
    integration_method="exponential")
p_pos, p_vel are (M,2); attacker_idx selects attacking rows; ball_trajectory is (T,3) with x, y and height sampled every dt. Control accumulates at or below z_max metres; the carrier is excluded before sharing mass. Returns scalar attacking success. Each supplied sample starts one integration interval: the benchmark’s 251 samples at 0..10 s use a 10.04 s left-step schedule. There is no parameter-dependent cutoff. This reconstructed-path likelihood estimates parameters; candidate-field inference uses target PPCF and its separately fitted isotonic map. Pass vignette.


Drive-loss integration
The final ball-drive solver is BallDriveModel, imported from PRESS.model. It evaluates the saved penalized spline model, including the approach-angle term. The frame API calls the same solver.
from PRESS.model import BallDriveModel

model = BallDriveModel.pretrained()
result = model.predict(r_defs, v_defs, x_bc, v_bc, horizon=1.0)
loss = result["loss_probability"]
causes = result["cause_probabilities"]
Defender positions and velocities are (D, 2) arrays; carrier position and velocity are (2,). Positions are centred metres and velocities m/s. predict_batch adds a leading state dimension. physics_kwargs permits explicit physical sensitivities; spline coefficients, knots, normalization and arrival dispersion are loaded from the fitted artifact. horizon accepts any finite nonnegative duration in seconds, using those same fitted parameters. The calibrated benchmark target remains one second; other horizons are model-implied forecasts.
At each left integration endpoint, the carrier is projected as \(x(t)=x_0+v_0t\). The solver evaluates the signed distance to the nearest boundary, each defender’s arrival probability \(F_j(t)\) and approach angle \(\phi_j(t)\). The tackle rate is
\[\lambda_j(t)=\exp\{\log\lambda_0+g_v(\|v_0\|)+g_B(B(t))+g_\phi(\phi_j(t))\},\]
where the saved spline functions include their fitted linear and nonlinear components. The angular contribution is set to zero when the carrier’s speed is below 1 m/s or the approach direction is undefined. The competing hazard is \(q_j(t)=F_j(t)\lambda_j(t)\) and \(H(t)=\sum_jq_j(t)\). Over a step of width \(\Delta t\), the solver holds these hazards fixed and updates
\[\Delta P_j=S\{1-\exp(-H\Delta t)\}\frac{q_j}{H},\qquad S_{\mathrm{new}}=S\exp(-H\Delta t).\]
A zero total hazard gives zero loss increment. Rates are reevaluated at every step; the default step is 0.04 s, with a partial final step when needed. Returned cause probabilities sum to total loss, and survival_curve includes the initial survival of one. This exponential update preserves the shared remaining probability mass; timestep convergence is a separate numerical question. See exponential integrators.
The drive vignette defines the spline model and uses this final solver. The superseded log-linear solver is retained only in archive/legacy_package/model/solver_intensity.py for research history; it is neither exported nor called by the package.


Ball flight and receiver arrival
Import time_flight from PRESS.physics.
time_flight(r_bc, r_target, p_attackers, v_attackers,
    v0_candidates=linspace(10,30,20),
    theta_candidates=linspace(0,pi/3,20),
    t_max_flight=10.0, dt_ball=0.04, grid_step=0.5,
    v_max=5.0, a_max=5.0, z_max=2.0,
    rho=1.2, Cd=0.25, A=0.038, m=0.43, g=9.81,
    distance_mode="exact")
The linspace notation describes default JAX arrays. Carrier position is (2,); targets (N,2); receivers (M,2). The receiver nearest in initial position to each target supplies the desired arrival time. A candidate flight is selected by matching that time, subject to reachability and controllable height. Exact target distances are the default; distance_mode="lookup" enables the corrected regular radial grid as an approximation. grid_step affects that approximation only. Drag parameters are air density rho, drag coefficient Cd, cross-section A, mass m, and gravity g, in SI units. Returns (N,) flight times. No receiver or reachable candidate gives infinite time and zero control. The class uses its saved flight configuration; see its defaults.
The flight ODE includes gravity and constant-coefficient aerodynamic drag. Below 5 cm while descending, height is held and horizontal aerodynamic drag continues; there is no bounce, fitted rolling friction or Magnus force. The latent vertical velocity is not reset by this ODE and is not interpreted as a post-impact velocity. The model consumes simulated positions and height. Flight equations and assumptions.


Fitted pass settings for the low-level solvers
The fitted pass model uses v_max=5.5, a_max=7, a_turn=7 and preserve_initial_overspeed=True consistently. The lower-level trajectory and target-control solvers accept the same a_turn and preserve_initial_overspeed keyword arguments. Their compatibility defaults remain unchanged; pass the fitted artifact settings to reproduce it. Physical λ,s are MLE estimates along reconstructed paths; isotonic knots are learned separately on cross-fitted hypothetical PPCF scores.

title: Reference: solvers
text:
BCOS formulations
compute_bcos defaults to the final transport-with-killing model. It returns destination accessibility, per-defender interception incidences, unresolved/reservoir/interior mass at a finite time, and the probability-weighted area. The default evaluates terminal probabilities (time=np.inf). The square-cell area is step**2; the 40 m disc is clipped to the physical pitch without rescaling its area.
Interception acts both while the carrier waits at the observed origin and while it moves along the route. Reservoir probability is the surviving mass still waiting at the origin, not a protected probability component. Use formulation="transport_reservoir" for the retained alternative with no interception before route entry; its model is PRESS.model.ReservoirBCOSModel in model/bcos_reservoir.py.
Use formulation="effective_hazard" to reproduce the preliminary BCOS field used in the existing benchmarks. Complete risk calculations evaluate only that preliminary feature once and store its area/map under BCOS; no final transport descriptor is computed in addition. To inspect final transport, call compute_bcos() explicitly. When final transport was explicitly calculated before standalone action selection, the classifier helper derives its required preliminary feature from the same physical settings. An explicit bcos_value remains a caller override. The configuration records the BCOS formulation and the action result records the classifier feature’s formulation. A different formulation in complete-call bcos_kwargs is rejected; use the standalone descriptor call instead. Changing that feature requires retraining; see the roadmap.
The final solver integrates the appendix’s characteristic solution. A positive quadrature over conditioned no-killing exit times includes both initial interior trajectories and later boundary inflow. Integrated killing determines survival along each trajectory. Ordered exponential competing-risk updates keep all cause incidences nonnegative and conserve probability. The implementation is checked against independent characteristic/density integrals, no-killing and constant-killing limits, finite-time reservoir balances and numerical refinement. arrival_order and path_order are numerical quadrature settings, not fitted coefficients.

title: Reference: solvers
text:
Physical parameter inputs
compute_ball_drive_risk(..., physics_kwargs=...) accepts v_max, a_linear, a_turn and the supported solver/pitch settings. compute_ppcf(..., physics_kwargs=...) accepts the pass model’s physical settings, including v_max, a_max, a_turn and ball-flight constants. Flight-time and pitch-control calculations use the same resolved pass settings.
compute_bcos(..., physics_args=...) accepts v_bc_max, v_def_max, a_bc_max, a_def_max, a_turn_bc, a_turn_def and s, plus numerical quadrature settings for final transport. Omitting settings uses the deployed physical conventions and ball-drive dispersion.
In a complete compute_risk_frame call these dictionaries are nested under ball_drive_kwargs, ppcf_kwargs and bcos_kwargs, respectively. Fitted parameters such as pass-control lambda, ball-drive spline coefficients and fitted dispersion are supplied through a named model dictionary, model object or manifest. Constructor inputs ball_drive_model and pass_risk_model accept the same named dictionaries. Changing inputs does not refit coefficients or calibration maps.

Named model parameters
press.compute_ball_drive_risk(frame_id, model={
    "s": 0.35,
    "gamma_v": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
})
press.compute_ppcf(frame_id, model={
    "lambda_control": 5.0,
    "s": 0.30,
})
These are explicit sensitivity inputs. Omitted entries inherit the model supplied at initialization, or the production fit otherwise. A dictionary is resolved for that call; omitting model on a later call restores the base model. Each call replaces its cached component result and invalidates dependent outputs. Motion settings can be supplied together through physics_kwargs.







Ball-drive key
Meaning




lambda_0, s
Positive baseline tackle rate and arrival-time dispersion, both in their natural scales.


beta_v, beta_B
Linear effects of speed and boundary distance in their original units.


gamma_v, gamma_B
Three nonlinear coefficients for each saved spline basis.


beta_angle
Linear coefficient for the saved standardized angle.


gamma_angle
Two nonlinear angle coefficients.


speed_basis, boundary_basis, angle_basis
Optional fitted basis dictionaries for another fit, including normalization, knots, projection and transformation. Supplying a basis also requires its corresponding coefficients.



Unspecified bases are reused without refitting. BallDriveModel.pretrained().parameters shows the production coefficients with these names. Full exported artifacts remain accepted as model dictionaries.
For pitch control/pass probability, named keys are lambda_control, s and optional calibration (method, x, y for an isotonic map). PassRiskModel.pretrained().parameters shows the physical-control parameters. Changing lambda or s changes the raw control field. If no new calibration is supplied, the saved map is still applied, and params["calibration_matches_parameters"] records whether the physical-control parameters match its reference. calibration_matches_model additionally requires matching movement/flight settings. These flags describe correspondence with the saved map, not a new validation of its performance.

title: Reference: plot functions
text:
1 · Initialization and classes · 2 · Solvers · 3 · Getters and saved results · 4 · Plot functions.
Import functions from PRESS.visualization. Every plot returns (figure, axes), draws observed tracking and consumes previously computed outputs. Plotting draws stored results and leaves models and stored probabilities untouched.

title: Reference: plot functions
text:
Shared options
The pitch functions accept pitch_length=None, pitch_width=None, figsize=(12,8), title_fontsize=9, legend_fontsize=8, plus keyword-only title=None, ax=None, show=True, legend=True, velocity_scale=1.0. Choice convenience functions retain their original title-size defaults. An explicit axis supports multi-panel figures; its figure is returned. show=False supports scripts and batch saving. Plot dimensions use native tracking metadata unless overridden for display.
Velocity arrows are drawing aids of length velocity_scale × velocity, indicating the current direction of movement. They can be hidden with velocity_scale=0. Missing players are omitted; a frame without a carrier can still be drawn with plot_frame.

title: Reference: plot functions
text:
Frames and scalar risks







Function
Contents




plot_frame(press, frame_id, ..., title=None)
Players, observed ball and velocity arrows. Works on observed tracking alone.


plot_action_selection(press, frame_id, ...)
Same observed frame with stored native P(pass) in the title.


plot_risk(press, frame_id, *, field="hazard", ...)
Same frame with stored h, residual_risk or xloss in the title. Requires that output to have been computed.


plot_ball_drive_risk(press, frame_id, ...)
Defender colors show their cause-specific loss probability divided by total drive loss, on a fixed 0–100% scale. Absolute loss appears in the title; zero loss gives zero shares. Defender IDs preserve the correct association when players are missing.

title: 3 · Use on a match
text:
This is the third part of the User guide. Part 1 describes the source data and one-match preprocessing; part 2 defines the segmentation and context labels.
The complete example follows Ivan Vujica’s possession 8_774 in Melbourne City FC–Macarthur FC, 7 March 2025. Vujica receives in his own third, carries and completes a pass to Luke Brattan. It is the first case in the case studies.
Here the models distributed with PRESS evaluate the observed frames. The case studies use held-out predictions, so their numbers can differ from this deployment example.

title: 3 · Use on a match
text:
1. Original match inputs
The loader expects the original match JSON, tracking JSONL and dynamic-event CSV in the match directory. It prepares velocities, possessions, context and actions in memory. A single call replaces a separate preprocessing command and precomputed Parquet files.

text:
7. Calculate h and xLoss at the generic frame
compute_risk_frame(..., include_residual=True) runs all five fitted components: pass execution, carry execution, pass destination, pass–carry choice and conditional residual risk. It calculates only the preliminary effective-hazard BCOS required as a feature by those fitted models. The final transport descriptor is available separately through compute_bcos() and is evaluated only when requested. The fitted xT surfaces and physical parameters are loaded from the model artifacts distributed with PRESS.
The current score is read from the prepared tracking context and is relative to Vujica’s team. Elapsed time is recovered from the observed individual interval. h describes loss on the current action; xLoss adds continuation risk to predict the terminal individual-possession outcome.

outputs = press.compute_risk_frame(
    frame_id,
    include_residual=True,
)

    press, frame_id, field="hazard", show=False,

)

section: 8. See where the object stores results
text:
8. See where the object stores results
Results are indexed by component, then frame ID. Complete risk calculations retain compact outputs by default: destination-weighted pass success/failure, carry risk, action choice, BCOS area, h with its band, residual risk and xLoss. Each frame refers to shared settings through configuration_id. Physical/numerical settings and xT inputs are stored in press.result_configurations; fitted coefficients, spline bases and tree models remain in press.result_models.
Use get_result_configuration(frame_id) and get_result_model(component, frame_id) to inspect the settings and fitted model actually used, including custom parameters. To retain spatial fields, defender contributions and feature records for inspection or plotting, use keep_details=True in the complete risk call. Separately called component methods retain their detailed outputs.
For many possessions, keep the default keep_details=False. Compact results support risk annotations; spatial maps require detailed results. Tree feature names, order and categories belong to the fitted model; their values belong to the frame calculation. The same storage convention applies to standalone components.








Level
Ball-drive example
BCOS example




Model
Estimated lambda_0, s, linear/spline coefficients, knots and basis transformations.
Uses the ball-drive model’s default dispersion.


Configuration
Defender maximum speed, accelerations, integration step and forecast horizon.
Separate carrier/defender maximum speeds, dispersion input, accelerations, spatial radius, grid and numerical orders.


Result
Loss probability for this frame; optional defender contributions and survival curve.
Accessible area for this frame; optional accessibility surface and interception diagnostics.

A model={"s": 0.35} changes the model parameter while retaining omitted coefficients and bases. Both produce a new result for the selected frame. Pitch control uses its own motion settings; BCOS distinguishes carrier v_bc_max from defender v_def_max. Per-call overrides apply to the named component only. Model, configuration and result: full contract and defaults.

title: Pass probability
text:
The pass probability component estimates the probability that the attacking team completes a pass to a candidate destination. It supplies the pass-success component of PRESS; its complement is the pass-failure probability. Destination choice is modelled separately.
The formulation follows two related contributions by Spearman. Physics-Based Modeling of Pass Probabilities in Soccer develops a physics-based pass model in which player interception times, uncertainty in arrival and competing control determine completion probabilities, with parameters estimated from observed passes (Spearman et al. 2017). Beyond Expected Goals extends the use of probabilistic player control to potential pitch control and hypothetical ball delivery (Spearman 2018).
PRESS implements two uses of the same physical control mechanism. First, it evaluates the competition for control along reconstructed trajectories of observed passes and estimates the control rate \(\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}\) and arrival dispersion \(s\) by maximum likelihood. Second, it generates hypothetical ball flights to candidate destinations and evaluates a potential pitch control field (PPCF) by initiating competition for control at the destination only after the selected flight time. Player reachability, however, is measured from ball release throughout. Because the second calculation differs from the trajectory-based fitting task, a subsequent isotonic calibration maps raw PPCF scores to observed pass-completion frequencies. Calibration leaves the fitted physical parameters unchanged.
The distinction is methodological. An observed trajectory specifies a sequence of possible interception locations, whereas a hypothetical destination defines a single location and a selected delivery time. Consequently, the two calculations can produce different scores even with identical player states and identical physical parameters. The observed-trajectory model supplies the estimation likelihood; the endpoint model supplies the raw score used for deployed destination-level inference.
The model is physics-informed: ball flight and player motion use explicit approximations, while control intensity and arrival uncertainty are learned from observed outcomes. The passer is excluded from the eligible receiving and competing control populations.
