title: Pass probability
text:
2. Player motion and interception time

Travel and turning time
Let \(\mathbf p_j\) and \(\mathbf v_j\) be the observed position and velocity of player \(j\), and let \(\mathbf r\) be a candidate interception position. Define \(d_j(\mathbf r)=\|\mathbf r-\mathbf p_j\|\) and \(u_j=\|\mathbf v_j\|\). Following the arrival-time modelling approach of Spearman (Spearman et al. 2017; Spearman 2018), PRESS approximates motion as a turning delay followed by linear acceleration and, if needed, travel at constant effective speed.
For \(u_j\le v_{\max}\), with linear acceleration \(a\), define
\[
t_{a,j}=\max\left\{\frac{v_{\max}-u_j}{a},0\right\},
\qquad d_{a,j}=u_jt_{a,j}+\frac12at_{a,j}^2.
\]
The estimated movement time is
\[
t_{\mathrm{move},j}(\mathbf r)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\sqrt{u_j^2+2ad_j(\mathbf r)}-u_j}{a},
&d_j(\mathbf r)\le d_{a,j},\\[6pt]
t_{a,j}+\dfrac{d_j(\mathbf r)-d_{a,j}}{v_{\max}},
&d_j(\mathbf r)>d_{a,j}.
\end{cases}
\]
If the observed initial speed exceeds \(v_{\max}\), the implementation retains that speed without further acceleration and sets \(t_{\mathrm{move},j}=d_j/u_j\). Thus \(v_{\max}\) is an effective acceleration target.
Following Pleuler’s heading-dependent turning penalty (Pleuler 2020), let \(\theta_j(\mathbf r)\) be the angle between the player’s current velocity and the target direction. PRESS adds
\[
t_{\mathrm{turn},j}(\mathbf r)=\frac{u_j\theta_j(\mathbf r)}{a_{\mathrm{turn}}}.
\]
This follows from the geometric turning radius \(R=u_j^2/a_{\mathrm{turn}}\) and arc traversal time \(R\theta_j/u_j\). It is a delay approximation of the turning manoeuvre. The total arrival time is
\[
\boxed{\tau_j(\mathbf r)=t_{\mathrm{move},j}(\mathbf r)+t_{\mathrm{turn},j}(\mathbf r).}
\]
At rest, the turning term vanishes. When \(d_j(\mathbf r)\le0.1\) m, the implementation sets \(\tau_j(\mathbf r)=0\).

title: Pass probability
text:
3. Probabilistic player reachability
As in Spearman’s pitch-control model, uncertainty around the estimated arrival time is represented by a logistic distribution (Spearman et al. 2017). At time \(t\), the reachability of player \(j\) at position \(\mathbf r\) is
\[
\boxed{
F_j(t,\mathbf r)=
\left[1+\exp\left\{-\frac{\pi[t-\tau_j(\mathbf r)]}{\sqrt3\,s}\right\}\right]^{-1}.
}
\]
Here \(s>0\) is the standard deviation of logistic arrival-time uncertainty; its logistic scale parameter is \(\sqrt3s/\pi\). Reachability equals \(0.5\) at \(t=\tau_j(\mathbf r)\). It is a player-specific arrival gate, and each \(F_j\) ranges over \([0,1]\) independently of the other players.

Motion parameters
The model uses \(v_{\max}=5.5\) m/s and \(a=a_{\mathrm{turn}}=7\) m/s\(^2\). These are effective common movement capabilities, motivated by published player-motion models and checked against the tracking distribution.








Parameter
Literature rationale
Tracking consistency check




Player speed \(v_{\max}=5.5\) m/s
The speed scale is informed by Spearman’s player-motion framework (Spearman 2018).
Off-ball player-frame speeds \(>2\) m/s: Q95 = 5.745 m/s (or 5.656 m/s excluding annotated ball-carrier frames).


Linear acceleration \(a=7\) m/s\(^2\)
The acceleration scale used in Spearman’s movement model (Spearman 2018).
Off-ball acceleration magnitudes \(>3\) m/s\(^2\): Q99 = 7.013 m/s\(^2\).


Turning acceleration \(a_{\mathrm{turn}}=7\) m/s\(^2\)
PRESS sets the turning-delay scale equal to the linear-acceleration parameter.
This equality is a modelling convention that sets the turning parameter from the linear-acceleration value.



The speed filter excludes stationary and walking observations for this descriptive check. These conditional quantiles assess the consistency of rounded model scales with observed movement. Observed positions and velocities are the movement inputs of the model.

title: Pass probability
text:
4. Shared ball-flight dynamics
Following the gravity-and-aerodynamic-drag formulation in Spearman (Spearman et al. 2017), let \(\mathbf R(t)\in\mathbb R^3\) and \(\mathbf V(t)\in\mathbb R^3\) denote ball position and velocity. The airborne trajectory satisfies
\[
\dot{\mathbf R}(t)=\mathbf V(t),\qquad
\dot{\mathbf V}(t)=-g\mathbf e_z-
\frac{\rho C_D A}{2m}\|\mathbf V(t)\|\mathbf V(t).
\]

Ball-flight parameters
The ball-flight model uses fixed physical constants. The values follow the gravity-and-quadratic-drag approximation adopted from Spearman (Spearman et al. 2017).








Quantity
Value
Role in the flight model




Air density \(\rho\)
1.22 kg/m\(^3\)
Determines the aerodynamic drag force.


Drag coefficient \(C_D\)
0.25
Dimensionless coefficient controlling drag magnitude.


Ball cross-sectional area \(A\)
0.038 m\(^2\)
Sets the area exposed to airflow.


Ball mass \(m\)
0.42 kg
Converts aerodynamic force into acceleration.


Gravitational acceleration \(g\)
9.81 m/s\(^2\)
Governs vertical acceleration.



The approximation neglects spin and Magnus forces, so the horizontal path is a straight line. Once the descending ball reaches 0.05 m, its height is held fixed while horizontal aerodynamic drag continues; bounce and rolling friction are omitted.

title: Pass probability
text:
5. Pass probability model: observed trajectories
The first model assigns a completion probability to an observed pass. The ball is reconstructed as a moving three-dimensional trajectory, and every eligible player competes to intercept it at successive positions along its path.

Reconstructing the observed ball trajectory
For parameter estimation, PRESS reconstructs each observed pass from its measured release position and initial ball observations. Launch speed and direction are estimated from the early observed ball positions, with release position fixed. The annotated target is not imposed as an endpoint constraint. The benchmark documents the initial-condition estimators and their selection.
The fitted initial conditions are propagated through the flight model to obtain \(\mathbf R_k(t)\) for observed pass \(k\). This reconstruction is an offline estimation procedure: it can use observations after release and is not presented as an online forecast available at the release instant.
For each reconstructed pass, the ball follows a time-indexed sequence of horizontal positions and heights. At every time step, each player’s arrival gate is evaluated at the ball’s current horizontal location. Thus a defender can contribute control probability at an intermediate point, before the ball reaches its annotated destination. The observed binary outcome is used only after these time-dependent contributions have been combined into a team-level completion probability.


Control along the moving trajectory
Let \(\mathbf r_k(t)=\mathbf R_{k,xy}(t)\) and \(z_k(t)=R_{k,z}(t)\) denote the horizontal location and height of the reconstructed ball for pass \(k\). Define \(P_{jk}^{\mathrm{traj}}(t)\) as the probability that player \(j\) has obtained first control by time \(t\), and
\[
U_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(t)=1-\sum_j P_{jk}^{\mathrm{traj}}(t)
\]
as the probability that nobody has yet obtained control. A player contributes only when the ball is at controllable height (at most 2 m). The instantaneous control intensity is
\[
h_{jk}^{\mathrm{traj}}(t)=\lambda_{\mathrm{control}} F_j(t,\mathbf r_k(t))\,\mathbb 1\{z_k(t)\le 2\,\mathrm m\}.
\]
The coupled competition equations are
\[
\boxed{\frac{dP_{jk}^{\mathrm{traj}}(t)}{dt}=U_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(t)h_{jk}^{\mathrm{traj}}(t),\qquad P_{jk}^{\mathrm{traj}}(0)=0.}
\]
Equivalently, writing \(H_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(t)=\sum_j h_{jk}^{\mathrm{traj}}(t)\),
\[
U_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(t)=\exp\!\left[-\int_0^t H_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(u)\,du\right],
\qquad
P_{jk}^{\mathrm{traj}}(T_{\max})=\int_0^{T_{\max}} U_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(t)h_{jk}^{\mathrm{traj}}(t)\,dt.
\]
The horizon \(T_{\max}\) is a time large enough for the ball to be controlled by someone; formally, \(T_{\max}\to\infty\).
The model’s observed-pass completion probability is the total first-control probability of eligible attacking teammates \(\mathcal A_k\) (excluding the passer):
\[
\boxed{p_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(\lambda_{\mathrm{control}},s)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal A_k}P_{jk}^{\mathrm{traj}}(T_{\max}).}
\]
Because the target position changes with \(t\), the model accounts for interception opportunities before the ball reaches its intended destination. The resulting \(p_k^{\mathrm{traj}}\) is the quantity subsequently used in the Bernoulli likelihood.

title: Pass probability
text:
6. Pitch control model: hypothetical destinations
The second model evaluates the probability that the attacking team would obtain first control at a chosen destination \(\mathbf r\). It constructs a hypothetical ball delivery and uses its arrival time to determine when competition at that fixed target may begin.

Selecting a hypothetical ball flight
For inference, PRESS chooses a feasible hypothetical flight to destination \(\mathbf r\). It evaluates a grid of 900 launch combinations: 30 speeds between 5 and 25 m/s and 30 elevation angles between 0 and 45 degrees. Among flights reaching the destination at controllable height, it selects the ball-arrival time closest to the estimated arrival time of the eligible teammate nearest in initial position to \(\mathbf r\).
This receiver-friendly timing convention follows the potential-pitch-control construction of Beyond Expected Goals, §3.1.2 (Spearman 2018). It models a hypothetical delivery, independently of the launch actually chosen by the passer.
In this use, the selected trajectory determines when the ball becomes available at the candidate destination. The competing-control calculation then uses that fixed point and begins accumulating control only after the selected arrival time. The selected flight provides the time \(T_{\mathrm{flight}}(\mathbf r)\) at which the ball becomes available for control at the target. Players may have reached that target earlier, but control competition at the endpoint begins only at this time.


Control at the fixed destination
Let \(T_{\mathrm{flight}}(\mathbf r)\) be the selected arrival time. Although a player can reach \(\mathbf r\) before the ball, first control at that location occurs only after ball arrival. Therefore, explicitly for \(t<T_{\mathrm{flight}}(\mathbf r)\),
\[
P_j^{\mathrm{PPCF}}(t;\mathbf r)=0,\qquad U^{\mathrm{PPCF}}(t;\mathbf r)=1,\qquad t<T_{\mathrm{flight}}(\mathbf r).
\]
At \(t=T_{\mathrm{flight}}(\mathbf r)\), control starts from \(P_j^{\mathrm{PPCF}}=0\) and \(U^{\mathrm{PPCF}}=1\). From ball arrival onward, the target stays fixed and the competing-control equations are
\[
\boxed{\frac{dP_j^{\mathrm{PPCF}}(t;\mathbf r)}{dt}=U^{\mathrm{PPCF}}(t;\mathbf r)\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}F_j(t,\mathbf r),\qquad t\ge T_{\mathrm{flight}}(\mathbf r),}
\]
with \(P_j^{\mathrm{PPCF}}(T_{\mathrm{flight}};\mathbf r)=0\) and \(U^{\mathrm{PPCF}}(T_{\mathrm{flight}};\mathbf r)=1\). Crucially, the time \(t\) in \(F_j(t,\mathbf r)\) is measured from pass release. Players who could have reached the destination earlier already have high reachability when the competition begins.
Setting \(H^{\mathrm{PPCF}}(t;\mathbf r)=\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}\sum_j F_j(t,\mathbf r)\) gives
\[
U^{\mathrm{PPCF}}(t;\mathbf r)=\exp\!\left[-\int_{T_{\mathrm{flight}}(\mathbf r)}^t H^{\mathrm{PPCF}}(u;\mathbf r)\,du\right].
\]
The raw attacking-team pitch control score is
\[
\boxed{C_{\mathrm{att}}(\mathbf r;\lambda_{\mathrm{control}},s)=\sum_{j\in\mathcal A}\int_{T_{\mathrm{flight}}(\mathbf r)}^{T_{\max}}U^{\mathrm{PPCF}}(t;\mathbf r)\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}F_j(t,\mathbf r)\,dt.}
\]
The difference from the observed-trajectory model is structural: control is evaluated only at the destination after the hypothetical ball arrives, so early interception opportunities along the flight are not explicitly integrated. Both models use the same player-reachability function and physical parameters.

title: Pass probability
section: 7. Parameter estimation from the pass probability model
text:
7. Parameter estimation from the pass probability model

Likelihood of observed pass outcomes
For observed pass \(k\), let \(Y_k=1\) indicate successful completion by the attacking team and \(Y_k=0\) indicate failure. Given the reconstructed ball path, the observed player state and physical parameters
\[
\psi=(\lambda_{\mathrm{control}},s),
\]
the competing-control model produces a trajectory-based team completion probability \(p_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(\psi)\) by summing the attacking players’ control probabilities along that reconstructed path.
Following the trajectory-likelihood approach of Spearman (Spearman et al. 2017), PRESS estimates the two parameters using the natural binary pass outcomes:
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal L(\psi;D)=
\prod_{k=1}^N
[p_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(\psi)]^{Y_k}
[1-p_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(\psi)]^{1-Y_k}.
}
\]
Equivalently, the log likelihood is
\[
\log\mathcal L(\psi;D)=
\sum_{k=1}^N
\left\{
Y_k\log p_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(\psi)
+(1-Y_k)\log[1-p_k^{\mathrm{traj}}(\psi)]
\right\}.
\]
A completed pass contributes the attacking team’s probability of obtaining control; an incomplete pass contributes its complement. The likelihood is evaluated on the reconstructed trajectories and uses only the pass outcome, regardless of the receiver’s identity or the time of first control.
The two fitted parameters influence the likelihood differently. Increasing \(\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}\) accelerates the transfer of remaining uncontrolled probability to players who are already reachable. Changing \(s\) changes how sharply each player’s reachability rises around the expected arrival time; it can therefore affect which team is likely to control the moving ball and when. The observed success/failure labels constrain these effects through their joint predictions across many different spatial and temporal configurations.


Maximum-likelihood estimation
PRESS estimates \(\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}\) and \(s\) jointly by minimizing the negative log likelihood. Positivity is enforced through logarithmic coordinates,
\[
(\eta_\lambda,\eta_s)=(\log\lambda_{\mathrm{control}},\log s),
\qquad
\hat\psi=\arg\max_{\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}>0,\,s>0}
\log\mathcal L(\psi;D).
\]
These are maximum-likelihood point estimates, fitted without parameter priors. Optimization procedures, initial-condition estimator selection, data splits and held-out results are documented in the pass-probability benchmark.

title: Pass probability
section: 8. Calibration of the pitch control model
text:
8. Calibration of the pitch control model
The parameters fitted on observed trajectories are transferred unchanged to the endpoint PPCF calculation. However, the likelihood uses competition along a moving observed ball path, whereas the PPCF evaluates competition at a fixed hypothetical destination after its selected flight time. Thus, a raw PPCF score \(C_{\mathrm{att}}(\mathbf r;\hat\psi)\) need not equal the empirical probability of completing a pass to that destination.
PRESS estimates a nondecreasing isotonic mapping \(c:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) from raw PPCF predictions and observed pass outcomes:
\[
\boxed{
p_{\mathrm{pass}}(\mathbf r)=c\!\left(C_{\mathrm{att}}(\mathbf r;\hat\psi)\right),
\qquad
p_{\mathrm{fail}}(\mathbf r)=1-p_{\mathrm{pass}}(\mathbf r).
}
\]
The mapping adjusts the empirical relationship between raw PPCF scores and completion frequencies. Its estimation, cross-fitting procedure and held-out assessment are documented in the pass-probability benchmark.

title: Pass probability
text:
9. Fitted parameters and deployed model
The deployed physical estimates are
\[
\boxed{
\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{control}}=5.437830\ \mathrm{s}^{-1},
\qquad
\hat s=0.294560\ \mathrm{s}.
}
\]
These are full-data refit estimates. Spearman (Spearman et al. 2017) reports a reference control rate of 4.30 s\(^{-1}\) and arrival dispersion of 0.45 s; Beyond Expected Goals reports a different fitted dispersion under its later specification (Spearman 2018). Such values depend on the movement, flight and control assumptions and the estimation dataset.

Arrival dispersion compared with ball drive
The full-data pass estimate \(s=0.294560\) s is close to the ball-drive estimate \(s=0.299632\) s. Both describe arrival-time uncertainty on a scale of approximately 0.3 s, but arise from different movement settings, likelihoods and estimation procedures (MLE for passes and MAP for ball drives). This is a descriptive comparison of the two scales. Parameter stability and uncertainty assessments belong to the respective benchmarks.

title: Pass probability
text:
10. Application to real tracking data
The package supports both physical calculations: the probability of attacking-team control along a reconstructed observed pass, and the calibrated PPCF for a hypothetical pass destination. The second calculation can be evaluated across a pitch grid to visualize the pass-success field from a given player state.
The two outputs are interpreted separately and need not agree for the same annotated endpoint, since their ball-control opportunities differ.

Brisbane Roar FC–Perth Glory, frame 54295
N. Acosta completes a pass to J. Hingert; the dashed line marks its observed destination. Set SKILLCORNER_OPENDATA to your local open-data repository.

from pathlib import Path
import os
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PRESS import PRESS

opendata = Path(os.environ.get("SKILLCORNER_OPENDATA", Path.cwd().parent / "opendata"))
match_dir = opendata / "data/matches/1925299"
press = PRESS.from_skillcorner(match_dir)
frame_id = 54295

from PRESS.visualization import plot_pass_map

press.compute_ppcf(frame_id)
plot_pass_map(press, frame_id, field="pass_success", pass_target=(-12.15, -28.05))
plt.savefig("figures/vignette_02_pass_real_field.png", dpi=170)
plt.savefig("figures/vignette_02_pass_real_field.svg")
plt.close()




Calibrated pass-success field and the observed pass, drawn by the package.

title: Pass probability
text:
11. Scope and limitations
The model assumes a fixed initial player state, common effective movement parameters, sequential turning and acceleration, logistic arrival uncertainty, and a shared control rate. Reconstructed ball trajectories omit spin and use a simplified ground-contact rule. The hypothetical-pass calculation optimizes a receiver-friendly arrival time and evaluates control at the target, without explicitly integrating all possible early interceptions along the flight. Its isotonic calibration corrects empirical score-to-outcome correspondence but cannot recover missing physical mechanisms or establish causal interpretation.

title: Pass probability
text:
12. References and next steps
Spearman’s pass-probability model (Spearman et al. 2017) motivates the observed-trajectory likelihood, uncertain player arrival, flight physics and competing control. Beyond Expected Goals (Spearman 2018) motivates hypothetical flight selection and potential pitch control. Pleuler (Pleuler 2020) motivates the turning-delay approximation. Fernández, Bornn and Cervone (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2019; Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021) provide the wider action-value context in which pass completion is a distinct component.
The equations describe the PRESS implementation of these two formulations. The separate pass-probability benchmark documents data selection, nested evaluation, calibration performance and numerical sensitivity. The complementary ball-drive vignette describes the possession-loss model for continued carrying.

title: Action selection
text:
At each moment of individual ball control, a player either releases a pass or keeps carrying the ball. Action selection estimates the probability of these two observed decisions from the current tracking state and match context. Stalpaert et al. (Stalpaert 2022) study the same binary pass–carry choice, while Fernández et al. (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021) treat a related problem with three actions (shooting, passing, carrying) inside a possession-value framework. PRESS models the pass–carry decision of outfield players.
Let \(s\) denote the current game state and \(A\) the chosen action. The target is
\[
q(s)=P(A=\mathrm{pass}\mid s),\qquad
P(A=\mathrm{carry}\mid s)=1-q(s).
\]
We model action selection as a binary classification problem and estimate \(q(s)\) with an XGBoost classifier (Chen and Guestrin 2016). The classifier takes a vector of features that summarizes the game state and returns the probability of passing. The features are described first, followed by the likelihood used to train the model.
The model describes observed behaviour across the sampled decisions. To characterize the pass–carry choice, PRESS represents both alternatives using features computed from tracking data and separately fitted execution and destination-choice models. The carry option is described by its immediate execution risk, the space available to the carrier and the tactical configuration along the direction of movement. The pass option is described by its probability of completion and the tactical consequences of its possible destinations, accounting for both successful and unsuccessful outcomes.

title: Action selection
text:
2. Model features
The model uses 30 features, 28 numerical and two categorical, organized into four groups. Several spatial descriptors are shared with Pass selection, where they characterize the current carrier position and individual candidate destinations. Here, these descriptors also characterize the projected carry position and are aggregated over possible passing outcomes. The four groups describe the two action alternatives and the context in which the decision is made.








Group
Question
Count




Carrier state and ball retention
How well can the player keep carrying?
6


Spatial and tactical configuration
Where does the carry lead, and how are the teams organized there?
8


Passing opportunities
What would a pass look like, and how would it end?
11


Possession and match context
How did control start, and what is the match situation?
5




Carrier state and ball retention (6 features)
These features describe the player and the room available to keep moving with the ball.

x, y position. Where the carrier is on the pitch, in the team’s attacking orientation: deep in the team’s own half or near the opponent’s goal, central or wide.
Speed. How fast the carrier is moving: running with the ball, or almost standing.
Velocity angle. The direction of movement relative to the attacking axis: forward, sideways or backward. It is missing when the player is effectively stationary. Velocity comes from the centred seven-frame tracking smoother, whose three-frame future support makes the current implementation suitable for offline analysis.
Carry-success probability \(1-d(s)\). The chance that the player still has the ball one second from now if carrying continues. A high value means carrying is safe in the current situation. It comes from the separate ball-drive risk model and measures execution risk; pass selection uses the carry-loss probability \(d(s)\) itself, an alternative encoding of the same information.
BCOS area. The probability-weighted area accessible to the carrier before interception by an opponent, in \(\mathrm{m}^2\). A large value means room to run, a small one means the carrier is boxed in. Ball carrier open space (BCOS) is a concept introduced for association football by Bandara et al. (Bandara et al. 2025). In PRESS, the BCOS model gives, for each point around the carrier, the probability that the carrier arrives there before an opponent can intercept; integrating this field over a 40 m surrounding domain gives the probability-weighted area.

The carry-loss probability is defined as
\[
d(s)=P(\mathrm{loss\ within\ 1\,s}\mid A=\mathrm{carry},s),
\]
The feature \(1-d(s)\) measures the probability of retaining control over the next second, while BCOS area measures the space accessible to the carrier. Both characterize the carry option from the same current state.


Spatial and tactical configuration (8 features)
These features describe where the carry would take the player and how the two teams are arranged around that place.
Six of them are evaluated at a projected position: where the carrier would be one second from now if the carrier kept the current velocity,
\[
\widehat x_{\mathrm{bc}}(1)=x_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)+v_{\mathrm{bc}}(0)\,(1\,\mathrm{s}).
\]
This is a hypothetical evaluation point. The spatial descriptors are evaluated at the projected position using the current player positions, following the conventions introduced in Pass selection.

Own-team xT. The expected threat of the projected position for the carrier’s team, that is, how much a possession at that spot tends to lead towards a goal. A high value means the carry heads into a dangerous attacking zone. xT was introduced by Singh (Singh 2018); its construction in PRESS is described in the xT vignette.
Opponent xT. The same quantity from the opponent’s point of view. It indicates how dangerous that spot would be for the carrier’s team if possession were lost there.
Nearest own-team line index and nearest opposition line index. These are the pressure lines of Fernández, Bornn and Cervone (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021). In PRESS, the current outfield longitudinal positions are clustered into three lines with complete linkage, excluding the original carrier from the own-team roster and the extreme-x goalkeeper proxy. The index says which line is closest to the projected position, for the carrier’s own team and for the opposition. As in pass selection, the three lines of each team are numbered from the attacking line (1) to the defensive line (3), with the intermediate line assigned index 2. Own-team lines are thus ordered along the opponent’s attacking direction, and opposition lines along the carrier team’s attacking direction.
Signed distance to the nearest own-team line and to the nearest opposition line. How far that line is from the projected position along the carrier team’s attacking direction, for both teams. A positive value means the line is ahead of the point and a negative value means it is behind. A small positive distance to the opposition line means the carrier is about to meet it.

The other two features use the carrier’s current position.

Teammates ahead and opponents ahead. How many players of each team are further up the pitch than the carrier, along the attacking direction. They show how many teammates are in front (potential forward options) and how many opponents are still to be beaten. For a set of players \(G\) and a point \(r\),
\[
N_G(r)=\sum_{k\in G}\mathbf 1\{\delta\,x_k>\delta\,r_x\},\qquad \delta\in\{-1,+1\},
\]
where \(\delta\) is the carrier team’s attacking direction for both rosters. The carrier is excluded and tracked goalkeepers are kept. The count is taken over the whole pitch width.



Passing opportunities (11 features)
These features characterize the passing alternative by combining the spatial descriptors introduced in Pass selection with the probabilities of choosing and completing a pass to each destination. The aim is to summarize both the feasibility of passing and its possible tactical consequences: where the carrier’s team would retain possession after a successful pass, and where the opponent would recover possession after a failed pass. Two separately fitted PRESS components provide the destination-choice and completion probabilities for every candidate destination \(j\) on the native one-metre pitch grid:
\[
\pi_j(s)=P(J=j\mid A=\mathrm{pass},s),\qquad
p_j(s)=P(\mathrm{completion}\mid J=j,A=\mathrm{pass},s).
\]
The first, \(\pi_j\), says how likely a passer in this situation is to target cell \(j\) and comes from the pass-destination model. The second, \(p_j\), says how likely a pass to that cell is to arrive and comes from the pass-probability model. The action model uses the flat destination model with its fitted validation temperature and isotonic-calibrated completion probabilities. Both are evaluated from the current game state.
Multiplying them splits every possible pass into two branches, a completed pass and a failed pass:
\[
w_j^+=\pi_jp_j,\qquad w_j^-=\pi_j(1-p_j).
\]
The weight \(w_j^+\) is the chance that the pass goes to cell \(j\) and succeeds, and \(w_j^-\) is the chance that it goes there and fails.

Expected pass success. The overall chance that a pass would succeed, averaged over the likely destinations. A high value means passing is easy right now.
\[
P(\mathrm{completion}\mid A=\mathrm{pass},s)=\sum_j\pi_jp_j=\sum_jw_j^+.
\]

The other ten features aggregate the destination-specific spatial descriptors from Pass selection: expected threat, nearest team-line indices and players ahead. For a spatial property \(\Phi(j)\), the two outcome-weighted sums are:
\[
\Phi^+(s)=\sum_jw_j^+\Phi(j),\qquad
\Phi^-(s)=\sum_jw_j^-\Phi(j).
\]
Branch + describes a completed pass, after which the carrier’s team retains possession at the destination. Branch − describes a failed pass, after which the opponent is assumed to recover possession near the destination assigned by the destination-choice model. The two branches describe the tactical consequences of the passing option.
The sums \(\Phi^+\) and \(\Phi^-\) are weighted by the joint probabilities of destination and outcome, conditional on attempting a pass, so each sum carries the probability of the corresponding outcome together with the spatial properties of its destinations. An unlikely branch therefore contributes little even when its destinations have large descriptor values.
The change in possession determines how the spatial descriptors are interpreted. Expected threat measures the offensive value of possession in a team’s attacking orientation, so each team has its own xT surface. We therefore use the carrier team’s expected threat \(X_{own}\) in the success branch and the opponent’s expected threat \(X_{opp}\) in the failure branch, evaluated in the opponent’s attacking direction.
For line indices and player counts, the spatial representation introduced in Pass selection is retained in both branches. The labels own and opp always refer to the original carrier’s team and its opponent, respectively. Each team’s lines retain their own numbering, from the attacking line (1) to the defensive line (3), and the ahead counts use the original carrier team’s attacking direction for both rosters. A player ahead in the carrier team’s direction is behind in the recovering team’s direction, so when possession changes the same descriptors are read from the recovering team’s point of view, as summarized below.
The table below summarizes the tactical interpretation of the spatial descriptors introduced in Pass selection in the two outcome branches.

Table. Tactical interpretation of destination-specific spatial descriptors under successful and unsuccessful passing outcomes. The labels own and opp refer to the original ball carrier’s team and its opponent, respectively. Ahead and behind are interpreted relative to the attacking direction of the team holding possession in each branch.

Expected threat (2 features). Expected threat is taken for the team that would hold the ball in each branch. \(\sum_jw_j^+X_{own}(j)\) measures the success-weighted offensive value of retaining possession at the possible destinations. \(\sum_jw_j^-X_{opp}(j)\) measures the failure-weighted offensive value of the opponent recovering possession there. Together, they describe the offensive opportunity of passing and the potential danger of losing the ball.
Pressure-line structure (4 features). The nearest own-team and opponent line indices, as defined in the previous group but evaluated at each destination from the current player positions, are aggregated once with \(w_j^+\) and once with \(w_j^-\). The line numbering of the previous group applies.
\[
\sum_jw_j^+L_{own}(j),\quad \sum_jw_j^-L_{own}(j),\quad
\sum_jw_j^+L_{opp}(j),\quad \sum_jw_j^-L_{opp}(j).
\]
For example, consider a pass directed towards the opponent’s third pressure line. If the pass succeeds, the receiver obtains the ball close to the opposition’s defensive line (line 3). If the pass fails, the opponent recovers the ball close to its own defensive line (the same line 3). Thus, weighting \(L_{opp}(j)\) by \(w_j^+\) summarizes the opposition line indices near possible successful receptions, while weighting it by \(w_j^-\) summarizes the recovering team’s own line indices near possible recoveries. The same interpretation applies to \(L_{own}(j)\). In the feature names, team_line_pass_success is the own-team index with \(w_j^+\) and opp_line_pass_failure the opposition index with \(w_j^-\).
Player positioning (4 features). The numbers of teammates and opponents ahead of the possible destinations, using the ahead-count convention defined in Pass selection. A backward destination can have more players ahead of it than a forward one. The ahead-count function \(N_G\) is evaluated at every candidate destination for teammates and opponents, with the carrier team’s attacking direction for both rosters, and aggregated the same way:
\[
\sum_jw_j^+N_{own}(j),\quad \sum_jw_j^-N_{own}(j),\quad
\sum_jw_j^+N_{opp}(j),\quad \sum_jw_j^-N_{opp}(j).
\]
In the success branch, \(N_{own}\) describes teammates ahead of the reception point (forward options), and \(N_{opp}\) describes opponents still to be beaten. In the failure branch, the same counts describe the configuration from the recovering team’s perspective: \(N_{opp}\) counts its own players behind the recovery point, and \(N_{own}\) counts opposing players behind that point, relative to the recovering team’s attacking direction.

Together, the eleven features give the classifier the likelihood, location and consequences of passing.


Possession and match context (5 features)
These features describe how the current individual control began and the match situation. The first four features follow the conventions of Pass selection; the number of completed carries is an additional feature specific to action selection.

Start type (categorical). The event that gave the player the ball: a reception, interception, recovery or restart.
Previous action (categorical). What the player did immediately before. It keeps the start context until the player completes a full one-second carry, and from then on it records ball_drive.
Match minute. Time elapsed in the match.
Score difference. Carrier-team goals minus opponent goals at that frame.
Completed carries. The number of complete one-second carry intervals already performed during the current individual possession, in other words how long the player has already been on the ball. It is a history summary available at decision time. A pass released after 0.4 s has zero completed carries and keeps its start context; a pass released after 2.4 s has two completed carries and ball_drive as previous action.

The two categorical variables keep their original labels, including unknown, and the encoded vocabulary is fitted on training data. The possession and checkpoint vignette describes the underlying segmentation.

title: Action selection
text:
3. Likelihood and learning
The model is trained on observed decisions. Each decision \(i\) has two ingredients: the feature vector \(z_i\) described above, which summarizes the game state at that moment, and its outcome \(y_i\), equal to 1 if the player passed and 0 if the player carried.
XGBoost learns the probability of passing from these pairs. It builds an additive ensemble of regression trees \(f_\psi\), in which each new tree corrects the errors left by the previous ones. The ensemble returns a score for every decision, and a logistic function turns that score into the probability of passing:
\[
q_i=P(y_i=1\mid z_i)=\frac{1}{1+\exp[-f_\psi(z_i)]}.
\]
Training chooses the parameters \(\psi\) that minimize the regularized Bernoulli negative log-likelihood, which penalizes confident predictions that disagree with the observed action:
\[
\mathcal L(\psi)=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[y_i\log q_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-q_i)\right]+\Omega(\psi),
\]
where \(\Omega(\psi)\) penalizes tree complexity and leaf weights to limit overfitting. The action-selection benchmark reports the hyperparameter search, match-wise validation and predictive performance.

title: Action selection
text:
4. Feature importance and interpretation
The contribution of each feature to the fitted model is measured with XGBoost split gain. The figure reports the total gain attributed to each conceptual feature, with one-hot encoded levels grouped under their original categorical input. These values describe how the trained ensemble uses its inputs.



Feature importance for the fitted action-selection model.


The carry-success probability \(1-d(s)\) (drive_success_1s) is the most influential feature: it accounts for 22.09% of total gain in the production model and ranks first in all five evaluation folds. Carrier speed follows at 8.00%, so the player’s immediate capacity to advance with the ball is central to the pass–carry decision. The passing-option summaries also contribute substantially: the own-team line index weighted by successful passing outcomes (team_line_pass_success) accounts for 6.85%, and the opposition line index weighted by failed outcomes (opp_line_pass_failure) for 5.32%. BCOS contributes 4.10% and the previous-action context 4.04%.
Together, these results are consistent with a classifier that combines the feasibility of continuing the carry with the spatial consequences of the available passing opportunities. Correlated features can share gain among themselves, and split gain depends on the opportunities a feature offers for tree partitioning. The full fold-wise analysis is documented in the feature-importance analysis.

title: Composed hazard and difficulty bands
text: PRESS describes the decisions and actions of the ball carrier through separately fitted components: the probability of passing or carrying, the risk of losing the ball in a one-second carry, the destination of a pass and its probability of completion. This page composes them into a single quantity, \(h\), that answers one question: given the current state, how likely is the team to lose the ball during the carrier’s next action? Because \(h\) is a probability, it has an absolute scale, which PRESS divides into four bands. The bands are used in the pressure case studies and player report.

title: Composed hazard and difficulty bands
section: 1. Possession as a discrete sequence of actions
text:
1. Possession as a discrete sequence of actions
PRESS segments a possession into a canonical set of on-ball actions, the segmentation described in Possessions and checkpoints. A player in possession either carries the ball for one second or passes it to a destination \(j\), so the set of actions is
\[\mathcal A_0=\{\mathrm{carry}_{1s},\ \mathrm{pass}(j)\},\]
where a pass runs until its completion. Shots are outside the action set.
Along a possession these actions form a sequence in which the team keeps the ball until, at some action, it loses it. A completed pass moves the ball to a teammate, and the sequence continues across successive carriers. Let \(T\) be the number of canonical actions until team possession is lost, and \(s_n\) the game state at the \(n\)-th decision. The probability that the loss occurs at the next action, given that possession has been retained so far, is the discrete hazard
\[h(s_n)=P(T=n+1\mid T>n,\ s_n).\]
This is the quantity that answers the question: how fragile is the possession here? A carrier with free space and safe passing options has a small \(h\), while a carrier whose carry is contested and whose passes are likely to fail has a large one. Defensive pressure acts on both branches at once, since it raises the risk of the carry and of the passes and it changes which action the player is likely to choose, and \(h\) summarizes these effects in a single probability. It is a probability per decision, indexed by actions, and its scale depends on the one-second horizon of the carry.
PRESS builds \(h\) from its components and marginalizes over the average decision-making policy learned from observed play, independently of the action the player actually chose, so \(h\) describes the difficulty of the situation. Local geometry and kinematics enter execution, and passing options and context enter choice. A high value indicates difficult modeled alternatives for an average player in the observed context.
\(h\) is evaluated at the conventional checkpoints of the segmentation, one for each canonical action, and these define the process and all the results of this page. Since the components depend on the current state, \(h\) can also be computed at intermediate tracking frames, which provides descriptive observations of how difficulty evolves within a possession without adding actions.

title: Composed hazard and difficulty bands
text:
2. Mathematical definition
Condition all quantities on the current state \(s\). Four separately fitted PRESS components enter:

\(q(s)=P(A=\mathrm{pass}\mid s)\) is the probability of passing from the action-selection model, and \(1-q(s)\) the probability of carrying;
\(d(s)=P(\mathrm{loss\ within\ 1s}\mid A=\mathrm{carry},s)\) is the loss probability of the one-second carry, from the ball-drive risk model;
\(\pi_j(s)=P(J=j\mid A=\mathrm{pass},s)\) is the probability of destination \(j\), from the pass-destination model;
\(p_j(s)=P(\mathrm{completion}\mid J=j,A=\mathrm{pass},s)\) is the completion probability of a pass to \(j\), from the pass-probability model.

Averaging pass failure over the destinations gives
\[f(s)=\sum_j \pi_j(s)\,\big(1-p_j(s)\big)=1-\sum_j \pi_j(s)\,p_j(s),\]
and the law of total probability over the two action branches gives
\[\boxed{h(s)=q(s)\,f(s)+\big(1-q(s)\big)\,d(s).}\]
The weighted pass contribution is \(qf\) and the weighted carry contribution is \((1-q)d\), and they add exactly to \(h\). A state can therefore have a high pass risk \(f\) and a low \(h\) when passing is unlikely, and vice versa. The sum \(\sum_j \pi_jp_j\) is the expected pass success of the action-selection features.
The composition is a project derivation, and the terminology follows the conditional failure probability of discrete-time survival analysis (Singer and Willett 2003; Suresh, Severn, and Ghosh 2022).

title: Composed hazard and difficulty bands
text:
3. Difficulty bands
The survival interpretation gives \(h\) an intuitive scale. If the current hazard stayed constant over the following actions, the probability of retaining possession for \(n\) more actions would be \((1-h)^n\). The half-life is the number of actions after which this probability falls to 50%,
\[n_{1/2}=\frac{\log(1/2)}{\log(1-h)},\]
so the higher the hazard, the shorter the half-life. It is a reference scale expressed in decisions; since difficulty changes throughout play, it summarizes the current situation as a constant-risk reference.
Along the canonical sequence, the corresponding model-implied survival profile is \(\widehat S_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}[1-h(s_k)]\). Intermediate tracking snapshots add no actions or survival factors, while \(h\) remains computable from any usable current state.
Following SkillCorner’s approach of classifying defensive pressure into bands (SkillCorner 2026), PRESS defines the difficulty bands from the hazard, through this half-life scale. The cutoffs are the values of \(h\) whose half-life is exactly 8, 4 and 2 actions, a geometric sequence in which each half-life is half of the previous one,
\[b_n=1-2^{-1/n},\qquad n=8,4,2.\]
Since \(b_n\approx \ln 2/n\) for small \(b_n\), halving the half-life approximately doubles the hazard, so the cutoffs are approximately equally spaced on a logarithmic scale of risk. This is a project design choice, with thresholds fixed by the half-life construction. The API keeps the labels below.



Band
\(h\) interval
Constant-risk half-life




None
\(0\le h<0.082996\)
More than 8 decisions; infinite at \(h=0\)


Low
\(0.082996\le h<0.159104\)
\(4<n_{1/2}\le8\) decisions


Medium
\(0.159104\le h<0.292893\)
\(2<n_{1/2}\le4\) decisions


High
\(0.292893\le h\le1\)
At most 2 decisions



The code uses the exact cutoffs, and a value on a cutoff enters the higher band. The same construction at \(n=1\) gives a cutoff at \(h=0.5\), which would define a fifth band. Only 36 of the 14,919 held-out states (0.24%) have \(h\ge 0.5\), too few to evaluate a separate band reliably, so High is kept as the highest band. The bands are defined on \(h\), whose per-action risk over a fixed window suits the constant-hazard half-life construction. xLoss is the probability of reaching an absorbing state, the terminal loss of the individual possession, and accumulates over a variable horizon, so these thresholds are specific to \(h\).

title: Composed hazard and difficulty bands
text:
6. Extension to xLoss
\(h\) concerns the next action. A complementary question concerns the eventual outcome of the current ball carrier’s individual possession, which can extend beyond the next action (SkillCorner 2025, 52). PRESS computes this object modularly, by composing the hazard with a residual-risk component. The distinction arises from the carry: a successful one-second carry preserves the individual possession but does not determine its outcome, since the player may keep carrying, pass or lose the ball later, while a successful pass ends the individual possession without a loss of team possession.
The residual-risk model accounts for this longer horizon with the residual risk
\[r(s)=P(\text{eventual individual possession loss}\mid s,\ \text{successful carry}).\]
Along the carry branch, the probability of an eventual loss combines the loss during the carry with the residual risk after its success, \(d(s)+(1-d(s))\,r(s)\). Marginalizing over the same average decision-making policy as \(h\) gives the expected loss
\[\boxed{\mathrm{xLoss}(s)=\big(1-q(s)\big)\big[d(s)+\big(1-d(s)\big)r(s)\big]+q(s)\,f(s),}\]
or equivalently
\[\mathrm{xLoss}(s)=h(s)+\big(1-q(s)\big)\big(1-d(s)\big)\,r(s).\]
The additional term is the probability of a successful carry followed by an eventual loss of the individual possession. xLoss incorporates this longer horizon through \(r(s)\), which absorbs the subsequent decisions into a single probability.
The two quantities are complementary. \(h\) characterizes the immediate difficulty of the situation and supports the difficulty bands, and xLoss estimates the probability that the current individual possession ends in a loss. Both are evaluated under the average decision-making policy, independently of the action actually performed.
Related work predicts possession outcomes over a time horizon: the loss of possession within four seconds (Gu et al. 2024), the rate of the next action and of possession loss (Dick and Brefeld 2023), and the goal probability of a possession over time (Le Coz, Boustila, and Imbach 2026).
The same Auckland FC–Newcastle Jets FC possession ends with L. Gillion losing the ball and K. Grozos starting the next individual possession.

area = press.get_bcos_result(frame_id)["BCOS area"]

from PRESS.model import ActionSelectionModel, ResidualRiskModel

    action_model=action_model, time_since_start=time_since_start,
    x_bc=state["x_bc"], v_bc=state["v_bc"],
    r_atts=state["r_atts"], r_defs=state["r_defs"],

title: 2 · Possession segmentation and context
text: This is the second part of the User guide, between datasets, installation and preprocessing and use on a match.

title: 2 · Possession segmentation and context
text:
1. Three distinct units

Individual possession: one player’s control interval, identified by (match_id, possession_id). Its observed start and end must be matched to tracking for the interval table used here.
Team possession: a chain of individual intervals connected by verified completed passes. A completed pass changes the carrier without ending this team interval. Unverified continuity starts a new reconstructed team interval.
Canonical action: a one-second carry attempt or an instantaneous pass release. Its start state is a checkpoint at which the hazard h, the probability that the team loses possession during the next action, is evaluated.

A checkpoint is the start state of a canonical action. An additional snapshot is any other evaluated state; it lies outside the action sequence.
Frame evaluation is more general than action segmentation. A usable frame can be evaluated even if it is not a checkpoint. Segmentation supplies the conventional discrete action sequence underlying h; extra evaluations leave that sequence unchanged (Fernandez, Bornn, and Cervone 2021).

title: 2 · Possession segmentation and context
text:
2. Canonical checkpoints

General rule
The checkpoints of an individual possession are the starts of its complete one-second carries, plus one terminal checkpoint that depends on how control ends: the release after a pass, the start of the final failed carry after a direct loss, and none after a foul suffered or a clearance.
Carries are anchored to the start of the individual possession, in successive one-second blocks. Each full successful carry supplies one checkpoint at its start. If control ends in a direct possession loss, the final failed attempt is retained even when it lasts less than one second. If loss occurs exactly at a full-second boundary, the last full block is the failed attempt.
A pass supplies a checkpoint at release, regardless of how much time has elapsed since the last full carry. A successful subsecond tail before a pass is an additional snapshot, left out of the final one-second carry benchmark and action-choice training.
Fouls suffered and clearances preserve preceding complete carries and end without a terminal pass/carry action; their terminal frames and short tails can be retained as additional snapshots. Shots are outside the fitted pass–carry task. The composed-risk benchmark separately defines the terminally covered cohort used for bands and reports.
get_actions() returns canonical actions; their frame_start values are the checkpoints. valid_only=True selects usable start states. include_snapshots=True also returns the annotated extras, marked by is_canonical=False. compute_risk_player_possession(..., include_snapshots=False) evaluates the canonical sequence only; frame_ids supports an explicitly chosen sampling. Extra overlapping forecasts stay out of a canonical survival curve.


Possessions shorter than one second
The way control ends decides which actions a short possession retains:

Pass before 1 s: only the release is a canonical checkpoint. The earlier control interval is shorter than a full carry, so it supplies no successful canonical carry. The start can be inspected as an additional snapshot.
Direct loss before 1 s: retain one failed carry attempt, with its checkpoint at the individual-possession start. It is a failure within the fixed one-second forecast horizon, even though the observed loss happens earlier. The loss endpoint closes the possession without starting another action.
Foul suffered or clearance before 1 s: no complete carry and no terminal pass/carry action are available, so there is no canonical checkpoint. Annotated snapshots remain available for inspection.

The canonical profile of a short pass or a short failed carry therefore contains one point: the release for a pass, the start of the possession for a failed carry. Any further evaluation frame is an additional snapshot.


A partial tail after full carries
For a possession lasting 2.4 s and ending in a pass, the successful canonical carries remain 0–1 s and 1–2 s. The last 2–2.4 s is a short control tail, shorter than a complete carry. Canonical checkpoints are 0, 1 and 2.4 s; 2 s is an optional snapshot.
If the same 2.4 s duration ends in a direct carry loss, retain the failed 2–2.4 s attempt. Canonical checkpoints are then 0, 1 and 2 s. The terminal action is evaluated at 2 s, before execution fails, and 2.4 s is the loss endpoint.
For a foul suffered or clearance at 2.4 s, only the carry starts at 0 and 1 s are canonical. The tail start at 2 s and terminal frame at 2.4 s are additional snapshots. The possession ends without a terminal canonical action. These timings are constructed to illustrate the segmentation rule.


Initial and final states
The initial state of an individual possession is its first canonical checkpoint. The final state is its last canonical checkpoint when control ends with a pass or a direct loss: the release in the first case and the start of the final failed carry in the second. A foul suffered or a clearance supplies no terminal action, so the possession has no final state in this sense. A possession shorter than one second has a single checkpoint, which is both its initial and its final state.

title: 2 · Possession segmentation and context
text:
3. Start type and previous action
The pass-selection, action-selection and residual-risk models use two possession-level context variables, start_type and previous_action. The table of context variables by task lists what each task reads. This section fixes the convention for both.
Start type describes how the player obtained control. It is taken without modification from the Dynamic Events of SkillCorner, which define the categories and their annotation (SkillCorner, n.d.). The labels are listed below.
Previous action follows the convention of (Stalpaert 2022): when an action is preceded by a complete carry, the previous action is the carry, named ball_drive in the code. Otherwise the previous action is the start type. With the one-second carries of this segmentation, the rule is applied to the observed prefix of the individual possession:

Before a complete second of control, previous_action equals start_type.
From 1.0 s of control onwards, after at least one complete carry, previous_action is ball_drive; the checkpoint at 1 s already carries it.
The same rule applies to a pass release or an arbitrary intermediate frame.

Thus a quick pass after reception keeps the reception context, such as pass_reception, while a pass after several seconds of carrying has previous_action="ball_drive". For example, a pass released at 2.4 s follows two complete carries and has previous_action="ball_drive", whereas a pass released before 1 s keeps the start type. The field depends only on the observed prefix of the individual possession.

title: 2 · Possession segmentation and context
text:
4. Context labels and their origin
The learned models use the granular start_type labels of the SkillCorner Dynamic Events without regrouping them. previous_action takes the same labels until a complete carry is observed, and then becomes ball_drive. In feature records these columns are named start_type_raw and previous_action_raw. SkillCorner defines the labels (SkillCorner, n.d.); the table gives a short general reading of each, and the football concepts (reception, interception, recovery and restart context) are common to providers.







Label
General meaning




pass_reception
Receiving an open-play pass.


pass_interception
Obtaining control by intercepting an opposing open-play pass.


recovery
Obtaining control of a loose or available ball.


keep_possession
Retaining or re-establishing control, as distinguished from a new reception or interception by the source annotation.


throw_in_reception, corner_reception, free_kick_reception, goal_kick_reception
Receiving the ball from the named restart.


throw_in_interception, corner_interception, free_kick_interception, goal_kick_interception
Gaining control from the opponent’s named restart.


unknown
The source explicitly leaves the start context unspecified.


ball_drive
Carrying after at least one complete canonical carry; generated by PRESS for previous_action only.



A possession may begin with a restart reception and continue in active play. Keeping that start context is a separate decision from admitting a dead-ball delivery into the open-play pass-execution cohort. Pass-link and outcome filters belong to the individual task benchmarks.
The fitted encoders also contain __missing__ and __unseen__ buckets for an absent value or a category outside the fitted vocabulary. They are encoding markers. Legacy _std columns group the raw labels into open-play/set-piece reception, open-play/set-piece interception and continuation; the deployed choice and residual-risk models use the granular vocabulary instead.
For another provider, map equivalent event meanings to these labels before using the pretrained models. Preserve genuinely unavailable context as missing. Action-choice context excludes future outcomes, intended recipients and remaining possession time.

title: 2 · Possession segmentation and context
text:
5. Context in the learned tasks
Only the tree-based tasks use context variables. The physical models, ball-drive risk and pass probability, use the tracking state alone.







Task
Context variables




Pass selection
Start type, previous action, match minute and score difference


Action selection
Start type, previous action, match minute, score difference and completed_canonical_drives


Residual risk
Start type, previous action, match minute, score difference and elapsed individual-control time



Match minute and score difference (carrier-team goals minus opponent goals) are read at the evaluated frame and do not depend on the segmentation. Start type and previous action are one-hot encoded, with buckets for missing and unseen values. The possession-level variables use only the observed prefix of the individual possession, before its eventual duration or outcome. Action selection uses the number of completed canonical carries. Carry checkpoints fall on whole seconds, whereas passes are released at arbitrary times, so the elapsed time would reveal which action follows. This follows from the segmentation choices and would be leakage. Residual risk predicts the terminal outcome of the possession, so it uses the elapsed time.

title: 2 · Possession segmentation and context
text:
6. An observed sequence
Ivan Vujica’s possession 8_774 in Melbourne City FC–Macarthur FC lasts 2.9 s and ends with a completed pass to Luke Brattan. The table below is read from the processed match, including the noncanonical short-tail snapshot. It illustrates both the segmentation and the change in previous_action.

from PRESS import PRESS

individual_id = "8_774"

    possession_id=individual_id,

actions["elapsed_seconds"] = (
    actions.frame_start - individual.frame_start.item()

title: Extra: Ball Carrier Open Space (BCOS)
text:
Ball Carrier Open Space (BCOS) is the space a player in possession can navigate without interference from an opponent. It was introduced by Bandara et al. (Bandara et al. 2025), who define it as the unoccupied area surrounding the ball carrier, study its spatial and temporal variation and relate it to match results, for which it is a predictor.
PRESS formalizes BCOS from tracking data in a transport-with-killing framework. Interference is interpreted as interception, more precisely as the first interception by an opponent before the carrier can arrive at a destination. The model is a timed race between the carrier and the defenders, who must intercept the carrier before the carrier reaches a point, and it assigns each point around the carrier the probability of being reached before interception. Each destination defines a hypothetical straight-line route along which the carrier moves while exposed to opposing players, so that arrival at the destination and interception are competing terminal events. This probability is the accessibility of the point, and the resulting accessibility surface describes the spatial organization and extent of the carrier’s movement opportunities.
To quantify the probability of arrival before interception, the model builds on the probabilistic representation of player movement introduced by Spearman (Spearman et al. 2017; Spearman 2018). In the ball-drive risk model, the carrier follows a deterministic trajectory while the movement of defenders is uncertain. BCOS represents the movement of both the carrier and the defenders through probabilistic arrival-time distributions.
In PRESS, the BCOS feature is a predictor of the possession outcome in residual risk and of the choice between passing and carrying in action selection. This vignette also uses BCOS as a descriptive statistic of the match.
The formulation developed below is the transport-with-killing model, including interception during waiting at the origin. The existing pretrained action-selection and residual-risk classifiers and their reported benchmarks use a preliminary effective-hazard formulation, which remains available in the package. Retraining and held-out evaluation with the transport-with-killing formulation are planned, and will also compare the predictive performance of the two formulations.
